title: UAE says FlyDubai co-pilot attacked captain with cockpit’s crash axe
text:
CAIRO (AP) — The co-pilot accused of attacking the captain of an Israel-bound flight with an ax and trying to seize the controls was an Omani national who had been barred from flying on his country’s airline because of concerns about extremist views, officials said Saturday.
The co-pilot has been identified as Hamam al-Hammami, according to three people with knowledge of the situation, including a Gulf and a Western diplomat, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to the media.
The United Arab Emirates, which is leading the investigation, said the co-pilot attacked with the cockpit’s crash ax and tried to take control of the plummeting plane in a “terrorist attack” Wednesday. His actions nearly crashed the flight with 182 people on board before passengers and others rushed in and subdued him.
The new details raised questions about how thoroughly FlyDubai vets potential employees, and how the co-pilot’s presence on a flight filled with Israeli passengers got past Israel’s strict security protocols.
Israel has said it has agreements with foreign carriers to keep pilots of nations without diplomatic ties from flying there. Israel and Oman don’t have formal diplomatic relations. The UAE government has earned a reputation for effective measures against extremist activities but has bristled in the past over criticism of security lapses.
The incident occurred at a sensitive time for Israel, a week before the anniversary of the Hamas-led attack on Oct. 7, 2023, that sparked the war in Gaza. It also came weeks before a highly contentious election in which security, and Oct. 7 security failures, have been central issues.
FlyDubai hired the co-pilot after Oman Air barred him
Separately, a regional official and a person familiar with the matter said the co-pilot had been barred from flying by Oman over concerns that he had adopted extremist views. The official said he was moved to an administrative job at Oman Air. Both spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss the ongoing investigation. They gave no details about the alleged extremist views.
The co-pilot was later hired by UAE-based airline FlyDubai, the person said. It wasn’t immediately clear to what extent the co-pilot was vetted. The Gulf diplomat said he had undergone standard security checks before being hired, but it appears that the checks focused on whether he had been convicted of criminal charges and didn’t go deeper into examining his background for potential signs of radicalization.
The regional official also said security agencies from four regional countries were working to establish the co-pilot’s motives, aided by the United States and other Western governments. The Gulf diplomat said the investigation, which hasn’t concluded, hasn’t found any connections with militant groups, suggesting that the co-pilot acted on his own.
The regional official said the co-pilot was born in the UAE and his mother is Syrian. He obtained Omani nationality from his father, also an Omani national. The regional official also said the co-pilot had traveled to Syria, with no details.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Friday said the co-pilot had undergone “Islamist radicalization,” but provided no evidence. There was no immediate comment Saturday from Israel’s government.
A social media account was deleted the day of the flight
A FlyDubai spokesperson said in an email that the airline could not comment beyond its official statements and acknowledged “there are many questions at this stage.” There was no immediate comment from Oman Air, and Oman’s government has said nothing publicly in response to repeated questions since the incident.
In a statement to The Associated Press, Royal Air Maroc, Morocco’s national carrier, said the co-pilot “completed a three-month theoretical training period with the airline in 2025, as part of the pre-employment process. At the end of this training period, his application was not selected for employment.” There were no details.
Keith Coles, a spokesperson for Buckinghamshire New University in England, told the AP that al-Hammami previously completed a distance-learning course in aviation management there but “did not undertake any pilot training.” There were no details on the timing.
Little else was immediately known about the co-pilot’s background. His Instagram account was active until the day of the flight and then deleted.
Philip Baum, a visiting professor of aviation security at Coventry University in England who wrote a book about aircraft hijackings and bombings, said background check systems differ from country to country and there are limits on what types of information can be shared.
“In terms of aviation security itself, obviously we want to have as robust background checks as possible. But there are huge limitations on doing background checks in any case, especially in cross-border checks,” he said.
Captain and passengers have described drama on board
Airlines are generally required to carry crash axes in the cockpit that could be used in an emergency to break open a window to escape or break open a panel to access a fire.
The captain, who was badly wounded, has said he used his remaining energy while being attacked to unlock the cockpit door, allowing people who had noticed alarming sounds to come in, tackle the co-pilot and stabilize the flight while passengers screamed.
In a phone call with Israel’s Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Saturday, the flight’s captain, Smit Machchhar, said that before the attack, the co-pilot wanted to pray, and that he turned away out of respect. He said he felt a blow to the back of his head a few minutes later, and then the blows kept coming.
Netanyahu told Machchhar that he was amazed at his courage and his ability to stay cool under impossible conditions. “You saved so many souls. ... You saved the spirit of the world,” he said.
The plane made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia after a descent so extreme that part of the rudder was torn away, and aviation experts have marveled that it didn’t crash. FlyDubai has said crew traveling on the plane helped to stabilize it and land. They haven’t been publicly identified.
The captain and co-pilot were later taken to the UAE. The passengers, most of them Israeli, flew home later Wednesday on a separate plane, to cheers.
___
Mednick reported from Tel Aviv, Israel, and Anna from Jerusalem. AP Washington bureau chief Anna Johnson in Washington, Transportation Writer Josh Funk in Omaha, Nebraska, and reporter Sam Metz in Jerusalem contributed.

title: Let’s get political flyers out of Maine, while we’re at it
text:
Thank you for the Sept. 27 op-ed “Free Maine’s yards from political yard signs,” by David Stein. I agree wholeheartedly. While we are at it, let’s ban political flyers from the USPS. I have taken at least three a day out of my mailbox for over a month and immediately threw them in the recycle bin without looking at them.
The post office is having a difficult time just getting mail I want delivered to my box — they don’t need the extra work.
If people want to know where the candidates stand, they should read a newspaper.
Beth Anne King
Durham

title: Trump posts Sen. Tom Cotton’s cellphone number amid clash over Daylight Saving Time
text:
President Trump urges calls to Arkansas Sen. Tom Cotton in push for permanent daylight saving time
President Donald Trump on Saturday pressured Sen. Tom Cotton of Arkansas to support a bill to make daylight saving time permanent, urging Americans to call what appeared to be the personal cellphone number of Cotton, the chairman of the Senate Intelligence Committee.
The Sunshine Protection Act passed the House in July, but it faces roadblocks in the Senate where some Republicans are strongly opposed. Proponents, including the White House, argue that the change would provide more daylight during the times that Americans are most active. Detractors said permanent daylight saving time would lead to darker and potentially more hazardous winter mornings when children will be waiting for school buses and parents will be driving to work in darkness.
It was a remarkable escalation on Trump's part of a longstanding fixation shared by both men — with Trump supporting making daylight saving time permanent, and Cotton vociferously opposed — at a time just weeks before the midterms, when Republicans would prefer that the president focus on talking about affordability issues and the party's achievements. Cotton is also up for reelection this November, although that race is not expected to be competitive.
Trump calls daylight saving time ‘depressing’
Daylight saving time is that period between spring and fall when clocks in most parts of the United States are set one hour ahead of standard time. Not all states observe it — and under the bill, states can opt out of the change if their respective legislatures act to do so before the bill’s enactment.
“For some reason, Tom is stopping the Bill and, in the Senate, it’s very easy to do, it only takes one!” Trump wrote on social media, noting that passing the bill would give professional golfers more time on the greens. “So, everyone in Arkansas, a State I love, and won 3 times, the last by by 34 points, tell Tom to, GET IT DONE! It will be appreciated by all,” Trump said.
Trump included a phone number with an Arkansas area code. The Associated Press called the number, but no one answered and the voicemail box was full.
Cotton, a member of Republican leadership, reiterated his opposition to permanent daylight saving time in a social media post of his own Saturday afternoon. He is not the only GOP senator who opposes the policy, though he has been among the most vocal opponents.
“No one likes changing the clock, me included, but Congress has enacted permanent Daylight Savings Time multiple times before and repealed it each time once Americans experienced absurdly late sunrises in the winter,” Cotton wrote. “Arkansans don’t want their kids going to school in the pitch dark, and I’ll always put Arkansas first.”
Trump, who is spending the day at his northern Virginia golf club before traveling to Ohio later Saturday, promptly fired back.
“If Tom Cotton were putting Arkansas first, he would give them an extra hour of daylight and, more importantly, they wouldn’t have to run all over their houses, farms, work places, and everywhere else, twice a year, having to change their Clocks, and often forgetting to do so,” Trump said, adding that “that is really putting Arkansas FIRST.”
As his motorcade was rolling back to the White House, Trump added that “a table full of very distinguished people just told me that they HATE, immediately after a mandatory time change, going home at night – and it’s DARK.”
“It’s depressing!" Trump continued. "One of the gentleman stated that, ‘I just hate going home in darkness.’ It’s also, in Crime Ridden Blue States, a lot more dangerous to be walking home in the dark!”
A 2025 poll from The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research shows that if forced to choose, most Americans would prefer to keep that extra hour of daylight in the evening. Only 12% of U.S. adults favor the current system of daylight saving time, which requires people in most states to change their clocks twice a year, while 47% oppose it and 40% are neutral.
Members of Congress have long been interested in the potential benefits and costs of daylight saving time since it was first adopted as a wartime measure in 1942. The Senate passed a bill four years ago to make daylight saving time permanent, but it stalled in the House.
This is not the first time Trump has released personal information about a senator
While competing for the 2016 Republican presidential nomination, the late Sen. Lindsey Graham of South Carolina described Trump as “unfit for office” after Trump denigrated the military service of Sen. John McCain of Arizona. Trump then released Graham’s personal cellphone number. That prompted a viral video in which the senator dramatically destroyed a series of flip phones.
Graham later became a close ally of Trump. In contrast, although they share many of the same policy positions, Trump and Cotton are not known to be close.
Cotton, one of the Republican Party's most prominent national security voices, has advocated for a more hawkish approach on Iran, particularly as Trump entertains pauses in military strikes amid the seven-month war. In Trump's first term, Cotton was a critic of the president's attempts at overhauling the nation's sentencing laws, calling the proposal a “jailbreak."
Earlier this year, Cotton had temporarily defied Trump's attempts at stalling the confirmation process for his own nominee for director of national intelligence, Jay Clayton. The president had wanted to ensure his interim pick for the intelligence job, Bill Pulte, would be able to serve in that role at least briefly when the former director, Tulsi Gabbard, left the job.
But the appointment of Pulte, who had no known national security credentials, drew bipartisan condemnation from Capitol Hill and Cotton had tried to expedite Clayton's confirmation process, which could have prevented Pulte from being installed as acting director.
But Trump ultimately ordered Clayton to not appear before Cotton's committee for his confirmation hearing, and Pulte served in the job for several weeks this summer. Clayton was eventually confirmed by the Senate in late July.
___
Associated Press writer Mary Clare Jalonick in Washington contributed to this report.

title: Letter: Amy Roeder works hard for Bangor
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
I have the privilege of knowing Amy Roeder not only as a great friend and neighbor, but also as my state representative for House District 23. I have seen firsthand the kind of legislator she is: thoughtful, hardworking, accessible, and focused on getting things done for the people she serves.
Now, as Amy runs for the Maine state Senate, her record matters. At a time when affordability is on everyone’s mind, Amy has worked on the issues that hit closest to home. As a leader on the Legislature’s Labor and Housing Committee, she helped advance LD 2003 to remove unnecessary zoning barriers and create more housing opportunities across Maine. She supported state investments in public education and municipalities that help ease pressure on local property taxpayers, and she supported LD 874 to protect essential workers from the financial hardship of missed paychecks during a government shutdown.
What I appreciate most about Amy is that she understands these aren’t simply bills and numbers. They’re about whether our neighbors can afford a home, pay their property taxes, heat their house, fill a prescription, or make a paycheck stretch far enough.
Amy shows up, she listens, and she works hard for Bangor. I know her personally, and I know how seriously she takes public service. I am proud to have had her represent me in the Maine House, and I’m proud to support her as she runs for the Maine Senate. Please join me on Nov. 3!
Marwa Hassanien
Bangor

title: Sacred Heart football rallies to beat UMaine
text:
ORONO, Maine — Coastal Athletic Association newcomer Sacred Heart overcame a nine-point deficit to beat the reeling University of Maine’s Black Bears 24-16 at Morse Field in Alfond Stadium on Saturday afternoon.
Sacred Heart is now 2-3 overall and 2-2 in the CAA while UMaine has now lost five in a row and is 1-5 and 1-2.
Sacred Heart junior quarterback Poochie Snyder completed 21 of 27 passes for 207 yards and two touchdowns and he also rushed for 73 yards on 15 carries.
Dean Hangey caught seven passes for 58 yards and Jason Palmieri caught six for 73 more.
Linebacker Myles Hamilton had two sacks and was one of three Pioneers with a team-high seven tackles along with linebacker Luke Hackett and strong safety Kymari Latney.
UMaine head coach Jordan Stevens alternated quarterbacks with Caden Drezek finally winning the job later in the game. Drezek completed 12 of 28 passes for 141 yards and Eddie Buehler was 1-for-5 for 13 yards.
Rashawn Marshall carried the ball 13 times for 67 yards and Nick Laughlin had four catches for 22 yards. Corey Rideout had three receptions for 47 yards.
Strong safety Jeremiah McGill and linebacker Sam Oppenheimer each had a game-high 10 tackles and linebacker Noah Carpenter and cornerback Jamaree Gibson had nine each. Carpenter had 1 ½ sacks.
Sacred Heart had a 382-259 edge in total yards and a 25-13 advantage in first downs.
“Our guys certainly played with more fight but our execution was poor on both sides of the ball at the end of the half and that bled into the third quarter. They really controlled the ball in the third quarter,” said Stevens, whose Black Bears ran only five plays in the third quarter compared with Sacred Heart’s 22.
“They were able to dominate that quarter. That being said, we had a chance to tie the game in the fourth quarter but we came up short,” Stevens said.
UMaine built a 9-0 lead on three Sam Tremblay field goals but the Black Bears’ inept offense couldn’t find the end zone and Sacred Heart made them pay by stringing together two second-quarter scoring drives that enabled the visitors to take a 14-9 lead into the intermission.
The offense had little to do with the field goals.
Sacred Heart’s Jack O’Sullivan shanked a 22-yard punt in the first quarter to give UMaine the ball at the Sacred Heart 30-yard line but three plays produced only 6 yards so UMaine had to settle for a 42-yard field goal by Tremblay.
The UMaine defense stopped Sacred Heart on a fourth-and-one on its 47-yard line with Bryce Purnell leading the charge and UMaine’s offense received two runs totalling 20 yards by Marshall before the drive stalled and Tremblay booted a 45-yard field goal.
Freshman Ty Boone’s 34-yard punt return to the Sacred Heart 34-yard line and a Buehler pass to Elijah Smalls moved it to the 21-yard line. Smalls tried to hurdle a tackler but got hurt on the play and didn’t return.
The next three plays generated just 1 yard, so Tremblay kicked a 37-yard field goal.
The UMaine defense had been stout up until that point and had done an excellent job containing Sacred Heart dual-threat quarterback Snyder.
But that all changed.
Snyder engineered drives of 79 and 81 yards to give the Pioneers a lead they would never relinquish.
The first drive was an eight-play affair and included a 33-yard pass from Snyder to Palmieri and their ability to pick up a first down on first-and-20 thanks to two Snyder completions and an illegal use of hands penalty on Maine’s Kye Pressley.
Dean Hangey’s 3-yard touchdown run on a sweep capped the drive.
The next drive took 12 plays and a 16-yard pass from Snyder to Hangey on third-and-nine from the Sacred Heart-30 extended it.
Snyder tossed an 8-yard TD pass to Palmieri to finish off the drive with 19 seconds left.
Sacred Heart opened the second half with another impressive and methodical drive that culminated in a 6-yard TD pass from Snyder to Brendan Errity. That completed a 12-play, 75-yard drive.
The UMaine offense finally came to life and Drezek orchestrated a six-play, 69-yard march completed by Nick Laughlin’s 2-yard run.
He completed a 24-yard pass to Major Leak and a 30-yard pass to Keyon Concepcion.
Sacred Heart expanded its lead to 24-16 on a 40-yard field goal by Ryan Bocklet with 6:48 left.
UMaine had a chance to tie it late in the game but a costly drop by Sebastian Rammery on what would have been a 30-yard gain inside the Sacred Heart-20 yard line was soon followed by a completion that came up just a yard short of a first down on fourth-and-15.
UMaine had one last chance in the last 1:30 but the Black Bears couldn’t convert.
“Offensively, too many dropped passes. We talk about the quarterback position so much but it’s hard for me to make an objective decision on the quarterback when we’re dropping balls all the time,” said the UMaine head coach. “It’s not Eddie or Caden that are the roots of inefficiencies in the pass game. It’s not fair to those guys if we aren’t going to catch the ball.”
The Black Bears had at least eight drops in the contest.
“We have to do a better job. We have to coach better. It starts with myself. I’ve got to be better for our players and our coaches. Some of the things we’ve done these past few games are unacceptable,” Stevens said.
UMaine will have next weekend off before hosting Bryant on Oct. 17 at 1 p.m. Sacred Heart will host Stonehill next Saturday at noon.

title: FBI has commissioned a classified, internal 'Patel Report' about times when it 'fell short'
text:
FBI has commissioned a classified and internal 'Patel Report' about times when it 'fell short'
The FBI is issuing a classified report to its workforce examining what it says are chapters from the bureau's history “where this institution fell short,” according to an internal message obtained Friday by The Associated Press.
It was unclear what episodes from the FBI's past are chronicled in the new “Patel Report.” But the document's existence is in keeping with Director Kash Patel's vocal criticism of the leaders who preceded him and with his determination to rid the FBI of agents he contends have politicized the bureau in the past. Patel's critics say he is the one who has weaponized the FBI and that his scrutiny of his predecessors and their decision-making is part of an effort to rewrite history in favor of President Donald Trump.
Patel pledged at his confirmation hearing last year that he would not look “backward," but as director, he has encouraged investigations of former senior officials and presided over sweeping terminations, including of employees who participated in years-old investigations of Trump, were photographed taking a knee during a 2020 racial justice protest and contributed to a disputed analytical memo about Catholic extremism.
“The Patel Report looks backward because accountability demands it,” says a message to the workforce signed by the FBI's co-deputy directors, Christopher Raia and Andrew Bailey. The message describes the report as marking the “closing of one chapter in our history and the beginning of another complete with a brighter future ahead.”
Bailey announced his resignation earlier this week, and his last day is Friday. The FBI declined to comment on the report.
The message also says, “We cannot change what happened before we arrived. But we can confront it honestly. We can recognize failures instead of protecting them. We can hold people accountable. We can fix what was broken. And we can build safeguards strong enough to ensure the mistakes of the past are never allowed to define this institution again. These steps are consistent with any institution of excellence that is constantly striving for improvement."
It was unclear if the report made recommendations or demanded any action to address what the FBI now regards as past shortcomings.
The FBI message says the report is meant to "promote fierce organizational accountability” and rebuild “public trust.” But Patel’s critics say the politically charged investigations into perceived adversaries of Trump that the FBI has embarked on under his watch, as well as the punishment of agents who participated in investigations into the Republican president to which they were assigned, have eroded faith in the nation’s premier federal law enforcement agency.

Maine paddleboarder’s 5-mile trip to photograph seals ends with rare lighthouse view
text:
This story was originally published Oct. 11, 2025.
Karl Ramsdell regularly paddles the ocean to photograph wildlife. A professional, he especially enjoys capturing seals, which he affectionately calls “chubmarines.”
Recently, Ramsdell paddled about five miles on his paddleboard from Harpswell to Halfway Rock Lighthouse in Casco Bay. He had previously visited the island from East End Beach in Portland, covering roughly 22 miles round-trip.
He warns that such trips are only for experienced paddlers. “It’s no joke,” he said. “It’s extremely dangerous.”
Ramsdell, who grew up surfing, has been paddleboarding for about 10 years and photographing seals from his board for seven. He relies on his ocean knowledge from surfing, carrying all his gear in a dry bag on his back.
Halfway Rock Lighthouse, built in 1871, was automated in 1975 and fell into disrepair before being restored by its current owner, Ford Reiche, earning top honors from the American Lighthouse Foundation in 2017.
While photographing seals loafing on the 2-acre barren ledge surrounding the lighthouse, Ramsdell was invited in by Reiche. From 76 feet up, he captured a rare panoramic view of the surrounding waters. He’s even spending the weekend in the lighthouse.
Access to the island is notoriously difficult. “I got beat up getting on the island,” Ramsdell said. Reiche has a specially equipped boat to make landings easier.
Ramsdell first discovered the seals in 2022 during a boat visit, and it had long been his dream to paddle there.

title: There is no ‘bipartisan’ way to organize the Senate
text:
Daniel M. Shea is the Marson-Moller-McNulty Professor of Government at Colby College.
Sen. Susan Collins wants to talk about her bipartisanship, an understandable strategy.
Maine leans blue, and few states value political moderation as much. Even as ticket splitting has nearly disappeared across America, many Mainers pride themselves on judging candidates rather than parties. Collins has built an entire Senate career on that instinct.
The go-to retort from Democrats is that Collins’ votes against her party are rare and, more importantly, strategic. She gets a pass from Republican leadership only after a measure’s success has been assured, or she votes for the procedural motions that decide a bill’s fate and against final passage once the outcome is settled.
So, what’s the skinny on Collins’ bipartisan record? As they say, it’s complicated.
The Lugar Center’s Bipartisan Index has ranked her at or near the top of the chamber year after year, and she has broken with Republican presidents on a few highly visible issues. At the same time, CQ Roll Call found that Collins supported President Trump’s position roughly 95% of the time in 2025.
Those facts are not contradictory. They reflect how much the Senate has changed. In today’s Congress, a senator who defects a handful of times per session can be deemed “the most bipartisan.” But has the definition of “bipartisan” also shifted? It has.
When Collins’ career began, moderate Republicans were part of the Senate’s fabric. Maine alone sent Bill Cohen and Olympia Snowe to Washington. Across the country, Republicans like John Chafee, Nancy Kassebaum, Mark Hatfield and Warren Rudman worked with Democrats to write legislation, broker compromises and assemble governing coalitions. No one called them bipartisan because they voted against their party here and there. They were bipartisan because they helped govern across party lines. They forged compromise solutions. That is a different model from the one Collins represents today.
Yes, the Senate has become much more polarized. The ideological overlap between the parties has nearly vanished, and genuine coalition-building is harder than it was in 1996, when Collins was first elected. In the new environment, moderation has come to mean something smaller. Instead of asking whether a senator can build bipartisan agreements, we ask whether she occasionally casts a dissenting vote. Those are not the same thing.
The old moderation changed legislation before it reached the floor. Today’s version of moderation usually amounts to dissent after decisions have been made. Collins sometimes casts votes against her party. Where the outcomes stay the same, the dissent makes little difference.
Maine watched this play out last summer. The Medicaid cuts in the 2025 budget law were drafted in committees chaired by the majority and moved on the majority leader’s schedule. Collins voted “no,” warning of what the cuts would mean for Maine’s rural hospitals. The bill became law anyway. Her dissent was real, but it changed nothing, because the decisions that mattered had already been made.
Which brings us to the most consequential vote Susan Collins has cast every two years, and will cast again if she returns to Washington. It comes before any debate over taxes, immigration, spending or judges — before the Senate takes up any legislation at all. It is the vote to organize the chamber: the vote that elects the Senate leader.
That single decision shapes every important vote that follows. Every senator casts the “organizing vote,” and no one crosses party lines. If reelected, Collins will vote for Republican leadership, a move that cannot be spun as moderate, bipartisan or centrist.
Collins would answer, fairly enough, that the organizing vote is exactly what makes her chair of the Appropriations Committee, and that the gavel delivers for Maine.
But the same organizing vote gives Ted Cruz the committee that oversees Maine’s fisheries, and it puts public lands and conservation policy under Mike Lee, who spent last summer trying to sell off millions of acres of the kind of land Collins helped protect with the Great American Outdoors Act. It hands the Special Committee on Aging — the committee Collins herself chaired for six years — to Rick Scott, whose 2022 plan would have sunset all federal laws, Social Security and Medicare included, every five years.
Some of the most strident Republican partisans in the Senate now run the committees Maine depends on. The chairmanship is the payment for the organizing vote, and the price includes every other chairman it installs — not just Collins. There is nothing bipartisan about it.
There is also no getting away from the fact that if the organizing vote puts Republicans in charge, it empowers Donald Trump’s agenda.
None of this makes Collins’ bipartisan claims unimportant. It makes them incomplete. Voters should weigh the times she has stood apart from her party — and ask what difference those votes made in the end. And they should weigh her pending vote to install a Republican majority. She’d be chair of Appropriations, but Trump and his hardcore partisans would be in charge of the rest.
For 30 years, Collins has asked Mainers to vote for the candidate, not the party. The first vote she casts in Washington does the opposite, and Maine voters should be clear-eyed about that.

Cat food investigation finds toxic contaminants across nearly all brands
text:
(CNN) - A new investigation into cat food found toxic chemicals in nearly all types and brands.
One hundred of the top-selling cat foods, including wet, dry and air- or freeze-dried foods, were tested for more than 120 contaminants.
Toxic plastic contaminants, the herbicide glyphosate and heavy metals such as lead, mercury and arsenic were found in all types of the foods tested.
Metal levels across brands
Of cat food samples across 62 brands, lead was found in 99% of samples. Cadmium, which harms the kidneys and bones, was found in 96% of samples. Arsenic was found in 94% of samples.
Differences by protein type
The report, by the nonprofit Clean Label Project, found fish and seafood proteins, especially wet versions, generally contained the most mercury and cadmium.
Chicken versions saw higher rates of lead and herbicides.
Nearly 85% of poultry-based foods met Clean Label Project’s purity standard, compared with 25% of fish and seafood products.
Recommendations from the report
According to the report, cat owners should try to vary their pet’s diet.
Wet or air-dried products are preferable to dry food for lower lead exposure.
Avoiding foods with plants in the top ten ingredients could help lower pesticide exposure.

title: Zach Bryan wears pro-Palestine shirt onstage at Gillette Stadium
text:
Zach Bryan wears pro-Palestine shirt onstage at Gillette Stadium
Country singer Zach Bryan and his bandmates wore pro-Palestine shirts onstage at a Gillette Stadium concert Friday night.
Video below: Robert Kraft responds to Macklemore's donation challenge
Bryan, who had two concerts scheduled at the Foxborough venue over the weekend, wore a black shirt with the phrases "Free Palestine. An appeal to heaven" on it.
"An appeal to heaven" is a phrase and symbol that dates back to the Revolutionary War. It was the maritime flag of Massachusetts until 1971.
Other members of Bryan's band wore Palestinian soccer jerseys.
In September, Robert Kraft, the CEO of the Kraft Group, which owns Gillette Stadium, barred rapper Macklemore from opening for singer Ed Sheeran in Foxborough.
That move came after Macklemore gave a speech at a concert in New Jersey where he said "Free Palestine" and claimed Israel was committing a genocide in Gaza.
In a statement at the time, Kraft said Macklemore's speech was deeply offensive to the Jewish community.
Bryan is set to return to Gillette for another concert Saturday night.

title: Doctors warn about risks energy drinks pose to kids. What families need to know
text:
Doctors warn about the risks energy drinks pose to kids. What families need to know
Sean and Heidi Cripe will never forget the call from their son's high school saying Davis was being taken to the emergency room.
Related video above: Back-to-school food tips focus on breakfast and balance
“He chugged an energy drink — like, just trying to be cool,” said Sean Cripe, recounting the day nearly a decade ago.
The teen's heart soon fell out of rhythm, and he died. While such deaths are rare, doctors across the country have warned for years that energy drinks contain high levels of caffeine that can seriously harm children, causing problems such as abnormal heartbeats, increased heart rate, sleep disturbances, dehydration, agitation, high blood pressure and seizures.
A newly formed coalition of doctors is highlighting these risks in the wake of a sponsorship deal between Monster Energy and the Big 12 Conference college athletic organization. The group has asked conference leaders to pause the sponsorship and the NCAA to review energy drink marketing to youths in general, citing the deaths of three children, including Davis, a 16-year-old from South Carolina.
The doctors stress that they are not just concerned about Monster but all energy drinks and any similar partnerships.
“Kids are going to see energy drinks now promoted by the universities and the athletes that they admire and want to emulate,” said Dr. Matthew Nelson, an Idaho cardiologist involved with the effort. “The kids will think of them as sports drinks, which they’re not.”
Too much caffeine can harm kids in many ways
Various medical groups, including the American Academy of Pediatrics, say children and teens should avoid energy drinks altogether. Yet many are not. According to the latest results of the federally funded Monitoring the Future survey, run by the University of Michigan, 23% of 12th graders, 20% of 10th graders and 18% of eighth graders reported consuming energy drinks daily.
Depending on the product, caffeine content can range from 80 to 300 mg per serving. By comparison, a typical 8-ounce coffee contains about 80 to 100 mg and some sodas contain 50 mg or less. Overall, the pediatrics academy recommends children ages 12 to 18 limit caffeine to 100 mg a day. Younger kids are discouraged from consuming any caffeine.
Caffeine and other stimulants increase heart rate and the reactivity of the nervous system – basically “how fast things go in the body, which can create an overload of the system,” said Dr. Tamara Hannon, an Indiana pediatrician who chairs the academy’s nutrition committee.
She likened it to running a blender until the motor heats up too much. “The same thing can happen when you deliver stimulants to people,” she said. “The heart can wear out, the nervous system can go haywire and you can have really serious consequences.”
While such cardiovascular dangers are real, Harvard Medical School experts say there is no scientifically valid evidence behind the common belief that caffeine can stunt a person's growth.
Mixing different types of caffeine can be risky
Children with preexisting conditions such as high blood pressure are at especially high risk, Hannon said, but even healthy children who get too much of a stimulant can have serious problems. That includes young athletes.
Another consideration: Kids often drink various types of caffeinated beverages. That was the case with Davis Cripe, who died in 2017. According to the coroner at the time, Davis had no prior heart condition and drank a Mountain Dew and a latte from McDonald’s earlier in the day. He experienced arrhythmia after having the energy drink.
It was not the first time Davis drank one, although he did not consume them regularly.
“We had talked to him and let him know that they weren’t healthy,” Sean Cripe said. “We didn’t understand they could be deadly.”
Trade group says the energy drink industry tries to protect kids
The American Beverage Association — which includes Monster and other companies comprising 94% of the energy drink category — said members voluntarily disclose caffeine totals on product labels, which carry advisories such as: “Not intended for children, pregnant or nursing women, or persons sensitive to caffeine.” Members also do not sell or market energy drinks in K-12 schools.
Monster Energy said in a statement that caffeine and other drink ingredients are found in a broad range of food products. “Mainstream energy drinks have been marketed worldwide for more than 30 years and more than 100 billion energy drinks have been sold and safely consumed globally,” the company added.
The deal between Big 12 and Monster calls for a co-branded logo on football and basketball jerseys, fields and courts, and across digital and social media channels.
“The energy drink category is not new to collegiate athletics,” the Big 12 Conference said in a statement, adding that beverage companies are always looking for ways to reach sports fans.
The NCAA does not have the authority to regulate conference or school sponsorship agreements, Dr. Deena Casiero, the association's chief medical officer, told the doctor group in a letter. She said the association offers schools educational resources on caffeine and student-athlete health, and caffeine has been a topic of interest for an NCAA committee, which recently commissioned a cardiac advisory group.
How to educate kids about excess caffeine
To protect children, teachers and coaches can educate them about the dangers of too much caffeine and the difference between energy drinks and sports drinks, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Sports drinks are designed to help replace water and electrolytes lost through sweating after activity.
Parents and other adults can also model good behavior by not consuming energy drinks in front of kids.
At well visits, parents should talk with pediatricians about all the beverages their children are consuming, said Hannon, who often advises families to “Rethink your drink.”
Sean Cripe said sharing stories like his could also help children understand that energy drinks are not for them. “We just pray parents will use our stories, our tragedies, our grief, to have an impact on their own kids.”

title: Officials encourage residents to decapitate, destroy invasive fish
text:
(CNN) - People are being encouraged to destroy an invasive fish.
The Missouri Department of Conservation says it recently removed a northern snakehead from a river.
MDC says it is a predatory fish from Asia and Africa that eats aquatic insects, snails and other fish -- and can have a negative impact on the Missouri River system.
The northern snakehead has been spotted in the Saint Francis and Eleven Point rivers.
Officials say anyone who encounters the fish should decapitate it to be sure it’s dead, or put it in a plastic bag and throw it away in the trash.

title: Weather Discussion 10/3/26
Maine runners from Scarborough, Falmouth win titles at Festival of Champions
text:
BELFAST — Scarborough’s Atticus Merriam knew he had a challenge on his hands in the boys race of the 25th Festival of Champions.
And Dirigo William Morris pushed him to the brink.
Merriam finished in 15:21.18 to beat Morris, who finished in 15:21.33 to win the annual cross country race at Troy Howard Middle School on Saturday. The meet included a record 100 schools and 1,800 runners from Maine, Massachusetts, Rhode Island, Vermont and Nova Scotia.
“I’m a little tired, but I feel good,” Merriam said. “(My thought was), ‘I just have to hold him off,’ because this is a bit of a state (championship) preview,” Merriam said. “It worked out today … I knew there was about six guys (to beat), but he was the one I had in my mind that was probably going to give me the most trouble.”
Falmouth senior Georgia Moon won the girls race by more than five seconds in 17:24.51, holding off Glastonbury (Conn.) junior Lauren Parrett (17:29.42). Last year’s girls winner, Portland sophomore Nora Schmidt, finished third with a time of 17:41.62.
Merriam and Morris kept pace with each other throughout the final mile of the race. The pair sprinted toward the finish line in the final 100 yards, gasping for air while trying to get ahead. Both runners collapsed to the ground, congratulating the other on a good race.
“I feel a little let down,” Morris said. “It came down to the wire, and it just wasn’t quite there. I’m happy with the time, but I was really shooting for that win and I was a little bummed I didn’t get it.”
Moon secured the victory with a strong finishing kick, using her prior success and knowledge of the course.
“Lauren and Nora, we ran together for a while,” Moon said. “I’m just really happy to finally make that jump. It means a lot. I didn’t want to burn out too soon. I sat for a bit until I knew I could kick it in and have (momentum) all the way through, because I think that’s something I’m really strong at.”
Parrett was pleased with her time and effort against Moon.
“This is a pretty flat course, so I was extremely excited about possibly beating my top time,” Parrett said. “I was definitely trying to push and catch up (to Moon), but my legs were starting to let up.”
Yarmouth High School won the boys team title with 114 points, followed by East Greenwich (Conn.) High School (139) and Portland (156). The Clippers were led by junior Bowen Mitchell, who finished sixth in 15:59.43.
Glastonbury dominated the field for the girls team title with 76 points, followed by Hampden Academy (196) and Mercy (Conn.) High School (236).
Temperatures were in the low 60s, slightly warm, but otherwise ideal for the relatively flat track at Troy Howard, allowing runners to post strong times.
“The full sun made it warm, but I would take weather like this any day,” Merriam said.
The girls course and race record still belong to Orono graduate Ruth White, who ran a time of 16:56.92 in 2023. The boys course and meet record is held by Sean Gray of Portsmouth (N.H.) High School, who ran a time of 14:55.56 in 2024.

title: Medical transport plane with 6 on board missing off Massachusetts coast
text:
Medical transport plane with 6 on board missing off Massachusetts coast
The U.S. Coast Guard is searching for a missing medical transfer plane off the coast of Nantucket, Massachusetts, that had six people on board, officials said early Saturday.
The Gulfstream G-100 aircraft departed L.F. Wade International Airport in Bermuda and was traveling to Boston's Logan International Airport.
A Massport spokesperson confirmed that the aircraft did not arrive at Logan Airport as scheduled.
The Bermuda government said it has been in contact with the families of those on board.
“My thoughts are with everyone on board and their families during this deeply worrying time," said Premier David Burt. "We are praying that all six people will be found safe, and we thank the search and rescue crews for their continuing efforts.”
In a statement from Skyport, the company who manages Wade International Airport, a spokesperson said that the aircraft was a Canadian-registered air ambulance that left their airport for Boston at 12:41 a.m. on Saturday.
The company said there were four crew members and two passengers on board.
"The U.S. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has advised that air traffic controllers subsequently lost contact with the aircraft off the coast of Nantucket Island, Massachusetts, and a search is currently underway," the spokesperson said. "Skyport has no further information to provide at this time."
The Federal Aviation Administration said it issued a search and rescue alert for the plane at 1:20 a.m.
The FAA notified the U.S. Coast Guard that it lost contact with the plane, which is registered to Canadian-based Latitude Air Ambulance. The company confirmed that the missing plane is among its fleet.
The Coast Guard's response includes crews from Air Station Cape Cod, a 47-foot motor lifeboat crew from Station Brant Point and the USCGC William Sparling -- a fast response cutter.
The search is about 13 nautical miles off the coast and extends from about 30 nautical miles wide and 20 nautical miles long, according to the Coast Guard.

title: Maine’s Democratic voters should not fall for Collins’ pitch
text:
Insanity, as the adage goes, is doing the same thing over and over again and expecting a different result. Yet — again and again — Maine voters send Susan Collins back to the U.S. Senate. The result of this action has never changed: always concerned but never taking action, always siding with Republican hardliners except when they have enough votes to let her appear centrist, always avoiding direct engagement with voters.
Compounding this insanity are numerous “lifelong Democrats” who will once again fall for it and vote for her, shirking the history of the party of FDR and the New Deal. We could have great things from paying our taxes: universal healthcare, infrastructure, social safety nets for retirement or life-altering events, free education and not one child ever going hungry again. Susan Collins desires none of this for Mainers. She will always do what Donald Trump tells her to do.
I, as a lifelong Democrat, am not falling for it. I am not falling for the relentless onslaught of mailers paid for by her billionaire donors. I am not falling for the empty words of a woman who willingly voted to take away the bodily autonomy of other women and girls. I am not falling for the promise that this time, this sixth term of a promised two, will be different. I want the world to substantially change for the better, for myself, for my daughters, for all Mainers. Join me in stopping this insanity. Vote Troy Jackson.
Andrew Swayze
Cape Elizabeth

title: Tennessee’s prisons chief is resigning after failed execution of Christa Pike, governor says
text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (AP) — The head of Tennessee’s prison system is resigning, Gov. Bill Lee announced Saturday, the first major staff shake-up since Christa Pike’s stunning failed execution left her unconscious and on a ventilator at a hospital.
Frank Strada, commissioner of the Department of Correction, will step down this month, Lee said. Some of the governor’s fellow Republicans and other elected officials had been urging a change in leadership.
It was the second time since May that Tennessee has not been able to execute a prisoner who was seemingly moments away from death.
The governor also announced that former U.S. Attorney Ed Stanton would lead a review of what happened in Pike’s death chamber. Stanton previously was named to conduct a review after Lee called off a different execution in 2022; he found in that case that Tennessee had not complied with its own lethal injection process.
Strada said in a statement that resigning was “in the best interest of Tennesseans” while Stanton’s review is conducted. The state failed to execute Pike despite administering two doses of a lethal drug, pentobarbital.
Strada defends execution protocol
There was no immediate response from Pike’s lawyers for an update Saturday on her condition at a hospital. They had disclosed Friday that she was on a ventilator and unconscious in the hours following the execution attempt and that hospital staff were trying to clear the two doses of pentobarbital.
The shocking failure has left both sides of the death penalty debate demanding answers. Lee has ordered an independent review and halted any new executions. Strada said he believes the state “carried out its responsibilities in accordance with the established protocol.”
Pike’s legal team welcomed Strada’s departure but said “it does nothing to help Christa now.”
“What happened to her Wednesday reflects a systemic failure that goes far beyond any one person,” the four-lawyer team said. “We hope the governor’s call for a full, independent review will expose the profound problems within Tennessee’s entire death penalty system.”
Second failed execution since May
Pike’s attorneys said they believed problems with the IV lines caused the pentobarbital to flow into her body instead of her bloodstream.
Pike was extraordinarily cooperative with the execution team, even instructing them to “please try here, please try here” as they tried to insert lines, lawyer Randy Spivey told reporters Thursday.
In May, Tennessee stopped the execution of Tony Carruthers after staff placed an IV into his right arm but couldn’t get a secondary IV line. The governor ordered officials to wait at least a year before trying to execute him again.
Strada took over the Correction Department in January 2023 after serving as deputy director of the Arizona Department of Corrections. In late 2024, he announced that Tennessee was changing its lethal injection protocol and would use only pentobarbital.
Four people have been executed in Tennessee since 2025, according to the Correction Department.
Some Arizona executions had snags
Court filings show that Strada’s job included overseeing executions in Arizona when they resumed in 2022 following an eight-year break.
Clarence Dixon was the first that year. The medical team had trouble finding a vein to administer the lethal drugs and finally made an incision in his groin area. The process took about 25 minutes.
That same year in Arizona, medical staff preparing Frank Atwood for execution initially could not locate a vein in his right arm but inserted the IV in his right hand — at Atwood’s suggestion, said Henry Brean, an Arizona Daily Star reporter who was a witness.
Strada announced Murray Hooper’s execution by lethal injection, the third in 2022. There was an unsuccessful attempt to insert an IV line in his right arm. The IV in Hooper’s leg was inserted into his femoral artery.
“When Governor Lee hired Strada to fix execution problems in Tennessee, his problematic history of executions in Arizona was well known,” said Kit Thomas, an attorney who has represented people on Tennessee’s death row.

title: Why I’m supporting Sen. Susan Collins
text:
Dennis Brockway of Winslow is president of North East Mobile Health Services and a member of the Maine Ambulance Association. The views expressed here are his own.
I want to voice my strong support for Sen. Susan Collins.
As a member of the Maine Ambulance Association and president of North East Mobile Health Services, I have had the opportunity to see firsthand the challenges facing emergency medical services in Maine, particularly in our rural communities. Over the years, Sen. Collins has sponsored, co-sponsored or supported numerous pieces of legislation aimed at strengthening EMS and improving access to emergency medical care.
Her commitment to rural healthcare goes well beyond words.
Sen. Collins played an important role in securing $50 billion for the Rural Health Transformation Program during congressional negotiations and pushed to expand the program and broaden the range of rural healthcare providers eligible to participate. Maine subsequently received approximately $190 million in first-year funding through the program.
When Maine’s award was later placed in jeopardy after the state missed federal milestones and the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) raised concerns about implementation, Sen. Collins personally intervened with CMS Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz in an effort to help preserve Maine’s funding.
Her work on behalf of rural EMS extends much further. Sen. Collins helped author the SIREN program, which provides grants to rural EMS agencies for recruitment, training, equipment and other critical needs. She has consistently supported efforts to strengthen the EMS workforce and improve access to emergency care in rural communities.
My support for Sen. Collins, however, is based on more than legislation.
In my dealings with her over the past 20 years, I have found her to be honest, respectful and willing to listen, even when people disagree with her. That matters to me. Maine has a long tradition of independent-minded public servants who put their responsibility to the state ahead of partisan politics. Sen. Margaret Chase Smith embodied that tradition, and I see much of that same Maine independence in Sen. Collins.
I recognize that many Mainers disagree with Sen. Collins on important issues. They have every right to do so. But after decades in public life and numerous hard-fought campaigns, she has been subjected to an extraordinary level of scrutiny. Through it all, she has maintained a reputation for integrity and a commitment to serving Maine.
Seniority also matters. Sen. Collins has accumulated decades of experience, relationships and influence in Washington. Maine is a small state, and having a senator in a position to influence federal policy and funding can have very real consequences for our rural hospitals, ambulance services and communities.
For me, this election should not simply be about party labels. It should be about who can most effectively represent Maine.
Based on what I have witnessed personally over the past two decades, I believe Susan Collins has earned the opportunity to continue doing that work.

title: Heisman Trophy makes its way to Bates
text:
LEWISTON — Jeff Price may not have won the Heisman Trophy as a football player at Bates College, but on Saturday brought college football’s most coveted award to his alma mater.
Price, who graduated in 1987, currently serves as the CEO of the Heisman Trophy Trust. He had the trophy near Garcelon Field where people could pose and take photos ahead of Bates’ football game against Tufts.
The Heisman Trophy is awarded annually to the top player in college football.
“As a proud Bobcat and someone who’s spent 35 years in the sports industry, now at Heisman, to have the opportunity to bring the Heisman here, it represents excellence, certainly something Bates represents,” said Price. “Empowerment, which is certainly core to who Bates is. And we at the Heisman want to create enduring impact and I know that’s what Bates wants to do.”
In leading the Heisman Trophy Trust, Price has had a chance to cross paths with many of the award’s former recipients.
“The Heisman winners have been incredible,” Price said. “Just 61 living Heisman winners and so many of them, since I’ve started, have given us hours and hours of their time. Because, as we’re creating the Heisman Club, it’s something that they care about deeply. It’s their club.
“Only one person a year gets into it. And so, we’re co-creating that and building it together so that we can drive charitable impact, we can do better storytelling around the Heisman winners and ultimately make a difference.”
One memorable occurrence with a former recipient was with last year’s winner, Fernando Mendoza, who led Indiana to the national championship and was selected with the top pick in the NFL Draft by the Las Vegas Raiders. Price said Mendoza asked for his phone number at the culmination of the Heisman Trophy ceremony weekend.
“I’ve been in sports for a long time, dealt with a lot of high-profile athletes,” said Price. “(Mendoza’s) the only athlete who at the end of a weekend, asked if he could get my cell phone number so that we could stay connected.”
The trophy display drew a crowd of students, alumni, parents and community members, many mimicking the pose of the player sculpted in the award.
Sheila and James McKinnon were on campus to watch their nephew, Bates offensive lineman Ryder Smith. They were just two of the many who stopped by the Bobcat Fan Zone and took a picture with the trophy.
“It’s kind of like the Stanley Cup, you don’t really see it a lot,” James said.
They had already planned to come for the game, so the trophy being on campus was an added bonus.
“It was fun watching everybody do the (pose),” Sheila said, miming the motion. “Everybody’s going to do the pose.”
The Heisman Trophy is the latest major award to make its way to Maine in the last couple months. The Boston Celtics’ 2024 NBA Finals trophy was displayed at a Jr. Celtics Academy basketball camp session at the Lewiston Armory in August and the Stanley Cup was at a Portland Sea Dogs game in September.
For Price, bringing it to Bates was a way to merge both of his worlds.
“Meeting of kind of two assets and two institutions of a long-standing stature and excellence, and just thrilled to be here,” Price said.

title: Colby College hosts #STRONGGIRLS day camp to empower young women
text:
WATERVILLE, Maine (WABI) - Instilling confidence in the next generation- that’s the goal of the #STRONGGIRLS day camp held at Colby College Saturday.
The camp is designed to give young girls ages 10-14 the tools to support themselves through life’s challenges.
“It’s kind of surreal in a way,” said Caroline Hartley, Colby College Athlete
“It just feels like, honestly, like just yesterday that I was one of these girls, kind of trying to figure out my life too, and I just remember how I would always look up to the girls that were older than me.”
60 middle school girls gathered to mingle with peers and mentors and learn about healthy relationships in all areas, from mind and body to social relationships and food.
“So, there are actually 6 modules. It’s strong mind, strong body, strong leadership, strong grit, strong relationships, and strong confidence,” said Leah Lawrence, Impact Program Manager with the Lindsey Vonn Foundation.
Vonn is an Olympic gold medalist skier who created the Lindsey Vonn Foundation as a way to empower young women and connect them with mentors.
“They also get to take home a strong girls journal that Lindsey actually put together a few years ago with some educators, and they are things that she uses to this day,” continued Lawrence.
“We’ve got over 20 student athlete mentors joining them throughout the day and really what our goal is to provide them with tools that can help them move through the world with confidence.”
Middle school can be one of the hardest times in a young girl’s life. Mentors say they hope that this camp can help to inspire confidence and strength in the minds of these young girls.
“It’s kind of like a key part of their life, you know, like growing. Going through middle school can be a really hard kind of phase of, being a little bit more judgmental of themselves or kind of just becoming more aware of what’s going on around them. So being able to grow their confidence and just being kind of receptive of like we were once those girls too, like trying to grow into one ourselves and just reminding them that there’s just so much more that we can reflect on and be grateful for within our lives.” said Hartley.

title: Driver hit and killed by their own dump truck, troopers say
text:
ONSLOW COUNTY, N.C. (WITN/Gray News) - Troopers say the driver of a dump truck was hit and killed by their vehicle in North Carolina, according to officials.
Officials say it happened around 1:30 p.m. on a private driveway near Old Folkstone Road near U.S. 17.
Troopers say the driver’s truck was stuck, and another dump truck at the scene helped them get unstuck.
Afterwards, troopers say the driver got out of their truck, and their vehicle moved forward and pinned them between the two trucks.

title: AI-generated robocalls? Why you could be seeing even more unwanted phone calls
text:
PHOENIX (KPHO/Gray News) — With the midterm elections quickly approaching, you may already be noticing more robocalls on your phone than usual.
Legal robocalls to cellphones require the recipient’s consent. But a group is now asking the federal government to waive that requirement.
The Club for Growth asked the Federal Communications Commission for an emergency waiver to make AI-generated robocalls without prior consent.
“As far as I’m concerned, if they’re handing out medals for bad ideas, this is a strong contender for the gold,” Patrick Crotty, an attorney with the National Consumer Law Center, said.
According to the petition, “the Club and its affiliated political committees would like to use AI-powered calling tools to engage in noncommercial, political speech to inform and gather input from potential voters more effectively (e.g., in more languages) and more efficiently.”
The Club for Growth says similar rules already apply to landlines.
Crotty said if the consent requirement is removed, political robocalls would increase by as much as 40 times compared with previous midterm elections.
“We’d probably expect something closer to 15 billion robocalls,” he said.
The Club for Growth did not immediately respond to a request for an interview.
The FCC is currently taking public comments on the petition.

title: How the Smithsonian is using AI to connect artifacts from the American Revolution
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The distance in the march from the American Revolution to the age of artificial intelligence is almost beyond comprehension. But leaders of the Smithsonian Institution are using AI to bridge the divide.
As the United States celebrates its 250th anniversary of independence, Smithsonian leaders are turning to AI to better understand items in its collection tied to the fight that led to the country’s founding.
The goal is to allow the public and scholars to both search the institution’s collection and draw connections across the Smithsonian and other organizations, such as the Library of Congress, to gain a deeper sense of how communities formed and functioned at the nation’s birth.
Since researchers on the project, known as Revolution Crossroads, began applying AI models in the spring, they have quickly drawn links that would have previously required extensive manual searches across multiple catalogs. They located, for instance, a silversmith who was running newspaper advertisements for a creamer around 1774, similar to one held at the Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History.
The ultimate ambition is to scour records and surface new stories about people whose lives have faded away over the centuries.
“An ideal scenario is that we get to a place where we’re actually adding to the public record,” said Becky Kobberod, the chief digital and innovation officer at the Smithsonian. “Maybe they’re not Thomas Jefferson or George Washington, but they did live in a community and build that community, and that name is now known.”
Since its founding in 1846, the Smithsonian has curated the nation’s history and culture across an operation that now spans 21 museums and galleries, including the National Zoo. It’s a role that’s taken on new significance as Republican President Donald Trump has questioned some of the institution’s portrayals.
Kobberod’s team has identified about 10,000 objects centered on people who lived during the 40-year period from 1770 to 1810. They have had to digitize — and in some cases redigitize — the objects to make them more accessible to AI. The public can search the records online.
For Natalie Buda Smith, the director of digital strategy at the Library of Congress, the project is a reminder that these institutions are deeply engaged in rapidly evolving technology. This work, she said, can help people researching materials who don’t know whether to begin at the Smithsonian, the Library of Congress or somewhere else.
The creamer example “illustrates that there’s a richness out there and you might find part of the story at the Smithsonian and part of the story at the library,” she said. “Open up those doors to people so they can understand, because they found it in the Smithsonian doesn’t mean it’s the end of the story.”
The work is unfolding at a sensitive time in the debate over how to properly harness AI. Some of the industry’s top leaders have issued increasingly dire warnings about the technology’s potential harm. Many were in Washington this week, where they met with Trump and signed a voluntary accord for reviews. Democrats and some Republicans are calling for a more robust response, including stronger regulation of AI.
Kobberod, the first person to hold her role at the Smithsonian, acknowledged a “healthy fear” of AI. She said the Smithsonian is not using any of the current frontier models that have received much of the scrutiny in recent weeks. She also emphasized the importance of human oversight in the research, noting that trained historians review the data and can recognize nuance that would be lost on an AI agent.
“What they might say is, ‘actually that is a known nickname for so-and-so’ or ‘that is a generic term that’s used for X, Y, Z,” she said. “That is the nuance that a historian or someone who’s spent their whole career studying that time period is going to know that a machine is not.”
Still, she said it is important to embrace the possibilities that surround AI.
“It’s not going away,” she said. “We do believe we need to lean in and figure out the part that this technology plays in our work.”

title: FBI has commissioned a classified and internal ‘Patel Report’ about times when it ‘fell short’
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The FBI is issuing a classified report to its workforce examining what it says are chapters from the bureau’s history “where this institution fell short,” according to an internal message obtained Friday by The Associated Press.
It was unclear what episodes from the FBI’s past are chronicled in the new “Patel Report.” But the document’s existence is in keeping with Director Kash Patel’s vocal criticism of the leaders who preceded him and with his determination to rid the FBI of agents he contends have politicized the bureau in the past. Patel’s critics say he is the one who has weaponized the FBI and that his scrutiny of his predecessors and their decision-making is part of an effort to rewrite history in favor of President Donald Trump.
Patel pledged at his confirmation hearing last year that he would not look “backward,” but as director, he has encouraged investigations of former senior officials and presided over sweeping terminations, including of employees who participated in years-old investigations of Trump, were photographed taking a knee during a 2020 racial justice protest and contributed to a disputed analytical memo about Catholic extremism.
“The Patel Report looks backward because accountability demands it,” says a message to the workforce signed by the FBI’s co-deputy directors, Christopher Raia and Andrew Bailey. The message describes the report as marking the “closing of one chapter in our history and the beginning of another complete with a brighter future ahead.”
Bailey announced his resignation earlier this week, and his last day is Friday. The FBI declined to comment on the report.
The message also says: “We cannot change what happened before we arrived. But we can confront it honestly. We can recognize failures instead of protecting them. We can hold people accountable. We can fix what was broken. And we can build safeguards strong enough to ensure the mistakes of the past are never allowed to define this institution again. These steps are consistent with any institution of excellence that is constantly striving for improvement.”
It was unclear if the report made recommendations or demanded any action to address what the FBI now regards as past shortcomings.
The FBI message says the report is meant to “promote fierce organizational accountability” and rebuild “public trust.” But Patel’s critics say the politically charged investigations into perceived adversaries of Trump that the FBI has embarked on under his watch, as well as the punishment of agents who participated in investigations into the Republican president to which they were assigned, have eroded faith in the nation’s premier federal law enforcement agency.

title: Gorneault, Graves Lead County At Festival Of Champions
text:
Gorneault, Graves Crack Top 10 At Festival Of Champions; Houlton Boys Finish Ninth
Aroostook County runners held their own against one of the largest fields they will see this fall Saturday at the Maine Cross Country Festival of Champions in Belfast.
The complete results included 940 boys and 611 girls, with schools from throughout Maine and New England taking part. Caribou’s Pierce Gorneault led the County boys with a seventh-place finish in 16:01.17, while fellow Viking Emma Graves placed eighth overall in the girls race in 19:06.96.
The County also had strong team showings. Houlton/GHCA placed ninth overall in the boys standings with 425 points, while Presque Isle was the top County girls team, finishing 12th with 401 points.
Gorneault Runs To Seventh
Gorneault stayed with the leaders and crossed the line seventh overall in 16:01.17.
Scarborough’s Atticus Merriam won an incredibly tight boys race in 15:21.18, just .15 seconds ahead of Dirigo’s William Morris at 15:21.33.
Houlton/GHCA also packed several runners high in the standings. Malachi Witmer finished 46th in 17:00.21, Brayden Drake was 50th in 17:01.89, Wyatt Quint placed 62nd in 17:09.53 and Logan Witmer was 66th in 17:12.16.
That depth helped Houlton/GHCA finish ninth out of 79 scoring boys teams with 425 points.
Presque Isle’s Paxton Darrell also broke into the top 100, finishing 78th in 17:20.05, while Caribou’s Peyton Gorneault was 91st in 17:33.39.
Graves Finishes Eighth In Girls Race
Graves produced another top-10 performance against a deep field, finishing eighth in 19:06.96.
Falmouth’s Georgia Moon won the girls race in 17:24.31, followed by Glastonbury’s Lauren Parrett and Portland’s Nora Schmidt.
Presque Isle had two more County runners near the front. Lillian Johnson placed 19th in 19:37.19 and Aleah Rideout followed in 23rd at 19:45.74.
Taylor York finished 64th for Presque Isle in 20:43.37, with Caribou’s Jenna Strid immediately behind her in 65th at 20:47.69.
Those performances helped Presque Isle take 12th in the girls team standings with 401 points. Caribou finished 18th with 595.

title: Cornell president calls alleged gang rape 'deeply disturbing,' pledges greater transparency
text:
Cornell president calls alleged gang rape 'deeply disturbing,' pledges greater transparency
Cornell's president called the alleged gang rape of a student at a fraternity house in 2024 “deeply disturbing” Saturday and said it would weigh on the university for years to come, as he pledged greater transparency amid mounting outrage over the school’s handling of the case.
In an eight-minute video message to the Cornell community, Michael Kotlikoff described the past week as one of the most difficult in the university’s history and acknowledged troubling questions about the investigations that followed the allegations.
Related video above: New York attorney general takes over the investigation
“My heart aches when I think of what she experienced,” Kotlikoff said. “It raises heartbreaking and troubling issues about sexual assault, dehumanization, and aspects of party culture, alcohol, and drug use.”
“I believe we as an administration and we as a community must do better,” he continued.
Kotlikoff reaffirmed his commitment to supporting an independent investigation of the case called for by New York Gov. Kathy Hochul and said Cornell’s Board of Trustees would announce details next week. He also expressed support for Hochul’s decision to turn the criminal investigation over to the state attorney general.
Scrutiny has mounted in recent days over Cornell’s response to allegations that the woman was sexually assaulted by multiple fraternity members in 2024. The woman, identified in court documents as Jane Doe, has sued the university and seven former students.
During a student assembly hearing Thursday that gave students an opportunity to voice concerns and discuss proposals to improve Cornell’s response to sexual assault, several speakers called for Kotlikoff’s resignation.
Kotlikoff acknowledged frustration that Cornell has not communicated enough about its handling of the case, saying that has led to distrust. While citing “real legal and privacy limits” on what the university can disclose, he pledged greater transparency and more opportunities for students, parents and others to engage with university leaders.
He also committed Cornell’s support to legislative efforts to change New York’s sexual assault laws.
The case has renewed scrutiny of a New York law that makes it difficult to prosecute sexual assaults involving people who voluntarily consume alcohol or drugs, even if they became too intoxicated to consent.
Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten cited the law in defending his initial decision not to pursue charges, saying the woman’s original statement to police described voluntary drug use and sexual activity.
Critics have long sought to close what they call the “voluntary intoxication loophole,” which distinguishes between people incapacitated by drugs administered without their consent and those who voluntarily became intoxicated. Hochul has pledged to push for changes to the law.

title: Eastern Maine Medical Center nursing class celebrates 50th reunion
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - A group of Maine nurses celebrated a golden milestone in Bangor today.
Around 15 graduates of the Eastern Maine Medical Center School of Nursing Class of 1976 gathered at EMMC for their 50th reunion.
And although many of them don’t get to connect too often, the laughs, memories and stories shared allowed the group to pick up right where they left off.
“It’s really fun. And it’s amazing. We’re all in our early 70s. And when you’re young, like you are, you don’t really think about what it’s going to be like to grow older. But now most of us are retired. And we’re looking back on our careers but really enjoying our lives now. And it’s fun to connect with old friends and just share what our lives have been like,” said Martha Eastman, a Class of 1976 EMMC nursing graduate.
“This is the first one that has said, ‘it’s our 50th and we want to come back.’ So it’s really pretty exciting that we can open up our doors and show them some of the places where they used to work and now how we deliver the care in our newer facilities,” said Deb Sanford, Chief Nursing officer at EMMC.
The nurses trained in the hospital’s diploma program, which operated for nearly a century before closing in 1985 and transitioning to Husson University.
Bangor’s nursing legacy dates back to 1892, with graduates serving through two World Wars.

title: Let’s get political flyers out of Maine, while we’re at it
text:

If people want to know where the candidates stand, they should read a newspaper.

title: Fallen trooper among 3 officers killed in action from the same training class
text:
LOUISVILLE, Ky. (WDRB+WAVE/Gray News) — A Kentucky father said he got chills when he learned Kentucky State Police Trooper Hayden Phillips was shot and killed Monday.
Phillips has a connection to two other officers killed in the line of duty. They all graduated from the same Department of Criminal Justice Training class at Eastern Kentucky University in December 2019.
“It’s weird for sure; my first thought the other day was, ‘Man, is that class cursed,’” Brian Shirley said.
Brian’s son, Jefferson County Sheriff’s Deputy Brandon Shirley, Kentucky State Police Trooper Hayden Phillips and Scott County Deputy Caleb Conley were among 33 graduates from DOJCT class 506.
All three were killed in action.
Brandon Shirley was ambushed in August 2021 while working private security in Louisville at a car lot off Rockford Lane. Conley was shot and killed while conducting a traffic stop on southbound Interstate 75 in Georgetown.
Conley’s murder is similar to what happened to Phillips, who died Monday in Warren County and was also shot during a traffic stop.
Shirley said the coincidence gave him chills.
“It definitely hits home every time I hear an officer has gone down,” he said.
He said when an officer dies, the loved ones left behind become part of a fraternity where no one wants membership, connected by grief.
“Heartache and sorrow, it’s just never going to shut off for them,” Shirley said. “My heart has a giant hole in it, and no matter what I pour into it, I’m never, ever going to fill it up.”
Shirley went to Conley’s funeral in 2023 and said he will connect with Phillips’ family as well.
“Those kids lost their dad,” Shirley said. “She lost her husband.”
They are new members in the club no one wants to join: law enforcement loved ones left behind.
“They say time heals all wounds,” Shirley said. “I don’t know if it gets better or you just get better at dealing with it.”
Police said Emonnie Branch, 51, of Portland, Tennessee, allegedly shot Phillips and fled, triggering a statewide manhunt.
Branch was later arrested in Louisville and charged with murder of a first responder in Phillips’ death. During his arraignment in Warren County Tuesday morning, a judge denied Branch bail.
According to court records from the Tennessee Department of Correction, Branch had at least one active warrant out for his arrest when Phillips stopped him. It was for a probation violation in a fraud case. He pleaded guilty to fraud and impersonation and was sentenced to five years’ probation in July of last year.
