title: There is no ‘bipartisan’ way to organize the Senate
text:
Daniel M. Shea is the Marson-Moller-McNulty Professor of Government at Colby College.
Sen. Susan Collins wants to talk about her bipartisanship, an understandable strategy.
Maine leans blue, and few states value political moderation as much. Even as ticket splitting has nearly disappeared across America, many Mainers pride themselves on judging candidates rather than parties. Collins has built an entire Senate career on that instinct.
The go-to retort from Democrats is that Collins’ votes against her party are rare and, more importantly, strategic. She gets a pass from Republican leadership only after a measure’s success has been assured, or she votes for the procedural motions that decide a bill’s fate and against final passage once the outcome is settled.
So, what’s the skinny on Collins’ bipartisan record? As they say, it’s complicated.
The Lugar Center’s Bipartisan Index has ranked her at or near the top of the chamber year after year, and she has broken with Republican presidents on a few highly visible issues. At the same time, CQ Roll Call found that Collins supported President Trump’s position roughly 95% of the time in 2025.
Those facts are not contradictory. They reflect how much the Senate has changed. In today’s Congress, a senator who defects a handful of times per session can be deemed “the most bipartisan.” But has the definition of “bipartisan” also shifted? It has.
When Collins’ career began, moderate Republicans were part of the Senate’s fabric. Maine alone sent Bill Cohen and Olympia Snowe to Washington. Across the country, Republicans like John Chafee, Nancy Kassebaum, Mark Hatfield and Warren Rudman worked with Democrats to write legislation, broker compromises and assemble governing coalitions. No one called them bipartisan because they voted against their party here and there. They were bipartisan because they helped govern across party lines. They forged compromise solutions. That is a different model from the one Collins represents today.
Yes, the Senate has become much more polarized. The ideological overlap between the parties has nearly vanished, and genuine coalition-building is harder than it was in 1996, when Collins was first elected. In the new environment, moderation has come to mean something smaller. Instead of asking whether a senator can build bipartisan agreements, we ask whether she occasionally casts a dissenting vote. Those are not the same thing.
The old moderation changed legislation before it reached the floor. Today’s version of moderation usually amounts to dissent after decisions have been made. Collins sometimes casts votes against her party. Where the outcomes stay the same, the dissent makes little difference.
Maine watched this play out last summer. The Medicaid cuts in the 2025 budget law were drafted in committees chaired by the majority and moved on the majority leader’s schedule. Collins voted “no,” warning of what the cuts would mean for Maine’s rural hospitals. The bill became law anyway. Her dissent was real, but it changed nothing, because the decisions that mattered had already been made.
Which brings us to the most consequential vote Susan Collins has cast every two years, and will cast again if she returns to Washington. It comes before any debate over taxes, immigration, spending or judges — before the Senate takes up any legislation at all. It is the vote to organize the chamber: the vote that elects the Senate leader.
That single decision shapes every important vote that follows. Every senator casts the “organizing vote,” and no one crosses party lines. If reelected, Collins will vote for Republican leadership, a move that cannot be spun as moderate, bipartisan or centrist.
Collins would answer, fairly enough, that the organizing vote is exactly what makes her chair of the Appropriations Committee, and that the gavel delivers for Maine.
But the same organizing vote gives Ted Cruz the committee that oversees Maine’s fisheries, and it puts public lands and conservation policy under Mike Lee, who spent last summer trying to sell off millions of acres of the kind of land Collins helped protect with the Great American Outdoors Act. It hands the Special Committee on Aging — the committee Collins herself chaired for six years — to Rick Scott, whose 2022 plan would have sunset all federal laws, Social Security and Medicare included, every five years.
Some of the most strident Republican partisans in the Senate now run the committees Maine depends on. The chairmanship is the payment for the organizing vote, and the price includes every other chairman it installs — not just Collins. There is nothing bipartisan about it.
There is also no getting away from the fact that if the organizing vote puts Republicans in charge, it empowers Donald Trump’s agenda.
None of this makes Collins’ bipartisan claims unimportant. It makes them incomplete. Voters should weigh the times she has stood apart from her party — and ask what difference those votes made in the end. And they should weigh her pending vote to install a Republican majority. She’d be chair of Appropriations, but Trump and his hardcore partisans would be in charge of the rest.
For 30 years, Collins has asked Mainers to vote for the candidate, not the party. The first vote she casts in Washington does the opposite, and Maine voters should be clear-eyed about that.

title: Editorial cartoon on write-in voting was misleading
text:
I’m writing to set the record straight after your misleading editorial cartoon on Sept. 20. Thanks to ranked-choice voting, if a voter casts a write-in vote, whether for the declared write-ins or Graham Platner, and votes for Troy Jackson as their second choice, Jackson can win.
Susan Collins needs to win by 50.01% of all votes cast. She only won last time with 50.98% of total first-place votes cast. The senator is even more unpopular this time, given her 95% voting record with Donald Trump, her support for tax breaks for billionaires paid for by cuts to health insurance subsidies and her vote to confirm Brett Kavanaugh.
And, if she’s so important as chair of Appropriations, why is Alaska getting more congressional spending per capita than Maine?
A big turnout of Platner supporters who would otherwise not vote would be most helpful in defeating Sen. Collins.
Karen Heck
Waterville

title: Foxcroft Academy bests John Bapst
Heisman Trophy makes its way to Bates
text:
LEWISTON — Jeff Price may not have won the Heisman Trophy as a football player at Bates College, but on Saturday brought college football’s most coveted award to his alma mater.
Price, who graduated in 1987, currently serves as the CEO of the Heisman Trophy Trust. He had the trophy near Garcelon Field where people could pose and take photos ahead of Bates’ football game against Tufts.
The Heisman Trophy is awarded annually to the top player in college football.
“As a proud Bobcat and someone who’s spent 35 years in the sports industry, now at Heisman, to have the opportunity to bring the Heisman here, it represents excellence, certainly something Bates represents,” said Price. “Empowerment, which is certainly core to who Bates is. And we at the Heisman want to create enduring impact and I know that’s what Bates wants to do.”
In leading the Heisman Trophy Trust, Price has had a chance to cross paths with many of the award’s former recipients.
“The Heisman winners have been incredible,” Price said. “Just 61 living Heisman winners and so many of them, since I’ve started, have given us hours and hours of their time. Because, as we’re creating the Heisman Club, it’s something that they care about deeply. It’s their club.
“Only one person a year gets into it. And so, we’re co-creating that and building it together so that we can drive charitable impact, we can do better storytelling around the Heisman winners and ultimately make a difference.”
One memorable occurrence with a former recipient was with last year’s winner, Fernando Mendoza, who led Indiana to the national championship and was selected with the top pick in the NFL Draft by the Las Vegas Raiders. Price said Mendoza asked for his phone number at the culmination of the Heisman Trophy ceremony weekend.
“I’ve been in sports for a long time, dealt with a lot of high-profile athletes,” said Price. “(Mendoza’s) the only athlete who at the end of a weekend, asked if he could get my cell phone number so that we could stay connected.”
The trophy display drew a crowd of students, alumni, parents and community members, many mimicking the pose of the player sculpted in the award.
Sheila and James McKinnon were on campus to watch their nephew, Bates offensive lineman Ryder Smith. They were just two of the many who stopped by the Bobcat Fan Zone and took a picture with the trophy.
“It’s kind of like the Stanley Cup, you don’t really see it a lot,” James said.
They had already planned to come for the game, so the trophy being on campus was an added bonus.
“It was fun watching everybody do the (pose),” Sheila said, miming the motion. “Everybody’s going to do the pose.”
The Heisman Trophy is the latest major award to make its way to Maine in the last couple months. The Boston Celtics’ 2024 NBA Finals trophy was displayed at a Jr. Celtics Academy basketball camp session at the Lewiston Armory in August and the Stanley Cup was at a Portland Sea Dogs game in September.
For Price, bringing it to Bates was a way to merge both of his worlds.
“Meeting of kind of two assets and two institutions of a long-standing stature and excellence, and just thrilled to be here,” Price said.

title: Thornton football dominates in second half to beat Portland
text:
SACO — For a quarter Portland High was the best football team on the field, bludgeoning Thornton Academy’s defense with a power run game featuring Alex Martin over and over.
At half it was an even battle with Thornton up by a point.
But high school football is a four-quarter game and Thornton dominated the second half with 29 unanswered points in to earn a 43-13 Class A win on Saturday afternoon.
Thornton quarterback Noah Fullerton threw four touchdown passes, the first three to Logan LeBlanc. Brennan Tabor scored the final three touchdowns, on runs of 5 and 30 yards that sandwiched a 30-yard screen pass score.
“We fixed some things we weren’t doing right in the beginning, the energy was off,” Fullerton said. “We came back in the second half, adjusted our energy, and showed we can be physical in this game.”
Portland (4-1) and Thornton (5-0) have met in Class A championship game three seasons straight, with Thornton winning in 2023 and 2025. Since 2023, Thornton now holds a 4-3 edge in head-to-head matchups.
There are obvious challengers in both the South (unbeaten Bonny Eagle, rising Massabesic, solid South Portland) and the North (unbeaten Oxford Hills), but a fourth consecutive Portland vs. Thornton Academy championship meeting is a strong possibility.
“We’re definitely planning on seeing them again,” said Martin, who rushed for 206 of his 219 yards and both Portland scores in the first half. “Now that we know what it’s like this year, because every year is a new team, we can learn from our mistakes, learn from where we might have an advantage and just try to get better.”
HOW IT HAPPENED
Martin had 14 consecutive runs to start the game. His eighth went 28 yards for the opening score. Portland was about to go up two scores when Thornton linebacker Josiah Blain forced a Martin fumble and Carter Moody recovered at the Trojans’ 3.
On the first play of the second quarter, Fullerton found LeBlanc behind single coverage on a deep throw that LeBlanc took 97 yards for the score.
Martin answered with an 84-yard sprint and a 13-6 lead. Thornton took a 14-13 lead on a 7-yard fade into the end zone that LeBlanc went up and snared.
Moody blocked a 33-yard field-goal attempt by Justin Bouchard just before half.
With Thornton’s defense adapted to a Portland offense that featured guard Dom Huntington and Bailey Jordan as twin fullbacks ahead of Martin, Thornton pulled away in the second half behind LeBlanc’s third touchdown on a 20-yard slant and Tabor’s touchdowns.
UNSUNG HERO
Thornton’s Blain was a force at inside linebacker, caused the pivotal turnover , and was an effective runner early when rushing yards were still hard to gain against Portland.
QUOTABLE
“I’m proud of our guys for playing with them as long as we did. I think it’s a conditioning thing. We need to play harder for four quarters. Neither us or Thornton had to play a four-quarter game up until today. It’s a great litmus test for where we’re at and we got better playing against them today.” — Dylan Rottkov, Portland head coach
“Getting to halftime with a lead, where we felt we didn’t play a great first half, was big. And then we stressed to our kids, ‘Play 48 minutes.’ You’re a tough team to beat when you play 48 minutes. We just kind of took control of the game in the second half.” — Kevin Kezal, Thornton head coach
STATISTICS
Portland: Alex Martin (30 carries, 219 yards, 2 TD); Reece Wildes (2 of 6 passing, 39 yards)
Thornton: Noah Fullerton (7 of 11 passing, 162 yards, 4 TDs); Logan LeBlanc (4 catches, 124 yards, 3 TDs); Brennan Tabor (14 carries, 85 yards, 2 TDs, 1 catch, 30 yards, 1 TD); Josiah Blain (13 carries, 82 yards)

title: Portland must be thoughtful about solutions to addiction
text:
I’m a Portland counselor who has worked in addiction treatment for 13 years, writing in response to Leslie Bridgers’ recent column (“Aggressive behavior by ‘addicts’ is testing Portland’s values,” Sept. 26).
Forcing people into treatment is neither “common sense” nor “practical.” We’ve also been doing it for almost 100 years already, and, needless to say, it’s not working. Mayor Dion’s “accountability” rhetoric resonates with a lot of people desperate for solutions. That doesn’t mean he’s right. 
I wrote the cover story for the July 2026 issue of The Bollard on this subject, “We All Need The Same Things.” For anyone interested in what real progress would look like, based in clinical experience and research, please check that out.
Rosalie Genova, LCPC, CCS
Portland

title: Officials encourage residents to decapitate, destroy invasive fish
text:
(CNN) - People are being encouraged to destroy an invasive fish.
The Missouri Department of Conservation says it recently removed a northern snakehead from a river.
MDC says it is a predatory fish from Asia and Africa that eats aquatic insects, snails and other fish -- and can have a negative impact on the Missouri River system.
The northern snakehead has been spotted in the Saint Francis and Eleven Point rivers.
Officials say anyone who encounters the fish should decapitate it to be sure it’s dead, or put it in a plastic bag and throw it away in the trash.

title: With two big defensive plays, Carter Moody helps Thornton football earn a big win
text:
SACO — There’s Carter Moody, stretched out to all of his 6-foot-3, practically horizontal to the Hill Stadium turf. The Thornton Academy junior is in the process of making the play of the game. Moody blocks Justin Bouchard’s try for a 33-yard field goal in the final minute of the first half, preserving his team’s one-point lead.
It’s the second time in the first half of this pivotal game against Portland that Moody makes the play of the game for the Golden Trojans. Late in the first quarter, with the Bulldogs threatening to turn a one-touchdown lead into a two-touchdown lead, Moody is there to fall on the ball inside his 5-yard line as Josiah Blain knocks it from Portland’s Alex Martin with a strong tackle.
This game between the teams that played in the last three Class A state championship games (won by Thornton in 2023, by Portland in 2024, and by the Trojans again last November) was a battle of two undefeated teams trying to reach another state final. For a half, it was as close as you’d expect. Eventually, Thornton wore down the Bulldogs. A one-point game at the half became a 43-13 blowout.
Moody was a big reason why his team clung to a one-point halftime lead. An all-SMAA defensive back last season as a sophomore, Moody is enjoying a bigger role this season.
“His role has increased. He’s on offense, defense, special teams. He made some great plays. He’s a great tackler,” Thornton coach Kevin Kezal said of Moody.
Portland scored quickly and with little resistance on the game’s first drive, with Martin leading the strong ground game. The Bulldogs were on the verge of putting the Trojans in a two-touchdown hole, a place with which they are unfamiliar, when Blain’s hit dislodged the ball in the final minute of the first quarter, inside Thornton’s 5-yard line.
Moody was there to pounce on the ball, evaporating the threat. He didn’t know who caused the fumble, only that it happened, and he needed to get the ball.
“It was right there in front of me and I just fell on it,” Moody said. “We battle. We stay strong. No matter where we are on the field.”
With Thornton up 14-13, the Bulldogs drove, and looked poised to take the lead just before the first half ended. Bouchard has the leg for the 33-yard field goal try. Before the play, Moody and teammate Brennan Tabor had a quick chat.
“(Tabor) was lined up next to me, and said ‘You go as tight as you can, and I’m going to try and take (the blockers) on so you’ve got a free shot,'” Moody said.
Then Moody described what happened in short, simple sentences, as if he was outlining a series of snapshots taken after the snap.
“It worked. I got around them. No one touched me. (I) put two hands up. Laid out. Blocked it. It felt amazing,” He said. “They were driving on us, but getting that stop right before halftime really helped us in the locker room.”
The Trojans spend a lot of time on special teams, both Moody and Kezal said. It’s something the team takes seriously and to heart. It was Moody’s first blocked kick, and it couldn’t have come at a better time. He held momentum in his outstretched body.
“Obviously, Carter is one of our best players, and he made a great play. It’s nice when the ball is on the hash because you have a better chance (to block it) with the angle,” Kezal said. “He took a good angle, and it was a huge play to get us into halftime with a lead.”
With two teams who have a recent history of playing big games against each other, don’t be surprised if Thornton and Portland meet again at Fitzpatrick Stadium on the Saturday before Thanksgiving.
“We knew somebody was going home with a loss,” Moody said.
With two big defensive plays in the first half, Moody helped ensure that wouldn’t be his team.

title: 16-year-old girl found strangled in 1969 identified 57 years later, police say
text:
OAKLAND, Calif. (Gray News) - A teenage girl found strangled inside a downtown Oakland hotel in 1969 has been identified 57 years later.
The victim was identified as 16-year-old Joann Yvonne Burdick, known to her family as Joanie.
Police have identified Taylor Morris Teaford, a former FBI 10 Most Wanted Fugitive known colloquially as the “Crew Cut Killer,” as a potential suspect in her murder, a press release said.
“We don’t have an actual answer as to where he’s at right now or if he’s even still alive,” Oakland Police Chief James Beere said.
Burdick was found dead inside a room at the St. Louis Hotel on the 500 block of 7th Street on Oct. 2, 1969.
Witnesses and hotel staff reported seeing the victim enter the room with a white or Native American male just after 2:45 p.m. Less than 30 minutes later, staff heard a scream.
An autopsy determined she had been strangled. Toxicology testing found no alcohol or drugs in her system.
“For decades, her family lacked the answers they deserved about what happened,” Beere said.
Investigative genetic genealogy eventually led investigators to Burdick’s brother, who voluntarily provided a DNA sample. That sample allowed investigators to confirm the unidentified victim was his sister.
Police are now working with other law enforcement agencies and say additional searches and technology could help determine what happened to Teaford.
Investigators also aren’t ruling out the possibility that he could be connected to other cold cases.

title: Time is running out for leadership on healthcare in Maine
text:
Tom Dunne of Cape Elizabeth was the first executive director of the Dirigo Health Agency during the administration of Gov. John Baldacci.
Last fall I wrote an op-ed headlined “Please don’t make me run for governor,” challenging the many candidates to declare how they would lead much needed improvements across Maine’s healthcare system.
After the op-ed appeared, I had conversations with a number of candidates, across party lines. A constant agreement was on the need for change; some had specific ideas; for others, healthcare reform was a relatively new topic.
As a reminder, healthcare makes up about a sixth of our economy — it is big and complicated and
important. The stress of illness is compounded by the stress of an overly expensive and overly complicated system. It is a major pocketbook issue for everyone (except, perhaps, for those taking advantage of the weaknesses and flaws in the current system, making so much more than their counterparts in any other economy of the world).
We are now down to three candidates, one of whom will be our governor, an elected official having formal legal authority and specific responsibilities defined by law. Based on their declarations to date, not one of the three candidates, in healthcare, is positioning to be a leader, someone who will influence, guide or inspire others to a goal.
These candidates are citing slogans, declining to dig in and declare what practical
actions they would take to improve the system. They seem to be throwing out umbrella
statements, hoping to appeal to those voters who will hear what they want to hear while avoiding having to make any statements or provide details that might negatively influence possible voters.
Boiled down, “a public option — funding reform,” “eliminate waste and fraud,” “expand
telemedicine and deal with medical debt” are at best important but small ideas when
compared to the scale of the reform needed across the system. It is almost as if the
candidates are tip-toeing to get elected and then thinking they will “figure it out” later.
Unfortunately, this does not give them a mandate to lead, it just makes them an elected official. As a reminder, we are not stuck in the current system. Maine can lead, adopting a system similar to what Maryland has been working on and similar to the underpinnings of most European systems.
No, it is not “single-payer.” Rather they treat their healthcare systems for what they basically are — geographic monopolies that operate primarily under a global budget system.
There are several ways to fund this type of system (including single-payer). Across the world there are different models to learn from, and to pick from, with an eye to fitting with Maine’s culture and values. There is no perfect solution but there are better options.
Shifting to this sort of system will require strong leadership. Sadly, unless someone steps up over the next 45 days, the Blaine House will soon have a new elected official but not a leader with a mandate for significant reform of this sector.
I think Maine voters are ready for major change and crave greater and more detailed communication from those who aspire to lead.

title: Cornell president calls alleged gang rape 'deeply disturbing,' pledges greater transparency
text:
Cornell’s president called the alleged gang rape of a student at a fraternity house in 2024 “deeply disturbing” Saturday, said it would weigh on the university for years to come and pledged greater transparency amid mounting outrage over the school’s handling of the case.
In an eight-minute video message to the Cornell community, Michael Kotlikoff described the past week as one of the most difficult in the university’s history and acknowledged troubling questions about the investigations that followed the allegations.
“My heart aches when I think of what she experienced,” Kotlikoff said. “It raises heartbreaking and troubling issues about sexual assault, dehumanization and aspects of party culture, alcohol and drug use.”
Kotlikoff reaffirmed his commitment to supporting an independent review of Cornell’s handling of the case called for by New York Gov. Kathy Hochul and said the school’s Board of Trustees would announce details next week. He also expressed support for Hochul’s decision to turn the criminal investigation over to the state attorney general.
“I want to acknowledge something that can be difficult for an institution to say,” Kotlikoff said. “We don’t have all the answers, but we are committed to investigating and finding the answers our community deserves.”
Scrutiny has mounted in recent days over Cornell’s response to allegations that the woman was sexually assaulted by multiple fraternity members in 2024. The woman, identified in court documents as Jane Doe, has sued the university and seven former students.
During a student assembly hearing Thursday that gave students an opportunity to voice concerns and discuss proposals to improve Cornell’s response to sexual assault, several speakers called for Kotlikoff’s resignation.
Hochul, asked at a news conference Friday whether she believed Kotlikoff should resign over the university’s handling of the case, declined to take a position, saying she did not yet have enough information.
Kotlikoff acknowledged frustration that Cornell has not communicated enough, saying that has led to distrust. While citing “real legal and privacy limits” on what the university can disclose, he pledged greater transparency and more opportunities for students, parents and others to engage with university leaders.
He also committed Cornell’s support to legislative efforts to change New York’s sexual assault laws.
The case has renewed scrutiny of a state law that makes it difficult to prosecute sexual assaults involving people who voluntarily consume alcohol or drugs, even if they became too intoxicated to consent.
Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten cited the law in defending his initial decision not to pursue charges, saying the woman’s original statement to police described voluntary drug use and sexual activity.
Critics have long sought to close what they call the “voluntary intoxication loophole,” which distinguishes between people incapacitated by drugs administered without their consent and those who voluntarily became intoxicated. Hochul has pledged to push for changes to the law.
Kotlikoff also called for a “serious look at the role of fraternities and sororities in campus life,” saying Cornell would engage students, alumni and others in examining how to preserve the benefits of Greek life while strengthening accountability and transparency.
“Being part of a group can never diminish individual responsibility for our own actions, for how we treat others or for speaking up when someone may be at risk,” he said.

title: A $28B hemp THC industry is fighting to save itself from a looming federal ban
text:
In a commercial kitchen outside Raleigh, North Carolina, Nicholas Hohns spreads a blue-green goo into a gridded mold, making one of his company’s signature products: potent THC gummies, featuring the primary intoxicating compound found in marijuana.
It’s a business he might soon have to give up. America’s multibillion-dollar market for impairing hemp products — from THC seltzers sold at some Target stores to smokable cannabis flowers — faces potential elimination after Congress voted to close a loophole in federal law that has allowed it to flourish.
Advocates for the industry, along with some lawmakers, are fighting to save it. The short-term government-funding bill signed by President Donald Trump last month delayed the effective date of the “hemp THC ban” from Nov. 12 to Dec. 11, giving Congress more time to consider regulating the products rather than banning them.
“It’s such a weird spot to be in,” said Hohns. “You worked 100 hours a week for the past four years, and, yeah, you made some money. But now you might have nothing to show for it.”
Sen. Mitch McConnell closed a loophole in the hemp law he championed
Marijuana and hemp are the same plant — cannabis. Marijuana is cultivated for high levels of THC in its flowers. Low-THC hemp has historically been grown for its sturdy fibers, food or wellness products. “Rope, not dope” was long the motto of farmers who supported legalizing hemp.
To give farmers a new cash crop, Kentucky Republican Sen. Mitch McConnell successfully pushed the legalization of industrial hemp in the 2018 farm bill.
But the way that law defined hemp — as having less than 0.3% of a specific type of THC, called delta-9, by weight — opened a huge loophole. Beverages or snacks could meet that threshold and still contain more than enough THC to get people high.
Vape oil, gummy candies, chips, sodas and other unregulated, untested products laden with hemp-derived THC spread around the country, including in gas stations or convenience stores, where they were available even to teens. Some businesses started selling marijuana under the theory that raw marijuana’s THC is in a form called THC-A, which only turns into impairing delta-9 when heated or burned.
The products evaded state prohibitions on recreational weed or undercut heavily taxed and regulated cannabis where it is legal.
Dozens of states responded by regulating or banning impairing hemp products.
McConnell finally closed the loophole late last year by inserting a hemp THC ban into a measure that ended the longest government shutdown in history.
The ban, which limits the amount of THC in hemp products to 0.4 milligrams per container, wouldn’t take effect for a year.
An industry tries to save itself
The ban “threatens to reduce retail revenues by $28.3 billion, displacing 225,000 jobs and reducing state sales tax potential by $2.1 billion,” according to a report last month from Whitney Economics, which studies the market.
The industry hopes to save itself by restricting impairing products to people 21 and older, limiting how much THC can be in a package, and banning imported cannabis compounds.
The owners of Kentucky’s Cornbread Hemp, Eric Zipperle and Jim Higdon, are prepared to cap their products at, say, 5 milligrams if that’s what it takes to win support from lawmakers. But the 0.4 milligram limit would destroy their business, they said.
“If it goes through in December, this place is toast — it’s gone,” Zipperle said.
They have 105 employees, sell hemp beverages in 18 states and expect to bring in $65 million this year.
The 0.4-milligram cap is so low that it would ban even some non-impairing CBD products, such as topical lotions, said Jonathan Miller, general counsel of the industry group U.S. Hemp Roundtable.
Some consider other work
Hohns, who runs Deutermann Farms in Clayton, North Carolina, entered the hemp industry after losing his job as a personal trainer during the COVID-19 pandemic. North Carolina has not legalized either medical or recreational marijuana, but many of the edibles Hohns makes are more potent than what’s available in states that have.
“When I started seeing THC edibles being sold … I was like, I got 18 months to two years to make money in this industry,” Hohns said. “No way is the government just going to sit here and let us do this when this was supposed to be for fiber, plastics, building materials, rope.”
That was more than four years ago. Hohns kept his capital investments minimal, fearing a shutdown. He has considered making other products, such as creatine gummies, if he has to get out of the hemp THC business.
Things have been more stressful for others. Drinkin’ Buds, a cannabis beverage company in Sheboygan, Wisconsin, has mothballed production. Co-founder Matt Swanson took himself off the payroll on Thursday.
“There’s just so much uncertainty,” Swanson said. “I’m actively looking for employment.”
Allies and opponents line up
Among those who have come to the defense of the hemp industry are alcohol retailers, including Total Wine & More. Sales of cannabis seltzers have helped offset falling alcohol sales.
Opponents include people who say the products are dangerous.
“I have sympathy for people losing their jobs, but I also have sympathy for the many, many more people whose lives are affected by this,” said Kevin Sabet, CEO of Smart Approaches to Marijuana.
The regulated legal marijuana industry, which sees hemp THC as unfair competition, also supports the ban. Cory Harris, a lobbyist for state-legal cannabis operators, suggested that dire predictions about its effect on the intoxicating hemp industry are overstated.
While the ban would end interstate sales of products like THC seltzers and gummies, some could find a home in legal in-state markets, he said. It’s possible THC drinks could be sold at stores in the states where they were produced. States like North Carolina could adopt legal hemp programs.
“If you go from having virtually no rules to suddenly having an awful lot of rules, that’s a buzzkill,” Harris said. “Welcome to our world. But if you establish your whole business within a legally questionable loophole, that’s just sort of the risk you take.”
___
Associated Press reporters Allen G. Breed in Clayton, North Carolina, and Dylan Lovan in Louisville, Kentucky, contributed.

title: Maine approved for Medicaid waiver that could help jails pay for addiction treatment
text:
Major changes in how Maine’s prisons and jails pay for addiction treatment and other health care services are on the horizon.
The U.S. Centers for Medicare and Medicaid recently approved Maine’s request to allow correctional facilities to bill MaineCare, the state’s Medicaid program, for certain medical and behavioral health services provided in correctional facilities up to 60 days prior to release.
Federal law prohibits the use of Medicaid to pay for health care services for incarcerated people, meaning that correctional facilities foot the bill for all medical costs. But that will soon change.
Under Section 1115 of the Social Security Act, states can seek approval from the federal Department of Health and Human Services to waive certain Medicaid requirements and restrictions. A bipartisan law passed during the first Trump administration gave states the ability to seek waivers specific to re-entry services in carceral facilities.
Gov. Janet Mills in July 2023 signed a law directing the Maine Department of Health and Human Services to apply for an 1115 re-entry waiver and after a long application process, it was approved on Sept. 25. Maine now joins 21 states and the District of Columbia with such waivers.
“This is one of the largest changes in the criminal-legal system in 30 years,” said Dr. Courtney Pladsen, the MaineCare medical director.
The new waiver will allow correctional facilities to bill MaineCare for certain services provided to individuals incarcerated in jails and prisons up to 60 days prior to their release and individuals in youth correctional facilities up to 90 days prior to release.
“This will make it easier when someone leaves to have access to medications and easier for them to see a doctor because those connections to services will start prior to release,” said Vikki Wachino, the executive director of the Health and Reentry Project, a national group focused on improving health and safety through re-entry policy. “We know that when people have access to health care and access to mental health care, they are less likely to experience the criminal justice system or to be reincarcerated. So I think that’s really the potential here, is these changes can make people healthier and make it less likely that they cycle through prisons and jails.”
On Thursday, the Health and Reentry Project launched a technical assistance center to help states with the implementation process.
Among the services eligible for coverage under the waiver are medications to treat opioid use disorder, such as buprenorphine and naloxone. The officials who run Maine’s jails have said that their budgets are increasingly strained by the cost of providing health care to the people in their custody, particularly given the high prevalence of substance use and mental health issues.
Officials have said that while they see the value in providing medication-assisted treatment to prisoners, which Maine jails and prisons have been required to do since a 2019 ruling, they face a year-after-year struggle to find funding, often turning to temporary sources such as opioid settlement funds.
“This is good news,” Somerset County administrator Tim Curtis said of the waiver approval. “This is beneficial to the county taxpayer but most of all it’s beneficial to the inmate that needs certain services and coverage.”
Curtis, as a member of the County Corrections Professional Standards Council, worked with each county to estimate the cost of providing substance use and mental health care in jails. The results were published in the council’s January report which showed, for the first time, that jails spent over $12.6 million on addiction and mental health treatment last year.
The waiver also opens up funding for some services that many jails do not currently provide, including case management, HIV and Hepatitis C treatment and family planning services. It also gives correctional facilities the ability to bill MaineCare for a 30-day supply of an individual’s prescription medications, to be provided to them at the time of release.
“We’ll be able to provide really much more comprehensive services within all the jails in the state of Maine in the pre-release period,” said Dr. Alane O’Connor, who works with the Maine Sheriffs Association and oversees the Franklin and Somerset jails’ extended-release buprenorphine programs.
“I think it’s still going to be a lengthy process in terms of getting everything up and running,” O’Connor said.
Putting the application together took a year and a half, Pladsen, the MaineCare medical director said, and involved gathering input from all 15 of Maine’s county-run jails, the Maine Sheriffs Association and the Department of Corrections, which oversees prisons.
“I heard very clearly from the sheriffs that what happens and works in Aroostook County is not going to work and what happens in Cumberland County,” she said. “And so rather than having one uniformed initiative and one uniformed implementation plan, we are going to work with each county individually.”
The state now has 120 days to put together an implementation plan to submit to the federal government. Pladsen said the implementation process will be a huge lift for jails.
As just one example: Most jails do not have electronic health record systems, so part of the challenge will be getting jails set up with the technology and systems they need to both provide the services and to bill for them.
Pladsen said the state expects correctional facilities to be able to start billing MaineCare on July 1, 2028, though the timeline for each of the jails to get their own systems up and running will likely vary.

title: ‘Please, don’t wait’: With weeks left to live, woman shares breast cancer story to help others
text:
BATON ROUGE, La. (WAFB/Gray News) - A Baton Rouge woman says she is sharing her breast cancer story in hopes of helping other women.
Whitney Brooks, 34, was diagnosed with Stage 3 breast cancer at age 27.
The disease has since progressed to Stage 4 and spread throughout her body, leaving her unable to walk, use the restroom or feed herself without help.
In July, Brooks was placed on hospice and given a 90-day prognosis.
“I think that’s one of the main reasons I don’t go to sleep,” Brooks said. “I just think, what if I don’t get up? What if this is my last breath?”
Brooks said she has days when she wants to keep fighting and moving forward, as well as days when she feels like giving up.
“I know some days I feel like I want to keep moving, keep going,” she said. “But some days, I want to throw in the towel and not want to do it anymore.”
Now, Brooks is using her final days to encourage other women to pay attention to changes in their bodies and seek medical care.
Brooks said she first noticed something was wrong when she was just 25 years old.
While taking a shower, she felt a lump in her breast.
“I just thought, oh, that’s a boil. It’ll go away,” Brooks said.
But the lump did not go away.
Brooks said her now-wife, Dana Foreman, eventually urged her to go to Woman’s Hospital to have it checked.
“It was positive for cancer,” Brooks said.
Two years later, Brooks was diagnosed with breast cancer.
“Cancer really doesn’t have an age. It doesn’t have a number,” Brooks said.
According to the American Cancer Society, about one in eight women will develop invasive breast cancer during their lifetime.
The five-year relative survival rate for breast cancer that has not spread beyond the breast is nearly 100%.
Brooks said fear played a role in why she did not initially get the lump checked.
“Please, don’t wait,” she said. “Don’t let fear sink in, because that’s what I did. I allowed fear to sink in and stop me.”
Doctors encourage women to be familiar with how their breasts normally look and feel and to talk with a health care provider about changes that concern them, including a new lump, changes in breast size or shape, skin changes or unusual discharge.
Despite the uncertainty surrounding what comes next, Brooks said she is trying to focus on the time she has left and to enjoy a nice vacation.

title: Family of man shot by ICE agent in Biddeford wants transparency, accountability
text:
It’s been almost three months since Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero‘s death, and his family is still not used to the quiet.
Martha Karolina Rojas Alvarez, his widow, said he used to come home from a day of work — mornings at PetSmart, afternoons and evenings driving for DoorDash — and talk about his day, then ask about hers. He doted on their young daughter, reserving Monday afternoons for time with her.
“He didn’t like to be alone,” she said. “He always liked to be with us, to go out, to eat, visiting the lake … or simply staying at home and watching movies.”
On July 13, a Monday morning, Durán Guerrero was shot and killed by a federal immigration agent in Biddeford.
His death, and others by agents for U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, have spurred protests and backlash across the country. Democratic members of Congress have held two forums since Durán Guerrero’s death, and his family is being represented by Gideon Asen, a law firm that has pursued high-profile lawsuits in Maine, including a recent complaint against several ICE agents accused of forcefully arresting a civil engineer in the country legally.
In an interview on Thursday, Durán Guerrero’s widow and his sister said they have been heartened by the support, and they want answers about what happened. They spoke in Spanish to the Portland Press Herald with their attorneys present, and a translator from Presente! Maine, a nonprofit that supports the state’s immigrant community.
“We would love to see above all a transparent investigation, that the people involved face consequences,” his sister, Daniela Durán Guerrero, said through translator Mae Hickey. “He was a good person, he was just working for his family.”
TAKING TIME FOR FAMILY
Durán Guerrero was the youngest of three siblings. He grew up in Bucaramanga, Colombia, hanging out with other kids in their neighborhood and riding his bike outside, his sister said. Daniela remembered helping him talk to their parents when he was scared of getting in trouble.
“Even though we were different, on separate paths, we were always together,” she said through an interpreter.
Durán Guerrero met Rojas Alvarez when they were teenagers. He lived in the same neighborhood and they would see each other every day, courting her and trying to catch her attention, she said. Years later, he was excited to learn she was pregnant and that they were starting a family. She said they came to the United States to work hard and give their daughter a better future.
Once here, Rojas Alvarez said, he worked long days but still took time for his family. His sister said he regularly helped bring her kids to school.
“He would put his work stuff on pause to help me do that,” she said.
He was the kind of uncle who spoiled her kids with video game gift cards and he liked getting everyone together.
“For me, it was really important, because me and him grew up together,” his sister said. “We were always together, so that’s why it was really important for me, for my kids to grow up together with their family, as well.”
‘TOOK A LITTLE PIECE OF EVERYONE’
The Office of the Maine Attorney General announced it was investigating the incident for deadly use of force and for any criminal activity. The office said it had no public updates on Friday. The Department of Homeland Security’s Office of the Inspector General announced an investigation into the shooting, as well, saying it was routine for all shootings involving one of its officers.
DHS has declined to identify the agents involved in the Biddeford shooting. David Brouillette of Manchester was identified by several people who know him, including an ex-wife, as the agent who shot Durán Guerrero.
Brouillette has not responded to numerous requests for comment and a phone number for him was still out of service on Friday.
Attorneys Benjamin Gideon and Sean Murphy, who are representing Durán Guerrero’s family, have criticized the Trump administration following a report from CBS that the FBI is not conducting a review for civil rights violations, citing a Department of Justice official. The New York Times also reported in July on guidance ICE agents received that month, saying that the FBI would no longer be investigating claims of assault against them.
The DOJ and DHS did not respond to requests for comment.
Murphy, a former federal prosecutor, told members of Congress during a forum on Sept. 22 that this was unusual.
Durán Guerrero’s sister and his widow say they, too, are calling for accountability.
“Through this community support we’ve come to understand it shouldn’t have happened this way, it should never have happened,” Rojas Alvarez said.
And while they wait for answers, they also want the world to know that Durán Guerrero was a good person who “took a little piece of everyone with him” when he was killed.
They said they honor him in their homes, where they keep small pictures of him near images of saints and a candle.
And, they said, by sharing his story.
“Because that’s what he would have wanted, is for us to keep going and to keep fighting,” his sister said.

title: Trump announces $90 payments for seniors on Medicare ahead of midterm elections for premium costs
text:
Trump promises $90 payments for seniors on Medicare ahead of midterm elections for premium costs
President Donald Trump is promising more payments to voters just ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections — this time, to more than 20 million seniors, giving them $90 each to help pay for Medicare premiums.
The announcement, made late Friday night by Trump on social media, comes after the president last month said about 1 million people would get rebate checks of $500 for Affordable Care Act premiums. He has also promised on the campaign trail to send every American adult $5,000 if Republicans retain control of the House and Senate in the midterm elections.
That pledge — which would require approval from Congress — would likely cost more than $1 trillion, adding to the deficit and worsening inflation.
Related previous coverage in the video at the top: President Trump’s $5,000 dividend could cost more than $1 trillion. Could it actually happen?
Polls show Americans increasingly blame Trump for the high cost of gasoline and groceries with just 17% approving of his handling of inflation. Trump has sought to shrug off concerns about affordability, saying the economy is booming.
Where is the money coming from?
The White House said the $90 payments for seniors will come from the Medicare Improvement Fund, established by Congress in 2008 as flexible funding to improve program operations and payments to health care providers.
Who is eligible for a payment and when should they expect them?
Medicare Part B enrollees can expect to receive a one-time payment in October, either through direct deposit or by check, the White House said. Total monthly costs for the program — which covers costs like doctor's visits, ambulance services and lab tests — start around $200 and vary with income.
To be eligible, seniors must be living in the U.S. and not be already receiving premium assistance from Medicaid or paying adjusted monthly premiums based on income, according to the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services. Seniors enrolled in Medicare Advantage, a private plan alternative to traditional Medicare coverage, are not eligible for the payment. More than half of eligible Medicare beneficiaries have Medicare Advantage, according to healthcare research nonprofit KFF.
Has the fund been used this way in the past?
Previous administrations have not used the Medicare Improvement Fund in this way, although Congress has periodically taken out money from the fund to pay for other priorities, said Larry Levitt, KFF's executive vice president for health policy. For example, $20.74 billion was used for the creation of the Affordable Care Act in 2010.
“The Medicare Improvement Fund language is quite broad and gives substantial discretion to the administration,” Levitt said.

title: Family of man shot by ICE agent in Biddeford wants transparency, accountability
text:
It’s been almost three months since Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero‘s death, and his family is still not used to the quiet.
Martha Karolina Rojas Alvarez, his widow, said he used to come home from a day of work — mornings at PetSmart, afternoons and evenings driving for DoorDash — and talk about his day, then ask about hers. He doted on their young daughter, reserving Monday afternoons for time with her.
“He didn’t like to be alone,” she said. “He always liked to be with us, to go out, to eat, visiting the lake … or simply staying at home and watching movies.”
On July 13, a Monday morning, Durán Guerrero was shot and killed by a federal immigration agent in Biddeford.
His death, and others by agents for U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, have spurred protests and backlash across the country. Democratic members of Congress have held two forums since Durán Guerrero’s death, and his family is being represented by Gideon Asen, a law firm that has pursued high-profile lawsuits in Maine, including a recent complaint against several ICE agents accused of forcefully arresting a civil engineer in the country legally.
In an interview on Thursday, Durán Guerrero’s widow and his sister said they have been heartened by the support, and they want answers about what happened. They spoke in Spanish to the Portland Press Herald with their attorneys present, and a translator from Presente! Maine, a nonprofit that supports the state’s immigrant community.
“We would love to see above all a transparent investigation, that the people involved face consequences,” his sister, Daniela Durán Guerrero, said through translator Mae Hickey. “He was a good person, he was just working for his family.”
TAKING TIME FOR FAMILY
Durán Guerrero was the youngest of three siblings. He grew up in Bucaramanga, Colombia, hanging out with other kids in their neighborhood and riding his bike outside, his sister said. Daniela remembered helping him talk to their parents when he was scared of getting in trouble.
“Even though we were different, on separate paths, we were always together,” she said through an interpreter.
Durán Guerrero met Rojas Alvarez when they were teenagers. He lived in the same neighborhood and they would see each other every day, courting her and trying to catch her attention, she said. Years later, he was excited to learn she was pregnant and that they were starting a family. She said they came to the United States to work hard and give their daughter a better future.
Once here, Rojas Alvarez said, he worked long days but still took time for his family. His sister said he regularly helped bring her kids to school.
“He would put his work stuff on pause to help me do that,” she said.
He was the kind of uncle who spoiled her kids with video game gift cards and he liked getting everyone together.
“For me, it was really important, because me and him grew up together,” his sister said. “We were always together, so that’s why it was really important for me, for my kids to grow up together with their family, as well.”
‘TOOK A LITTLE PIECE OF EVERYONE’
The Office of the Maine Attorney General announced it was investigating the incident for deadly use of force and for any criminal activity. The office said it had no public updates on Friday. The Department of Homeland Security’s Office of the Inspector General announced an investigation into the shooting, as well, saying it was routine for all shootings involving one of its officers.
DHS has declined to identify the agents involved in the Biddeford shooting. David Brouillette of Manchester was identified by several people who know him, including an ex-wife, as the agent who shot Durán Guerrero.
Brouillette has not responded to numerous requests for comment and a phone number for him was still out of service on Friday.
Attorneys Benjamin Gideon and Sean Murphy, who are representing Durán Guerrero’s family, have criticized the Trump administration following a report from CBS that the FBI is not conducting a review for civil rights violations, citing a Department of Justice official. The New York Times also reported in July on guidance ICE agents received that month, saying that the FBI would no longer be investigating claims of assault against them.
The DOJ and DHS did not respond to requests for comment.
Murphy, a former federal prosecutor, told members of Congress during a forum on Sept. 22 that this was unusual.
Durán Guerrero’s sister and his widow say they, too, are calling for accountability.
“Through this community support we’ve come to understand it shouldn’t have happened this way, it should never have happened,” Rojas Alvarez said.
And while they wait for answers, they also want the world to know that Durán Guerrero was a good person who “took a little piece of everyone with him” when he was killed.
They said they honor him in their homes, where they keep small pictures of him near images of saints and a candle.
And, they said, by sharing his story.
“Because that’s what he would have wanted, is for us to keep going and to keep fighting,” his sister said.

title: We served with Troy Jackson. We’re excited to support him for US Senate.
text:
The BDN Opinion section operates independently and does not set news policies or contribute to reporting or editing articles elsewhere in the newspaper or on bangordailynews.com
Cathy Breen is a former state senator, who represented Falmouth, Cumberland, Yarmouth, Gray, Long Island, Chebeague Island and part of Westbrook. Rebecca Millett is a former state representative and former state senator, representing South Portland, Cape Elizabeth and parts of Scarborough.
If you really want to get to know a person, the last two months of a U.S. Senate race of national significance might not be the best time.
Between the media back and forth and the relentless barrage of negative — and misleading — ads, it can be hard to find the truth.
We both served side by side with Troy Jackson in the Maine Senate. And we couldn’t be more excited about him representing us in the U.S. Senate.
Mainers know Jackson’s working-class story and his passion for taking on the billionaires. But we want Mainers to know that Jackson also led the effort to elect more women to the Maine Senate than at any time in Maine history.
As a result, women like us chaired the most powerful committees in Augusta since Democrats won the senate majority in 2018 — Appropriations, Judiciary, Education, and Environment and Natural Resources.
With Jackson’s leadership and strategic smarts, we have programs that make a real difference in the lives of women, children, and all of Maine’s families.
During COVID, Jackson saw that families in his community were leaving coolers out by the road so that bus drivers could drop off school lunches for their kids. People were struggling and kids were having a hard time getting enough to eat.
Jackson rallied Republicans and Democrats to pass universal free meals for all Maine public school students. Kids can’t learn if they’re hungry, and Jackson recognized more quickly than many that providing universal meals would ensure that kids in Maine — no matter where they live — can get at least one healthy, nutritious meal a day.
He worked hard for paid family and medical leave to make sure families can take the time they need to be with a sick child or an aging parent, can have a baby, can recover from an injury or illness without losing a paycheck.
When moms and dads came to the State House looking for help, Jackson was there. He worked to make childcare more affordable, he stood up to corporations who were trying to weaken child labor laws while investing in apprenticeship programs.
After Sen. Susan Collins’ pivotal support of Justice Brett Kavanaugh, and the U.S. Supreme Court rolled back constitutional protections for abortion care, Jackson led the effort to strengthen Maine’s protection for women.
While Republicans in Washington have been taking rights away and making life harder for Maine families, Jackson was fighting to protect our state and the people who live and work here.
There’s a lot more: Maine leads the nation in addressing climate change and dealing with the scourge of PFAS in our soils. We conserved thousands of acres of land and working water fronts through the Land for Maine’s Future program.
He helped to create a retirement savings program for workers whose employers don’t offer such plans.
And because of Jackson’s belief in science, Maine maintains a high rate of vaccination against childhood diseases such as measles.
In short, Troy Jackson invested in women leaders and championed issues that matter most to us.
And when tensions arose in Augusta, as they always do, Jackson had our backs.
Jackson is much more than a working-class hero from The County. He is kind and funny. He cares about people and works for us every day. He’s one of the most savvy, tenacious and accomplished legislators we’ve known, and he would serve us well in the U.S. Senate.

title: Voters favor Democrats on key issues but lack faith in either party to solve problems: AP-NORC poll
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Aaron Siever was never a single-party voter. But now, the 41-year-old from southwest Virginia is more frustrated than ever with the two political parties whose chief accomplishment, he says, is blaming each other for getting little done.
“There’s so much turmoil,” said Siever, a former police officer who now guides Civil War battlefield tours. “It really messes up chances of getting anything done. It gets really disgusting.”
Voters are deeply dissatisfied with President Donald Trump and his Republican Party heading into the Nov. 3 midterm elections, according to an Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research poll, and Democrats have built a clear advantage on pressing issues such as the cost of living and healthcare over just a few months.
But the survey also points to a bigger problem for both parties: Few registered voters think either party is able to solve important problems or help Americans like them.
That undercurrent of cynicism will be a challenge for Democrats and the Republicans, no matter which party controls Congress. Frustration with Republicans is growing, but voters do not appear to think Democrats have a long-term solution to the country’s problems, either.
Democrats have gained on key issues, survey shows
Voters give Democrats the advantage when it comes to which party would be better to handle the cost of living, an issue that has proved to be a weak spot for Trump.
The survey finds that 38% of registered voters say the Democrats would be better for costs, compared with 27% who say that about the Republicans. The issue was about evenly split among U.S. adults in February, with about 3 in 10 saying each party would be better.
Democrats have also gained ground on the economy. About 4 in 10 registered voters now pick the Democrats, compared with 26% of U.S. adults in February.
These shifts are good news for Democratic candidates who are hammering an increasingly unpopular president — and by extension, his party. Few Americans approve of Trump’s handling of the cost of living, and views of his performance on the economy are only a little better.
Voters appear to view Republicans, in particular, as focused on the wealthy. The survey finds that about 6 in 10 registered voters say the phrase “focused on helping rich and powerful people” describes the Republican Party “extremely” or “very” well. Only about 3 in 10 registered voters say the same about the Democratic Party.
Few voters think either party is focused on people like them
While voters expressed deep dissatisfaction with Republicans, the survey indicates that voters have relatively little confidence Democrats have their problems in mind.
Democrats are less likely to be described as corrupt or focused on the wealthy than are Republicans, but not more likely to be seen as focused on ordinary people or capable of solving problems.
Only about 2 in 10 registered voters say that “able to solve important problems” or “focused on helping people like me” describes the Democratic Party “extremely” or “very” well. That is similar to the percentages who say this about the GOP.
Democrats are out of power in Washington, and that may contribute to the perception that they are unable to get traction in solving problems.
In the last year alone, the federal government partially shut down twice for weeks because of partisan disputes in Congress over spending on healthcare and immigration enforcement.
But gridlock has not been exclusive to Republican control. Despite Democratic majorities early in Democratic President Joe Biden’s administration, the party did not achieve its goals on key priorities such as abortion rights, voting rights and raising the minimum wage.
Siever is frustrated by what he sees as a commitment to partisanship in Congress at the expense of progress at a time when consumers are paying higher prices for daily necessities such as groceries and gasoline.
Driving around the region to lecture and guide tours, his travel costs have soared and led him to raise his prices.
“I’ve really become tired of the idea that, if you’re in this party, you have to be loyal to this but, if you’re in that party, you have to be loyal to that,” he said. ”There’s big problems and neither side seems able to fix them.”
Meanwhile, 55% of registered voters say the Republican Party is “too extreme.” Some 45% say the same about the Democratic Party.
Democrats are divided on their party’s path forward
Voters overall do not see an abundance of moderate sentiment in either party. But they are more likely to say Democrats are “too moderate” than Republicans — a reflection of the lack of unity within Democratic Party about its strategy.
Slightly fewer than half of Democratic voters say their party is “too moderate,” while a similar share say it is “about right.” That is a sharp contrast with Republican voters, who mostly say their party is “about right.”
Voters such as Meagan Ludwig of Milwaukee illustrate the party discontent that has emerged in Wisconsin and other closely contested states this year.
Ludwig, a 41-year-old real estate broker, voted for democratic socialist Francesca Hong in the Democratic primary for governor in August, arguing the candidate seemed more committed to a policy agenda aimed at helping working families than Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley.
Crowley won the primary by a half percentage point — roughly 3,800 votes — illustrating Democrats’ soul-searching in the Upper Midwestern swing state.
In the November general election, Ludwig is “reluctant,” but plans to vote for Crowley rather than Republican Tom Tiffany, a congressman. Ludwig hopes that Crowley, if elected, perceives the discontent about his party.
“We need to seize the opportunity to boldly enact policies that will improve the lives of Americans,” said Ludwig, who is married and has an elementary school-age child. “I’m tired of us pursuing incremental change.”
___
Beaumont reported from Des Moines, Iowa.
___
The AP-NORC poll of 2,140 adults, including 1,766 registered voters, was conducted Sept. 24-28 using a sample drawn from NORC’s probability-based AmeriSpeak Panel, which is designed to be representative of the U.S. population. The margin of sampling error is plus or minus 2.9 percentage points for adults overall and plus or minus 3.1 percentage points for registered voters.

title: 49ers owner Jed York suspended for 6 games after his arrest in prostitution sting
text:
49ers owner Jed York suspended for 6 games after his arrest in prostitution sting
The NFL suspended San Francisco 49ers owner Jed York for six games Friday following his arrest earlier this year in a prostitution sting in Ohio.
Video above: Body-camera video shows Jed York’s arrest in Ohio prostitution investigation
The league announced that York also was fined $500,000 for violating the league's personal conduct policy. York has not attended any games or league meetings so far this season and was credited with three games served. He is eligible to return on Oct. 20, following the team's game the previous night against Washington. The NFL's fall league meetings begin that day in New York.
York said in a statement released by the team that he accepts the punishment given by the league and apologized for his actions.
“To my family, to the players, coaches, and employees of the San Francisco 49ers, to our fans and partners, I am deeply sorry,” he said. “This was an inexcusable mistake and I take full responsibility. What I did does not reflect my values or the man I strive to be for my family. While I fell short of the model I want to set for my sons, I now hope to show them the importance of owning up to one’s failures, and that even our worst moments teach us to be better. Leading the 49ers is a privilege, and one I don’t take lightly. Your trust will have to be earned back over time, and I look forward to that work ahead.”
Coach Kyle Shanahan said later Friday that he didn't believe anything would change from the operation of the team on the field over the final three weeks of the suspension. Shanahan said that if he and general manager John Lynch wanted to make a major move during that time, they probably would tell York's father, John, about it, but that ownership has always deferred to Shanahan and Lynch on those decisions.
“There’s never been a situation where we’ve gone to him with a trade or anything like that and then him say no or anything like that,” Shanahan said. “If it’s something that the football people believe and think we should do, he’s always been fully supportive. So, I expect it to be no different if something like that comes up.”
York was arrested in a mobile home park by the Mahoning Valley Human Trafficking Task Force after police said he was attempting to pay $160 for sex with a woman he believed to be a prostitute.
York was booked into jail and was released after posting a $5,000 bond. York was initially charged with engaging in prostitution, but prosecutors amended that to disorderly conduct. He pleaded no contest to that charge and to possessing criminal tools for using his phone to respond to an undercover online prostitution advertisement.
He was sentenced to one day in jail for both offenses to be served concurrently and was credited with one day served when he pleaded no contest. He also was fined $1,150. Police seized the $160 from York and that was later given to the human trafficking task force as part of the plea. York also completed an online course.
Owners have been previously punished for violating the personal conduct policy. The late Indianapolis Colts owner Jim Irsay was suspended for six games and fined $500,000 following a guilty plea to driving while impaired in 2014.
New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft was investigated but not punished by the league after he was arrested in Florida in 2019 for allegedly paying for sex with a woman at a massage parlor. The charge was later dropped after a court ruled that police violated the rights of Kraft and the other customers when they secretly installed video cameras inside massage rooms at the spa.
York spent most of the summer in Ohio, where he grew up near Youngstown and had been away from the team even before his arrest. He had filed for divorce from his wife, Danielle, in May, according to court records.
York took over day-to-day control of the 49ers from his parents in 2008. He became the team’s principal owner in 2024. After some initial struggles under York’s leadership, the team has been a consistent contender since hiring Shanahan and Lynch in 2017.
The Niners have made the Super Bowl three times under York’s leadership, losing in the 2012 season under coach Jim Harbaugh and the 2019 and ’23 seasons under Shanahan and Lynch.
York also oversaw the building of Levi’s Stadium in Santa Clara. The team moved from San Francisco to the new stadium in 2014. The stadium has hosted two Super Bowls, a World Cup and a College Football Playoff title game.

title: Maine Historic Preservation Commission receives federal grant
text:
The Maine Historic Preservation Commission (Commission) is pleased to announce that it has received a grant award of $877,873 from the National Park Service for the 2026 federal fiscal year. These funds are appropriated from the Historic Preservation Fund by Public Laws 118-83 and 119-4 and are used to support the program of the State Historic Preservation Office in Maine. This award was made contingent upon raising a non-federal match of $585,249.
The Commission anticipates awarding a minimum of $100,000 from these federal funds as sub-grants to non-profit organizations, municipalities or state agencies for historic preservation projects. Funds will be available through a competitive grant process that is expected to begin later this year.
The Historic Preservation Fund grant supports the Commission as it undertakes programing for the protection and conservation of State and local cultural and historic assets and to assist it in implementing and fulfilling the program areas outlined in the National Historic Preservation Act and the National Park Service approved statewide historic preservation plan.
The Commission is the largest repository for information about historic buildings, sites, structures, objects and districts in the State of Maine. Established through a legislative act in 1971, the Commission is the state agency that functions as the State Historic Preservation Office in Maine. The Commission nominates properties to the National Register of Historic Places; reviews and comments on the effect of federal undertakings on historic properties; assists owners of income producing properties to obtain federal and state rehabilitation tax credits; oversees the identification and evaluation of archaeological sites as well as historic buildings, objects, and districts; and promotes historic preservation through planning and public education.
For more information contact Kirk F. Mohney, director, at kirk.mohney@maine.gov or 207-287-3811.
