title: Python swallows peacock in Florida backyard
text:
Python swallows pet peacock in Florida backyard
Python swallows pet peacock in Florida backyard
A Burmese python slithered into a backyard enclosure in Florida last week and swallowed a pet peacock named Violet, leaving a Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission agent to remove the invasive predator with his bare hands.
Rhett Stanberry, a python agent for FWC, responded to a frantic call from his neighbor about the massive snake.
"It's hard for me to see people hurting with their pets being lost. Right. So that's that's like the part that's difficult about that. But then, you know, I can go in, and I can remove the invasive predator," Stanberry said.
The python, a nearly 9-foot-long female, had already consumed half of the peacock by the time Stanberry arrived.
"By the time that my neighbor had found the peacock, the python had already consumed the first half of it, so it was too late," Stanberry said.
The pet peacock, Violet, was a female. Stanberry said he is unsure how the snake entered the enclosure but noted that sightings of Burmese pythons are becoming more frequent.
"They're expanding their range. And so they're now being found outside of the Everglades as humans are moving closer to the Everglades. So we're having a conflict of people and pythons," Stanberry said.
FWC confirmed that it is legal for homeowners to humanely kill invasive pythons year-round if spotted.

title: LifeFlight hosts event to reunite flight crews and patients
text:
LifeFlight hosts event to reunite flight crews and patients
LifeFlight of Maine hosted an event on Saturday that brought together flight crews and the patients whom they cared for.
It's a nonprofit statewide organization that attempts to hold these events every 3-5 years.
Staff at LifeFlight said it can be incredibly gratifying for the staff who don't always have the chance to further connect with the people they've saved and their families.
They also said it can, at times, bring a sense of closure to the patients.
"I know this is incredibly important," answered LifeFlight of Maine CEO Joe Kellner. "It can oftentimes be emotional for the crews to reconnect with the patients. I know our staff. I know they enjoy meeting the patients that they took care of and learning their story."
The day was hosted at Unum's Portland Campus. They say the company aims to help the working world thrive through life's moments.
"I was watching some of the patients and the families talk to the crews, and it truly gave me goosebumps. These were life-changing moments," said Unum Corporate Social Responsibility Manager Kelly Thayer.
Kellner added that the day can also work as an education tool. By seeing the helicopters touch down and learning the ins and outs of one of their ambulances, attendees can learn a lot about what a day looks like for LifeFlight staff.

title: Maine runners from Scarborough, Falmouth win titles at Festival of Champions
text:
BELFAST — Scarborough’s Atticus Merriam knew he had a challenge on his hands in the boys race of the 25th Festival of Champions.
And Dirigo William Morris pushed him to the brink.
Merriam finished in 15:21.18 to beat Morris, who finished in 15:21.33 to win the annual cross country race at Troy Howard Middle School on Saturday. The meet included a record 100 schools and 1,800 runners from Maine, Massachusetts, Rhode Island, Vermont and Nova Scotia.
“I’m a little tired, but I feel good,” Merriam said. “(My thought was), ‘I just have to hold him off,’ because this is a bit of a state (championship) preview,” Merriam said. “It worked out today … I knew there was about six guys (to beat), but he was the one I had in my mind that was probably going to give me the most trouble.”
Falmouth senior Georgia Moon won the girls race by more than five seconds in 17:24.51, holding off Glastonbury (Conn.) junior Lauren Parrett (17:29.42). Last year’s girls winner, Portland sophomore Nora Schmidt, finished third with a time of 17:41.62.
Merriam and Morris kept pace with each other throughout the final mile of the race. The pair sprinted toward the finish line in the final 100 yards, gasping for air while trying to get ahead. Both runners collapsed to the ground, congratulating the other on a good race.
“I feel a little let down,” Morris said. “It came down to the wire, and it just wasn’t quite there. I’m happy with the time, but I was really shooting for that win and I was a little bummed I didn’t get it.”
Moon secured the victory with a strong finishing kick, using her prior success and knowledge of the course.
“Lauren and Nora, we ran together for a while,” Moon said. “I’m just really happy to finally make that jump. It means a lot. I didn’t want to burn out too soon. I sat for a bit until I knew I could kick it in and have (momentum) all the way through, because I think that’s something I’m really strong at.”
Parrett was pleased with her time and effort against Moon.
“This is a pretty flat course, so I was extremely excited about possibly beating my top time,” Parrett said. “I was definitely trying to push and catch up (to Moon), but my legs were starting to let up.”
Yarmouth High School won the boys team title with 114 points, followed by East Greenwich (Conn.) High School (139) and Portland (156). The Clippers were led by junior Bowen Mitchell, who finished sixth in 15:59.43.
Glastonbury dominated the field for the girls team title with 76 points, followed by Hampden Academy (196) and Mercy (Conn.) High School (236).
Temperatures were in the low 60s, slightly warm, but otherwise ideal for the relatively flat track at Troy Howard, allowing runners to post strong times.
“The full sun made it warm, but I would take weather like this any day,” Merriam said.
The girls course and race record still belong to Orono graduate Ruth White, who ran a time of 16:56.92 in 2023. The boys course and meet record is held by Sean Gray of Portsmouth (N.H.) High School, who ran a time of 14:55.56 in 2024.

title: Michael Jordan's 'Last Dance' 1998 Finals jersey sells for a record $12.26 million
text:
Michael Jordan’s ‘Last Dance’ 1998 Finals jersey sells for a record $12.26 million
A jersey worn by Michael Jordan during one of the most famous seasons of his career sold at auction for $12.26 million on Tuesday to become the most expensive basketball jersey to ever cross the block.
The white mesh top emblazoned with Jordan's iconic number "23" was worn by the star during Game 3 of his legendary 1998 NBA Finals run. It was the end of his time with the Chicago Bulls, known as "The Last Dance," which was chronicled in a 2020 ESPN and Netflix documentary series of the same name.
During the pivotal game against the Utah Jazz, Jordan delivered a crushing performance in front of a home-court crowd that helped shift the series in the Bulls' favor, with Jordan ultimately leading the team to win its sixth championship in eight seasons.
The shirt is the only publicly known white game-winning jersey from the 1998 Finals ever put on sale, making it an extremely rare piece of memorabilia, according to Joopiter, the online auction house that hosted the sale.
"The significance of this jersey extends well beyond the box score," Joopiter had written on its online auction listing.
"This is the type of object collectors wait a lifetime for — an irreplaceable artifact that transcends basketball to become a piece of global cultural history," said Caitlin Donovan, the auction platform's global head of sales, in a press release prior to the sale's conclusion.
In becoming the most expensive basketball jersey ever sold at auction, the shirt surpassed the previous record set by another Jordan jersey from Game 1 of the same finals.
In 2022, a red jersey worn during that matchup where the Bulls lost, sold for $10.1 million, more than double initial estimates, CNN previously reported.
In 2021, a jersey also worn by the player during his sophomore season at the University of North Carolina set an auction record at the time when it sold for $1.38 million.
The current record for the most expensive sports collectible ever sold is held by Babe Ruth's "Called Shot" jersey, which sold for $24.12 million in 2024. Ruth wore the jersey during Game 3 of the 1932 World Series, when he appeared to gesture toward something in center field just before hitting a fifth-inning home run into the bleachers, a story which is now part of baseball lore.
Still, Jordan remains one of the most celebrated athletes, with online memorabilia sales consistently topping current top stars.
eBay users have spent more than $115 million on Jordan playing cards this year alone, according to Gemrate, a site that tracks trading card grading and sales dates — beating out every other current and previous NBA player and putting him only below Los Angeles Dodgers' baseball star Shohei Ohtani.

title: Husson football gets first win of season
text:
Daniel Ruiz Cantu rushed for 65 yards and two touchdowns as Husson held on to beat Western New England College, 26-21, on Saturday in Bangor for its first win of the season
The Golden Bears (2-3, 1-1 Conference of New England) pulled within five points on Carey Kilroy’s 29-yard scoring pass to John De Camps with 2:17 left, but the Eagles (1-4, 1-1) were able to run out the clock to preserve the win.
Husson quarterback Brody Gibson was 16-of-26 passing for 143 yards and a score to Jacob Lenz (four catches, 55 yards).
AMHERST 22, BOWDOIN 13: The Mammoths (3-0, 3-0 NESCAC) overcame an early 10-point deficit and beat the Polar Bears (0-3, 0-3) in Amherst, Massachusetts.
Clinging to a 15-13 halftime lead, Amherst scored on a 2-yard rush by Demetrius Smith to extend its lead with the only points of the second half.
Bowdoin had a fourth-and-1 at the Amherst 9-yard line with 1:16 left, but was turned the ball over on downs. The Polar Bears got their only touchdown in the first quarter on an interception return by Ferris Collins. Quarterback Soren Hummell finished 23 of 39 for 171 yards.
ENDICOTT 55, UNIVERSITY OF NEW ENGLAND 27: Quarterback Shea Lynch completed 20 of 34 passes for 369 yards and two touchdowns, and also rushed for 75 yards and a pair of scores, as the Gulls (5-0, 2-0 Conference of New England) beat the Nor’easters (0-5, 0-2) in Biddeford.
Bryan Ferreira rushed for 196 yards on 20 carries and had two touchdowns for the Gulls.
For UNE, Damien Jones rushed for 78 yards on 14 carries and scored a touchdown. He also had two receptions for 104 yards, including a 73-yard score. Javin Willis added a 9-yard scoring run and CJ Cooper returned an interception for a touchdown.
MIDDLEBURY 32, COLBY 2: Connor McClennan rushed for 121 yards and four touchdowns as the Panthers (2-1, 2-1 NESCAC) beat the Mules (0-3, 0-3) in Middlebury, Vermont.
Aidan Moss was 15-for-29 passing for 163 yards, including a 13-yard scoring pass to Luis Kuehberger.
The Mules scores on a safety in the third quarter.
TUFTS 22, BATES 21: With three seconds left, the Bobcats (0-3) lined up for a field goal with a chance to earn their first win of the season, but Marcos Ruiz’s kick was blocked by the Jumbos (2-1), who held on for a road victory Saturday night in Lewiston.
Tufts led 14-7 at halftime, backed by two touchdowns from Christian Shapiro, but Bates battled back in the second half to jump ahead by a score, 21-14, with just over three minutes to go in the third quarter.
Shapiro caught a touchdown pass for his third score of the game with 51 seconds left in the game. Tufts then converted its 2-point conversion to go ahead by one point before stopping Bates on its near game-winning drive.

title: Family of man shot by ICE agent in Biddeford wants transparency, accountability
text:
It’s been almost three months since Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero‘s death, and his family is still not used to the quiet.
Martha Karolina Rojas Alvarez, his widow, said he used to come home from a day of work — mornings at PetSmart, afternoons and evenings driving for DoorDash — and talk about his day, then ask about hers. He doted on their young daughter, reserving Monday afternoons for time with her.
“He didn’t like to be alone,” she said. “He always liked to be with us, to go out, to eat, visiting the lake … or simply staying at home and watching movies.”
On July 13, a Monday morning, Durán Guerrero was shot and killed by a federal immigration agent in Biddeford.
His death, and others by agents for U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, have spurred protests and backlash across the country. Democratic members of Congress have held two forums since Durán Guerrero’s death, and his family is being represented by Gideon Asen, a law firm that has pursued high-profile lawsuits in Maine, including a recent complaint against several ICE agents accused of forcefully arresting a civil engineer in the country legally.
In an interview on Thursday, Durán Guerrero’s widow and his sister said they have been heartened by the support, and they want answers about what happened. They spoke in Spanish to the Portland Press Herald with their attorneys present, and a translator from Presente! Maine, a nonprofit that supports the state’s immigrant community.
“We would love to see above all a transparent investigation, that the people involved face consequences,” his sister, Daniela Durán Guerrero, said through translator Mae Hickey. “He was a good person, he was just working for his family.”
TAKING TIME FOR FAMILY
Durán Guerrero was the youngest of three siblings. He grew up in Bucaramanga, Colombia, hanging out with other kids in their neighborhood and riding his bike outside, his sister said. Daniela remembered helping him talk to their parents when he was scared of getting in trouble.
“Even though we were different, on separate paths, we were always together,” she said through an interpreter.
Durán Guerrero met Rojas Alvarez when they were teenagers. He lived in the same neighborhood and they would see each other every day, courting her and trying to catch her attention, she said. Years later, he was excited to learn she was pregnant and that they were starting a family. She said they came to the United States to work hard and give their daughter a better future.
Once here, Rojas Alvarez said, he worked long days but still took time for his family. His sister said he regularly helped bring her kids to school.
“He would put his work stuff on pause to help me do that,” she said.
He was the kind of uncle who spoiled her kids with video game gift cards and he liked getting everyone together.
“For me, it was really important, because me and him grew up together,” his sister said. “We were always together, so that’s why it was really important for me, for my kids to grow up together with their family, as well.”
‘TOOK A LITTLE PIECE OF EVERYONE’
The Office of the Maine Attorney General announced it was investigating the incident for deadly use of force and for any criminal activity. The office said it had no public updates on Friday. The Department of Homeland Security’s Office of the Inspector General announced an investigation into the shooting, as well, saying it was routine for all shootings involving one of its officers.
DHS has declined to identify the agents involved in the Biddeford shooting. David Brouillette of Manchester was identified by several people who know him, including an ex-wife, as the agent who shot Durán Guerrero.
Brouillette has not responded to numerous requests for comment and a phone number for him was still out of service on Friday.
Attorneys Benjamin Gideon and Sean Murphy, who are representing Durán Guerrero’s family, have criticized the Trump administration following a report from CBS that the FBI is not conducting a review for civil rights violations, citing a Department of Justice official. The New York Times also reported in July on guidance ICE agents received that month, saying that the FBI would no longer be investigating claims of assault against them.
The DOJ and DHS did not respond to requests for comment.
Murphy, a former federal prosecutor, told members of Congress during a forum on Sept. 22 that this was unusual.
Durán Guerrero’s sister and his widow say they, too, are calling for accountability.
“Through this community support we’ve come to understand it shouldn’t have happened this way, it should never have happened,” Rojas Alvarez said.
And while they wait for answers, they also want the world to know that Durán Guerrero was a good person who “took a little piece of everyone with him” when he was killed.
They said they honor him in their homes, where they keep small pictures of him near images of saints and a candle.
And, they said, by sharing his story.
“Because that’s what he would have wanted, is for us to keep going and to keep fighting,” his sister said.

title: Cat food investigation finds toxic contaminants across nearly all brands
text:
(CNN) - A new investigation into cat food found toxic chemicals in nearly all types and brands.
One hundred of the top-selling cat foods, including wet, dry and air- or freeze-dried foods, were tested for more than 120 contaminants.
Toxic plastic contaminants, the herbicide glyphosate and heavy metals such as lead, mercury and arsenic were found in all types of the foods tested.
Metal levels across brands
Of cat food samples across 62 brands, lead was found in 99% of samples. Cadmium, which harms the kidneys and bones, was found in 96% of samples. Arsenic was found in 94% of samples.
Differences by protein type
The report, by the nonprofit Clean Label Project, found fish and seafood proteins, especially wet versions, generally contained the most mercury and cadmium.
Chicken versions saw higher rates of lead and herbicides.
Nearly 85% of poultry-based foods met Clean Label Project’s purity standard, compared with 25% of fish and seafood products.
Recommendations from the report
According to the report, cat owners should try to vary their pet’s diet.
Wet or air-dried products are preferable to dry food for lower lead exposure.
Avoiding foods with plants in the top ten ingredients could help lower pesticide exposure.

title: 16-year-old girl found strangled in 1969 identified 57 years later, police say
text:
OAKLAND, Calif. (Gray News) - A teenage girl found strangled inside a downtown Oakland hotel in 1969 has been identified 57 years later.
The victim was identified as 16-year-old Joann Yvonne Burdick, known to her family as Joanie.
Police have identified Taylor Morris Teaford, a former FBI 10 Most Wanted Fugitive known colloquially as the “Crew Cut Killer,” as a potential suspect in her murder, a press release said.
“We don’t have an actual answer as to where he’s at right now or if he’s even still alive,” Oakland Police Chief James Beere said.
Burdick was found dead inside a room at the St. Louis Hotel on the 500 block of 7th Street on Oct. 2, 1969.
Witnesses and hotel staff reported seeing the victim enter the room with a white or Native American male just after 2:45 p.m. Less than 30 minutes later, staff heard a scream.
An autopsy determined she had been strangled. Toxicology testing found no alcohol or drugs in her system.
“For decades, her family lacked the answers they deserved about what happened,” Beere said.
Investigative genetic genealogy eventually led investigators to Burdick’s brother, who voluntarily provided a DNA sample. That sample allowed investigators to confirm the unidentified victim was his sister.
Police are now working with other law enforcement agencies and say additional searches and technology could help determine what happened to Teaford.
Investigators also aren’t ruling out the possibility that he could be connected to other cold cases.

title: Maine Marathon 2026: What runners, spectators and drivers need to know for Sunday’s race
text:
Maine Marathon 2026: What runners, spectators and drivers need to know for Sunday’s race
Thousands of runners will take to the streets of Greater Portland Sunday for the 35th Maine Community Bank Marathon, Half Marathon and Marathon Relay.
Maine Marathon 2026: What runners, spectators and drivers need to know for Sunday’s race
Thousands of runners will take to the streets of Greater Portland Sunday for the 35th Maine Community Bank Marathon, Half Marathon and Marathon Relay.
Thousands of runners will take to the streets of Greater Portland Sunday morning for the 35th running of the Maine Community Bank Maine Marathon, Half Marathon and Marathon Relay.
The races begin at 7:45 a.m. Oct. 4 at Baxter Boulevard in Portland, with the full marathon, half-marathon and relay all starting and finishing near Back Cove.
The overall field is expected to approach a record 5,500 entries, according to race organizers.
For anyone cheering on a participant or simply trying to get around Greater Portland, organizers are warning of road closures and traffic changes throughout the morning.
When and where does the race start?
All three races begin at 7:45 a.m. near Pedro Field on Baxter Boulevard, between Forest Avenue and Preble Street Extension. The finish line is at the same location.
The marathon is a USATF-certified course and an official Boston Marathon qualifying event. The out-and-back course takes runners through Portland, Falmouth, Cumberland and Yarmouth.
An early 6:30 a.m. start is available only for marathon walkers expecting to maintain a pace of 13 minutes per mile or slower. Those early starters are not eligible for awards.
Race organizers say dogs, baby strollers and bicycles are not allowed on the course, and bikes are prohibited.
Road closures and traffic impacts
In Portland, Baxter Boulevard and Payson Park will be closed from 5 a.m. to 2 p.m. West Kidder Street, East Kidder Street and Sherwood Street will be closed from about 7:45 to 8:30 a.m., while Veranda Street will be closed in both directions from 7:45 to 9 a.m.
In Falmouth, Depot Road between Route 1 and Route 88 will be closed from 8 a.m. to 1 p.m. Route 88 between Route 1 and north of Depot Road will be closed from 7:40 to 10:30 a.m. Johnson Road will be limited to local traffic from 8 a.m. to 1 p.m.
In Yarmouth, Gilman Road between Route 88 and Prince's Point Road will be closed from 9 to 11 a.m.
Race organizers also ask spectators not to park along Route 88 because runners will be traveling in both directions.
Where can spectators watch?
Organizers say there are limited areas where spectators can easily reach the course because of the road closures.
One recommended spot is the intersection of Depot Road and Route 88 in Falmouth. Spectators can park at Walmart or another shopping center on Route 1 and walk about 0.3 miles to the course.
Another viewing location is Route 88 and Tuttle Road in Cumberland, with spectators encouraged to park along Route 1.
In Yarmouth, spectators can reach Gilman Road from Route 88 south, using either Route 1 or Interstate 295.
More than just a race
This year's event is expected to be one of the largest in its history, and it also has a significant charitable component.
Camp No Limits, Day One, Nanna's House and the Pine Tree Society are the four designated beneficiaries for 2026. The local nonprofit organizations all support Maine children in different ways and will split $65,700 from the race proceeds.
Camp No Limits is in Wales and supports young people with limb loss/limb difference, helping them build an independent lifestyle.
Day One is based in Windham and aims to improve the health of Maine teens and families by offering direct help with substance use, mental health and wellness needs.
Nanna's House, a nonprofit in Portland, helps foster families and provides supply kits to caseworkers so children have what they need.
Pine Tree Society, located in Scarborough, has spent 90 years creating opportunities for Maine children and adults with disabilities to live full, engaged lives through programs that promote independence, communication and inclusion.
The Maine Marathon says the event and its participants have raised more than $8.9 million for charity since 1997, including more than $793,000 donated in 2025.
"When we have more runners, we have more money to give away," said Maine Marathon Race Director Bob Dunfey. "We end up supporting about 50 other charities in addition to them, because we have many groups that provide volunteers that are nonprofits. Last year, we wrote more than $200,000 in checks."
WMTW is a proud sponsor of the 2026 Maine Marathon and has several employees taking part Sunday, including anchor Terry Stackhouse, reporter Jacob Murphy, meteorologist Ted McInerney and sales team members Sam Chipman and Andy Cartwright.
For the latest race information, including course maps, parking, spectator locations and runner tracking, visit the Maine Marathon website.

title: There is no ‘bipartisan’ way to organize the Senate
text:
Daniel M. Shea is the Marson-Moller-McNulty Professor of Government at Colby College.
Sen. Susan Collins wants to talk about her bipartisanship, an understandable strategy.
Maine leans blue, and few states value political moderation as much. Even as ticket splitting has nearly disappeared across America, many Mainers pride themselves on judging candidates rather than parties. Collins has built an entire Senate career on that instinct.
The go-to retort from Democrats is that Collins’ votes against her party are rare and, more importantly, strategic. She gets a pass from Republican leadership only after a measure’s success has been assured, or she votes for the procedural motions that decide a bill’s fate and against final passage once the outcome is settled.
So, what’s the skinny on Collins’ bipartisan record? As they say, it’s complicated.
The Lugar Center’s Bipartisan Index has ranked her at or near the top of the chamber year after year, and she has broken with Republican presidents on a few highly visible issues. At the same time, CQ Roll Call found that Collins supported President Trump’s position roughly 95% of the time in 2025.
Those facts are not contradictory. They reflect how much the Senate has changed. In today’s Congress, a senator who defects a handful of times per session can be deemed “the most bipartisan.” But has the definition of “bipartisan” also shifted? It has.
When Collins’ career began, moderate Republicans were part of the Senate’s fabric. Maine alone sent Bill Cohen and Olympia Snowe to Washington. Across the country, Republicans like John Chafee, Nancy Kassebaum, Mark Hatfield and Warren Rudman worked with Democrats to write legislation, broker compromises and assemble governing coalitions. No one called them bipartisan because they voted against their party here and there. They were bipartisan because they helped govern across party lines. They forged compromise solutions. That is a different model from the one Collins represents today.
Yes, the Senate has become much more polarized. The ideological overlap between the parties has nearly vanished, and genuine coalition-building is harder than it was in 1996, when Collins was first elected. In the new environment, moderation has come to mean something smaller. Instead of asking whether a senator can build bipartisan agreements, we ask whether she occasionally casts a dissenting vote. Those are not the same thing.
The old moderation changed legislation before it reached the floor. Today’s version of moderation usually amounts to dissent after decisions have been made. Collins sometimes casts votes against her party. Where the outcomes stay the same, the dissent makes little difference.
Maine watched this play out last summer. The Medicaid cuts in the 2025 budget law were drafted in committees chaired by the majority and moved on the majority leader’s schedule. Collins voted “no,” warning of what the cuts would mean for Maine’s rural hospitals. The bill became law anyway. Her dissent was real, but it changed nothing, because the decisions that mattered had already been made.
Which brings us to the most consequential vote Susan Collins has cast every two years, and will cast again if she returns to Washington. It comes before any debate over taxes, immigration, spending or judges — before the Senate takes up any legislation at all. It is the vote to organize the chamber: the vote that elects the Senate leader.
That single decision shapes every important vote that follows. Every senator casts the “organizing vote,” and no one crosses party lines. If reelected, Collins will vote for Republican leadership, a move that cannot be spun as moderate, bipartisan or centrist.
Collins would answer, fairly enough, that the organizing vote is exactly what makes her chair of the Appropriations Committee, and that the gavel delivers for Maine.
But the same organizing vote gives Ted Cruz the committee that oversees Maine’s fisheries, and it puts public lands and conservation policy under Mike Lee, who spent last summer trying to sell off millions of acres of the kind of land Collins helped protect with the Great American Outdoors Act. It hands the Special Committee on Aging — the committee Collins herself chaired for six years — to Rick Scott, whose 2022 plan would have sunset all federal laws, Social Security and Medicare included, every five years.
Some of the most strident Republican partisans in the Senate now run the committees Maine depends on. The chairmanship is the payment for the organizing vote, and the price includes every other chairman it installs — not just Collins. There is nothing bipartisan about it.
There is also no getting away from the fact that if the organizing vote puts Republicans in charge, it empowers Donald Trump’s agenda.
None of this makes Collins’ bipartisan claims unimportant. It makes them incomplete. Voters should weigh the times she has stood apart from her party — and ask what difference those votes made in the end. And they should weigh her pending vote to install a Republican majority. She’d be chair of Appropriations, but Trump and his hardcore partisans would be in charge of the rest.
For 30 years, Collins has asked Mainers to vote for the candidate, not the party. The first vote she casts in Washington does the opposite, and Maine voters should be clear-eyed about that.

'Water was, like, up to my chin': Neighbors work together to escape rising floodwaters
text:
'Water was, like, up to my chin': Neighbors work together to escape rising floodwaters
Isaac Guzman said he woke up around midnight to his dad banging on the door, with water already flooding their home.
"I had gotten up, I had put my feet on the floor and, like, the water was already up to, like, my ankles," Guzman said.
As the water continued to rise, Guzman said his family decided to move to a neighbor's house.
"The water on the inside was, like, coming up to our knees. So, we decided, like, it would be best if we walked up to the neighbor's house," he said.
The family had to move again as the water kept rising, carrying what they could, including their dogs.
"By then the water was probably, like, up to, ran into my nose. So, my dad was struggling with, like, the dogs, keeping them up as they were setting up the backpack. So, I had swam back in, like, picked both of the dogs up," Guzman said.
Firefighters eventually encountered the family and helped them make their way out.
"Firefighters use the tools that we have and the experience that they have to do the best job possible and, you know, try to help the citizens that need it," firefighter Trevor Towey said.
While firefighters were conducting rescues, neighbors also stepped in to help. Jeffrey Jimerson said he came to the area after his mom called for help.
"I came down here to rescue her. And then after I got her out, I figured I might as well just try to get a couple other people out," Jimerson said.
Jimerson said he helped a family with two young girls and a dog, placing them in a kayak and pushing them through the water.
"They would just sit in it, and I'd just push behind it. Water was, like, up to my chin," he said.
Firefighters eventually helped get those people out of the kayak. They said rescues in water like this are dangerous, even for trained crews.
"The main thing is ropes. That helps secure us to make sure that we don't get washed away and keep us safe," Towey said.

title: How Jon Ossoff and Susan Collins are turning a mundane part of their jobs into a reelection pitch
text:
ATHENS, Ga. — After Hurricane Helene barreled through Georgia in the fall of 2024, Sen. Jon Ossoff was the first high-ranking official on the ground in Valdosta, where he took in the damage and promised locals he’d help them get the federal recovery assistance they needed.
“Just about every week, I dial up Georgia mayors and pastors and farmers to find out how I can help,” Ossoff said at a recent campaign rally for his reelection bid against Republican Rep. Mike Collins.
Up the Eastern Seaboard, Maine Sen. Susan Collins keeps a regular itinerary of local events, including ribbon-cuttings and groundbreakings for projects she helped finance as Senate Appropriations Committee chair.
“There’s not a community in Maine that can’t say Susan helped us,” intones the voiceover in a campaign ad for Collins. The five-term senator, who’s not related to the Georgia congressman, is facing Democratic former state legislative leader Troy Jackson in November.
The two senators — Ossoff the Democrat, Collins the Republican — began this election cycle widely viewed as their respective parties’ most vulnerable members. But as Republican Donald Trump’s second presidency and partisan fights on Capitol Hill dominate national political conversation, the senators’ campaigns have played out differently than expected in part because of the more mundane part of their jobs: helping the people back home.
“We in the political world tend to think about the strength of incumbency through the lens of fundraising and national media attention, and those do matter,” said Republican Chris Hartline, once a top adviser at the National Republican Senatorial Campaign Committee. “But the ability to help the local communities you actually represent still matters.”
For Ossoff, it means attracting endorsements from Republican officials, including Valdosta Mayor Scott James Matheson, that have made it harder for Mike Collins to land attacks claiming that the liberal first-term senator from Atlanta doesn’t represent Georgia. For Susan Collins, it means a go-to buffer argument as she runs with the weight of Trump’s lagging popularity and her support for various parts of his agenda.
A month from Election Day, Ossoff has gone from a top GOP target to a widely perceived favorite to defend a seat that Democrats cannot afford to lose as they try to regain a Senate majority. And as Republican incumbents like Ohio Sen. Jon Husted are increasingly viewed as underdogs, strategists in both parties still view Susan Collins’ race as a tossup.
Ossoff draws begrudging respect from Republicans
Ossoff and his aides say the senator tries to deliver on every aspect of what Washington calls “constituent services.”
That could mean federal appropriations, disaster assistance or nuts-and-bolts matters like assisting a voter who is seeking Social Security disability benefits or a missing Social Security check. It includes surprise notes of congratulations or condolences to constituents — something Ossoff sends even to aides of Republican elected officials.
Endorsing Ossoff earlier this year, Matheson, the Valdosta mayor, described himself as a lifelong conservative. But he praised Ossoff for his Helene response. The senator recalled “going block by block” with the mayor and serving “hot meals to folks who had just lost their homes.”
Ossoff points to money secured for a dialysis center in nearby Tifton, Georgia. Mayor Julie Smith, another Republican, has endorsed Ossoff, too, explaining that “he’s been very good for south Georgia.”
Courtney Eskew, whose husband, Joshua, was injured during an Army tour in Afghanistan, pointed to Ossoff’s work for veterans’ care. The couple both grew up in Republican households but said they were volunteering for Ossoff’s campaign.
“Senator Ossoff has been passionately vocal about VA funding, and any time we’ve needed to call to advocate or to ask a question about benefits, his office has done everything we needed,” Eskew said after the couple attended an Ossoff event.
Eskew said it’s a powerful counter to opponent Mike Collins’ attacks that Ossoff is too liberal for the historically conservative state.
Ossoff “doesn’t vote the way I want him to vote” on contentious issues, added Chan Jones, who chairs the Georgia Republican Party’s 8th Congressional District committee. “But as far as the office and the way they’ve carried themselves and handled other aspects of the job, I can’t knock that.”

title: The Supreme Court will hear a major climate change case involving a devastating Colorado wildfire
text:
LOUISVILLE, Colo. (AP) — Less than an hour after the first warning that a wildfire was headed for her suburban street, Tawnya Somauroo’s Colorado home was in ashes.
She has worked tirelessly for nearly five years to rebuild her house and help ensure her neighborhood can withstand the next blaze. But as climate change contributes to more frequent wildfires, she worries that the careful landscaping, metal fencing and flame-resistant siding are not enough.
“We lost our homes and they left us to figure out for ourselves how to make our neighborhoods safe again,” Somauroo said. “At the end of the day, it comes out of our pockets, you know? And it does feel like maybe the oil and gas industry should have a part in this.”
She lives in Boulder County, one of dozens of jurisdictions across the United States suing oil and gas companies to help pay for damage from disasters linked to climate change.
The case is part of a wave of climate change litigation across the country and the world, with billions of dollars at stake. On Monday, the first day of the Supreme Court’s new term, the justices will hear the Boulder case that could decide the fate of others like it.
The city and county of Boulder first sued two oil companies in 2018, years before the fire. They argued that Suncor Energy and ExxonMobil had violated state law by deceiving the public about their contributions to climate change and sought unspecified damages to help cover the cost of worsening disasters.
The companies say that a flood of lawsuits in state courts is not the way to deal with the global issue.
“The problem is that climate change is caused by pretty much everybody living on earth,” said Phil Goldberg, special counsel for the Manufacturers’ Accountability Project, an industry group. “We need to figure out how to address that. We need to address it in a very meaningful way. This litigation doesn’t do that.”
The companies have the backing of the Trump administration. Federal government attorneys say the lawsuits are a backdoor way to regulate heat-trapping greenhouse gas emissions and amount to an unconstitutional power grab.
“No one state can superimpose its own regulatory preferences on the rest — least of all to address a global problem that exists almost entirely outside its borders and affects the world at large,” they wrote.
The Clean Air Act, they say, allows the federal government, rather than states, to regulate emissions. The Republican administration has largely used that power to roll back environmental regulations.
Last month, the Environmental Protection Agency ceded some of its climate authority by repealing rules that limit planet-warming greenhouse gas emissions from power plants fueled by coal and natural gas. The move could complicate its argument.
Boulder says it is not trying to regulate emissions beyond its borders, only holding companies accountable for local costs.
“Boulder County and city aren’t trying to change what’s happening in Texas or New York, they’re trying to get compensation for things happening now in Colorado,” said Sam Sankar, senior vice president at Earthjustice, which filed an amicus brief in the case.
Climate change was considered a factor in the 2021 Marshall Fire that destroyed Somauroo’s home, after the county’s suit was originally filed. The total damage was estimated at $2 billion. It was the costliest wildfire in Colorado history.
“Local county municipal governments play a very important role in helping front line communities adapt to climate change. This case could very well set a precedent,” said Chris Winter, executive director of the Getches-Wilkinson Center, an environmental research group in Colorado.
The case will come before a conservative-majority Supreme Court where environmental regulations have not always fared well, including a 2022 decision that limited the EPA’s authority to regulate carbon dioxide emissions from power plants.
Only eight of the nine justices will be on the bench, though. Justice Samuel Alito recused himself just a week before arguments after facing calls to step aside because he owns stock in oil companies.
That creates the possibility of a tie vote in the case, though it’s unclear how likely that might be. The court is also weighing a question that experts say is a potential “off-ramp”: whether the justices have jurisdiction to hear the case at this stage.
___
Whitehurst reported from Washington.

title: Video shows students rushing to stop school bus when driver suffers medical emergency
text:
(Gray News) - Students in Pennsylvania are being praised for their actions in helping stop their bus after the driver suffered a medical emergency.
Video from the Hollidaysburg Area School District has recently been released, showing the heart-stopping moments from the students’ ride home when the driver appeared to pass out while behind the wheel.
The students said they knew something was wrong when the bus started rolling during a stop.
In the video, the bus is seen starting to roll as students are exiting at a stop.
The students at the front of the bus are then seen jumping into action, bringing it to a stop, calling dispatch for help, and checking on the driver.
The Hollidaysburg Area School District thanked those students for their actions, including 10th grader Alexis Smith.
“Alexis took immediate action, safely bringing the bus to a stop, using the radio to call for emergency help,” the school district said.
School officials said Alexis also checked the driver’s pulse and respiration until medical responders arrived.

title: Editorial cartoon on write-in voting was misleading
text:
I’m writing to set the record straight after your misleading editorial cartoon on Sept. 20. Thanks to ranked-choice voting, if a voter casts a write-in vote, whether for the declared write-ins or Graham Platner, and votes for Troy Jackson as their second choice, Jackson can win.
Susan Collins needs to win by 50.01% of all votes cast. She only won last time with 50.98% of total first-place votes cast. The senator is even more unpopular this time, given her 95% voting record with Donald Trump, her support for tax breaks for billionaires paid for by cuts to health insurance subsidies and her vote to confirm Brett Kavanaugh.
And, if she’s so important as chair of Appropriations, why is Alaska getting more congressional spending per capita than Maine?
A big turnout of Platner supporters who would otherwise not vote would be most helpful in defeating Sen. Collins.
Karen Heck
Waterville

title: How Jon Ossoff and Susan Collins are turning a mundane part of their jobs into a reelection pitch

title: Marine veteran to receive new home built on National Mall
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - A 76-year-old Marine Corps veteran is set to receive a brand new home built in just seven days on the National Mall.
The 480-square-foot modular home is being constructed piece by piece on America’s Front Lawn, in full public view of visitors to the nation’s capital.
“It’s been a great experience to be here on the National Mall and watching this home coming together and knowing that it’s going to be mine,” said Jim Taylor, the veteran receiving the home.
Taylor was nominated and chosen to receive the home from Purple Heart Homes, an organization dedicated to building safe, affordable housing for veterans. He said the decision came as a surprise.
“I was like, oh really? Why?” Taylor said.
The founders of Purple Heart Homes were on hand to walk Jim through the building process, explaining how the build symbolizes more than just a house.
“Every veteran just wants to be at home,” said John Gallina with Purple Heart Homes.
“They want to have a safe, accessible home that’s not going to cause them worries, that’s going to be affordable for them. And that’s what these homes represent,” Gallina said.
Taylor works with veterans in North Carolina on a daily basis and has seen firsthand the housing struggles of many.
“I work at a place called Fifth Street Ministries… and we have homeless veterans sleeping five beds to one room,” Taylor said. “People don’t realize that many veterans need help.”
The final unveiling of the finished home is Monday. The home will then be loaded up and sent to Glasgow, Va., where Taylor will move into his new neighborhood.

title: Birds are behaving strangely in my backyard this fall
text:
Outdoors
The BDN outdoors section brings readers into the woods, waters and wild places of Maine. It features stories on hunting, fishing, wildlife, conservation and recreation, told by people who live these experiences. This section emphasizes hands-on knowledge, field reports, issues, trends and the traditions that define life outside in Maine. Read more Outdoors stories here. 
We are ten days into autumn. Where once the backyard was alive with bird song, the neighborhood now buzzes with the sound of leaf blowers.
It’s time to get my bird supplies ready for winter. It’s time to clean all the bird feeders, or in my case, just one.
For the last month, I’ve dared to keep just one feeder stocked with sunflower seeds. I’m training the local birds that my backyard is a good food source, while training my local bears that it isn’t. I’m keeping a small quantity of seed inside a hanging platform feeder. If a bear wanders in, it’ll find a quick snack but not a big meal, and it won’t tear apart the open feeder.
This strategy has worked better than I expected. Usually, there’s enough natural food in the treetops this time of year that the birds ignore my feeders. However, I’ve had families of red-breasted and white-breasted nuthatches chowing down at the platform with wild abandon, accompanied by chickadees and titmice. Weirdly, local hordes of blue jays have totally ignored the feeder. Usually, they’re swallowing and caching every seed they can get this time of year. I think the birds are sending a message about what kind of winter this will be, but I haven’t figured out exactly what they’re telling me.
As soon as bears den up for the winter, I’ll put out more feeders — some nyjer seed for the tiny finches, and a basket of suet for all the others. This is a good time to clean all the feeders — the one I’m currently using, and the ones I will be.
Feeder cleaning is an important seasonal chore. Seed can mold over the summer, especially at the bottom of the feeder. Nyjer seeds are tiny and prone to going rancid. Nyjer is often called thistle, although it’s an unrelated seed imported from Africa. American goldfinches are fond of it, as are their close cousins, pine siskins and redpolls.
Feeders may also become unhealthy if too many bird droppings accumulate in and around them. Droppings spread disease, especially salmonella. Finches — especially house finches — can contract a bacterial infection that causes swollen and crusty eyes.
You’ll find plenty of feeder cleaning instructions online. I soak mine in a mild solution of dish soap and water. For tougher jobs, I substitute a little bleach for the soap.
I’d recommend leaving your hummingbird feeders up for a couple more weeks before cleaning and storing them. Most of our ruby-throated hummingbirds have left by now, but several western species may wander into the state. It’s rare, but we find vagrant hummingbirds somewhere in Maine every year. Any hummer at the feeder this late should be greeted with suspicion.
Bird houses also demand seasonal maintenance, especially bluebird boxes. Different species have different housekeeping strategies. House wrens are meticulous about removing old nesting material before building new nests in the spring. Bluebirds aren’t. They will just build on top of the old nest, and live with any of the mites and parasites that may have wintered over.
Open the nest box and remove all nesting material. Unlike the metals and plastics in most feeders, wood has a rough, grainy surface that can harbor germs. Scrape with a brush, wash thoroughly, and leave open till completely dry. A weak solution of bleach usually does the trick — nine parts water to one part bleach. Inspect wood, screws, and hinges for sharp edges. If a woodpecker has widened the entry hole, repair it. Wider holes allow entry by bigger predators.
Autumn is a natural time to clear brush — in my case, as little as possible. Feeder birds need protective cover so they can dash in, grab a seed, and dash back. I also leave leaf litter in place over the winter. It shelters bugs and other natural food until migrants return in the spring. Plus, I’m too lazy to rake. However, letting ticks overwinter in excess leaf litter becomes less desirable.
A heated bird bath in winter is irresistible to backyard birds, providing fresh drinking water and a chance to bathe. Some folks swear by them, but honestly, it’s never worked for me. Birds get enough water from snowmelt off my metal roof and out of my frequently muddy driveway.
Finish up your fall chores by bolstering squirrel defenses. I’ve had limited success with “squirrel-proof” feeders in the past. Lately, I’ve had longer-lasting triumphs with baffles. One baffle on a pole defeats most squirrels. Two, properly spaced, vanquish all.

title: Goodfellas moves across the bridge to former Taylor’s Drug Store location in Madison
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
For the Abdelrihim family, a restaurant is more than a place to just get a meal, it’s a place for families and communities to come together.
Goodfellas, which serves a mix of American and Italian dishes, recently moved from Anson to Old Point Avenue in Madison, opening in the former Taylor’s Drug Store and giving the family more space for the restaurant.
Owner Alex Abdelrihim decided to make the move after learning the building was for sale.
“He wanted to open Goodfellas to provide breakfast, lunch and dinner because his Anson location was too small,” said Brandie Abdelrihim, Alex’s 37-year-old daughter-in-law.
Brandie Abdelrihim manages the dining room for Goodfellas. Her husband, Sharif, helps in the kitchen when needed while also operating Good ‘N’ Plenty 2 Diner on Lakewood Road in Madison with his wife.
Goodfellas’ Anson location had limited space and a parking lot that was not ideal for business. The move to Madison has given Goodfellas more visibility and foot traffic from area residents and people passing through.
“Since moving from Anson to Madison, we have definitely seen an increase in business,” Brandie Abdelrihim said. “Madison gives us more visibility and traffic, and we’re serving a much larger mix of both familiar faces and new customers.”
Before Goodfellas opened, the Abdelrihims made extensive renovations to transform the space into a restaurant.
“It needed commercial kitchen equipment, a hood system, new flooring, a bathroom, and an added emergency exit,” Brandie Abdelrihim said.
The business opened briefly Aug. 10, but technology issues forced the restaurant to close for the day. It reopened the following day, welcoming customers, both old and new.
“The community has been very welcoming and has offered some great feedback on where to make improvements,” Brandie Abdelrihim said. “We are listening and doing what we can to provide what our patrons want.”
One of the most common requests has been a liquor license, which the family plans to work on.
The restaurant business has been a part of the Abdelrihim family for decades.
Alex Abdelrihim, originally from Cairo, moved from Egypt to the United States in 1984 for more economic opportunities. He learned the restaurant business from a mentor who ran the Golden Eagle restaurant in New Jersey before opening his own diner in Connecticut in 1993.
He later moved to Maine and in 2004 opened Good ‘N’ Plenty 2 in Anson. He bought the former Ole Sole Mio building the following year and opened it in 2008 as the Golden Eagle. The restaurant was later renamed Good ‘N’ Plenty 2.
Brandie Abdelrihim, who was born and raised in Madison, and her husband took over Good ‘N’ Plenty 2 in 2023. They are now helping Alex Abdelrihim establish Goodfellas in its new location.
“We want people to feel like they’re more than just customers when they walk through our doors,” Brandie Abdelrihim said. “Whether it’s supporting local families, giving back through community events, or simply creating a place where people feel welcome and taken care of, we’ve really tried to make Good ‘N’ Plenty 2 a place that feels like home, and we plan to help carry that same energy over to our father’s restaurant.”
The restaurant will also sell the family’s viral trompe l’oeil desserts designed to realistically resemble other foods or objects. The Abdelrihims hope to offer trivia nights, throwback nights, music events, and other activities.
“We want to be a place families can come for a good meal and celebrate milestones,” Brandie Abdelrihim said. “We really want to lean into the Goodfellas name and have some fun with it.

title: VIDEO: Police bodycam footage of Luigi Mangione’s arrest released
text:
VIDEO: Police bodycam footage of Luigi Mangione’s arrest released
Police bodycam footage released Friday shows the moment officers located and arrested Luigi Mangione at a Pennsylvania McDonald’s in connection with the shooting death of United Healthcare CEO Brian Thompson in Manhattan.
In one video, officers ask Mangione to lower the face mask he was wearing to hide his identity.
“That’s 100% him,” one officer says eagerly as they step outside to speak out of Mangione’s earshot.
“I told you, man,” another responds off camera.
Later, an officer searches Mangione’s belongings and smiles widely as she pulls out a gun cartridge, seemingly confirming they’d found their suspect.
Video below: Bodycam video shows moment ammo magazine found during Luigi Mangione's arrest
The trove of videos comes from Mangione’s Dec. 9, 2024, arrest in Altoona, five days after Thompson, a 50-year-old Minnesota executive, was gunned down as he walked to a midtown Manhattan hotel for his company’s annual investor conference.
A Manhattan judge unsealed the recordings Friday after CNN petitioned for their release. Parts of the videos were shown during a December court hearing as Mangione’s lawyers unsuccessfully sought to get key evidence thrown out, including his initial statements to police and items seized at the time of his arrest.
Mangione pleaded guilty in August to federal stalking charges and faces life in prison when he's sentenced in December. He also faces murder charges in New York state court, though those proceedings have been postponed indefinitely as his lawyers seek to have the case thrown out.
The videos released Friday begin as officers descend on the McDonald’s in central Pennsylvania, nearly 300 miles from Manhattan.
They find Mangione, the Ivy League-educated scion of a wealthy Maryland family, seated at a table wearing a ski hat, surgical face mask and winter coat. The officers say they're responding to a call about a suspicious person and ask for his name and identification.
“You’re a little nervous right now. Why are you nervous?” an officer asks at one point.
They order him to put his hands on his head and ask him if he’s been in New York recently. They confront him about a phony New Jersey driver’s license he offers up bearing the name Mark Rosario.
“You’re under official police investigation right now,” one officer warns. “You give a false name to us again, you’re gonna be arrested for false ID.”
When Mangione finally comes clean, they ask why he had lied.
“I clearly shouldn’t have,” he responds as he’s asked to write his real name and spell it aloud.
Other videos show officers patting Mangione down, reading him his rights, placing him in cuffs and taking him to the police station.
As an officer searches him more thoroughly at the station, another officer goes through his backpack.
The officer finds the 9 mm handgun authorities would later confirm was used in the killing, as well as a silencer and another ammo magazine. They also recover the journal that prosecutors would later say revealed Mangione’s intent to “wack” a health insurance executive, as well as his other handwritten notes.
“He has a checklist for today,” another officer says, ticking off the seized items to someone on the phone. “Tomorrow he’s supposed to do an intel check-in and get a survival kit.”

title: Woman told Cornell investigators she ‘felt like bait’ during alleged gang rape
text:
(AP) - A woman who says she was gang-raped at a Cornell University fraternity told the school’s investigators last year that she “felt like bait” as the attackers were “like lions around me,” according to records from the school’s disciplinary investigation.
The documents, reviewed Friday by The Associated Press, include excerpts of interviews Cornell’s investigators did with the woman and the men she accused and shed more light on the university’s handling of the case.
While heavily redacted, the records offer a fuller but sometimes conflicting timeline of events and a glimpse at how the men responded to the allegations. Some disputed the woman’s account and said they weren’t involved in any assault.
The woman, identified in court papers only as Jane Doe, sued Cornell and seven former students last month, alleging she was given ketamine and repeatedly assaulted at a fraternity house in October 2024.
She went to campus police three weeks after the encounter and gave a detailed account of what happened, but the local district attorney decided not to file criminal charges or push for more investigation after reviewing a police summary of her interview.
Only the school’s investigation, under the federal Title IX law, persisted, with a goal of deciding discipline for the students involved.
Lawsuit by one of the accused men reveals details on investigation
This week, a lawyer for one of the accused men filed documents from the school’s investigation in a lawsuit that seeks to overturn the university’s punishment and remove it from his academic record. They include a 99-page report on a campus hearing panel’s disciplinary findings and a summary of events submitted by the university’s lawyers.
Though only a fraction of the thousands of pages amassed in the investigation, the records show the breadth of the university’s inquiry — including 50 interviews with 32 witnesses and 12 days of hearings.
Late Thursday, Gov. Kathy Hochul appointed Attorney General Letitia James as a special prosecutor to lead a renewed criminal investigation, saying she had lost faith in Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten.
According to the Title IX documents filed in court, which are only a portion of the entire investigation, the woman and several of the men gave investigators similar accounts of drug use and sexual activity that took place at the Chi Phi fraternity house — but differed sharply in how much of it was consensual.
Snapchat messages drew other men
The woman had been invited there by a fraternity member for whom she had long held strong romantic feelings and sexual interest, according to the disciplinary panel’s findings. The panel found that she initially consented to sex with that man and one of his friends, though she later alleged in her lawsuit that she had been pressured into taking ketamine, marijuana and alcohol and was too intoxicated to consent.
Then other men began showing up in the room, some drawn by a message one of the fraternity brothers sent to a Snapchat group at 1:42 a.m. using a vulgar term to advertise that a woman’s body was freely available. Later, another person in the chat asked if the “shop” was still open.
The woman told investigators that her intoxication had rendered her partly defenseless. She said she remembered smoking marijuana and said she knew she took ketamine, her first time doing so, but didn’t have an independent memory of it. The drug, she said, left her in a state of “vague consciousness.”
“You look like an operating human being,” she told school investigators at a hearing in May of 2025. ”You don’t look dead or asleep necessarily. So, lights are on, but nobody’s home. Your brain is not functioning at its proper level.”
She said some of the men inhaled drugs off her unclothed body.
“I felt like bait. I felt like lions around me. It just was a totally debilitating place to be in,” she told investigators.
Accused student says he only entered room for a wellness check
One of the men the woman accused of snorting drugs off her body — but not participating in other elements of the assault — denied her account.
He told investigators he was in the room for no more than five minutes, and didn’t go there for sex.
“That was not our intentions at all. We were just checking out to see if everything” was OK, he said.
He insisted that he did not see the woman naked at any time — she was under bed coverings, he said — and did not partake in drug use. He said he sat on a couch and chatted for a few minutes, then left after the woman and another man there both indicated they were all right.
A Cornell disciplinary panel later cleared him of sexual assault or exploitation allegations, but found him responsible for attempted sexual exploitation because it didn’t believe his claim to have gone to the room for altruistic reasons.
The fraternity member, who is challenging Cornell’s disciplinary process in court, also posted in the Snapchat conversation, saying what was happening in the room was not a joke, adding: “Firsthand pov not a bit.” The student later told investigators he did not remember sending the message, according to Cornell’s account.
Woman’s lawsuit seeks tougher penalties
In her lawsuit, Jane Doe accused two of the other men who entered the room of performing sex acts on her without her consent, while she was partially incapacitated. She accused another man of kissing her without her consent. According to the Title IX documents, Jane Doe told investigators two other men stood at the foot of the bed acting “more like voyeurs than anything.”
The lawsuit seeks to hold all seven men liable for rape. She is asking for unspecified damages.
Cornell hasn’t detailed the results of its investigation, but said it resulted in some students being expelled.
The man who filed the lawsuit challenging his punishment was allowed to stay at Cornell, but he was ordered to stay away from the woman, take a class on sexual harassment and bystander intervention, and write a paper reflecting on the circumstances for which he was found responsible and include a proposal to train other students on preventing sexual harassment.

title: ‘I just want to be a child again’: Boy overcomes rare condition through stem cell transplant
text:
NEW ORLEANS (WVUE/Gray News) - A boy from Gulfport, Mississippi, is dreaming big after receiving what doctors call a lifesaving stem cell transplant.
Peyton Stewart is an 11-year-old with big dreams. One of them is to play in the NBA. It’s a dream the staff at Manning Family Children’s hospital quickly learned about when Stewart arrived there in 2024 suffering from a rare mutation called STAT1 gain-of-function.
“At that time, we didn’t know the cause of it. We knew his red blood cells were getting destroyed, but we didn’t know why,” said Dr. Benjamin Watkins, pediatric hematology oncologist at Manning Family Children’s Hospital.
Stewart’s doctor said the condition caused his immune system to attack his own red blood cells, and his only hope for a cure was a bone marrow transplant. Stewart’s older brother, Acie, was a match for the procedure. Their mom worried.
“It touched my heart to see the siblings pull together like that, and I was nervous during the process because I had two children going through something at the same time,” said Laurie Stewart, Peyton Stewart’s mother.
During the six months Peyton Stewart spent at the hospital, he seemingly won over everybody, including its CEO, who found himself going one-on-one with the aspiring hooper.
“Somewhere along the way, he stopped being a kiddo I visited in the hospital, and he became my buddy. We played basketball, me not very well, so he taught me a lot,” said Lucio Fragoso, president and CEO of Manning Family Children’s Hospital.
On Thursday (Oct. 1), the hospital held a special bell ringing ceremony exactly one year after Peyton underwent the life-changing transplant. With a basketball hoop, brass band and a room full of hospital staff, Peyton rang the bell celebrating his so-called “re-birthday.”
Sitting just a few feet from the second line, Stewart’s grandmother Yvonne Hill thought of just how far he has come and what he said when he was sick.
“He said, ‘I just want to be a child again...I want to go to school,’” said Hill.
When Peyton took the podium during the ceremony, he thanked the brother that made the moment possible.
“Acie, thank you for being brave and helping me get better. I love you,” he said.
There weren’t many dry eyes among the people who took care of him.
“Thank you for helping me through the hard days and giving me reasons to smile. You held my mom too and made us feel like family,” Peyton told the hospital staff.
Peyton’s doctor said his immune system is now healthy, and there’s not much holding him back. He told the crowd he’s ready to take a shot at his new life.
“Today, ringing this bell means I get to look forward to being home, playing basketball and following my dreams, including becoming the future CEO of Manning Family Children’s Hospital, only after my NBA career, of course,” he said.
Stewart’s father, Christopher Stewart, said he feels fortunate his son now has the possibility of pursuing dreams.
“He’s obsessed with the NBA. I’m hoping for a CEO, but chances are it’s going to be the NBA,” he said.
Whatever path Peyton chooses, he’ll have support from the home team.
“He’s just full of life, and I just love to see him just be him. I just love it,” said Stewart’s grandmother.

title: Pets of the Week
Editorial cartoon on write-in voting was misleading
text:
I’m writing to set the record straight after your misleading editorial cartoon on Sept. 20. Thanks to ranked-choice voting, if a voter casts a write-in vote, whether for the declared write-ins or Graham Platner, and votes for Troy Jackson as their second choice, Jackson can win.
Susan Collins needs to win by 50.01% of all votes cast. She only won last time with 50.98% of total first-place votes cast. The senator is even more unpopular this time, given her 95% voting record with Donald Trump, her support for tax breaks for billionaires paid for by cuts to health insurance subsidies and her vote to confirm Brett Kavanaugh.
And, if she’s so important as chair of Appropriations, why is Alaska getting more congressional spending per capita than Maine?
A big turnout of Platner supporters who would otherwise not vote would be most helpful in defeating Sen. Collins.
Karen Heck
Waterville

title: Thieves steal almost entire field of pumpkins from first-year family farm
text:
CAPRON, Ill. (WIFR/Gray News) - A family farm has cut pumpkin season short after owners say a major theft wiped out the remainder of its unharvested crops.
Last week in a Facebook post, Meyers Family Farm in Illinois said thieves entered its field and stole almost all of its pumpkins. This included only regular orange ones, as other specialty pumpkins were already harvested.
The farm says after the recent theft, it will no longer be able to participate in pumpkin picking at this year’s Boone County Farm Stroll.
As a first-year farm, owners shared they did not carry crop insurance. Despite this, they plan to continue looking to the future.
“Financially, this is not a setback for our farm. We will continue to move forward, learn from this season, and prepare for the next. However, what hurts the most is thinking about the families and children who could have enjoyed these pumpkins, spent time outdoors, and made memories with us and their families,” the post said.
The farm also says these pumpkin thefts continue to affect multiple farms in the Poplar Grove and Capron area.
Owners say the best thing the community can do is to keep an eye out around area farms and report anything suspicious to police, as well as continue to support local farmers.
