title: A pulse of warm water hitting the Pacific coast could mean erosion and flooding
text:
SEATTLE (AP) — Sea levels along the West Coast will begin to rise by up to a foot this month as a series of pulses of warm water called Kelvin waves hit the shoreline and move north, sparking concerns about beach erosion and flooding in areas already impacted by climate change and El Niño.
Kelvin waves are not like tsunamis, and they don’t curl over and crash on the beach. A better image is water sloshing in the bathtub or a swimming pool during an earthquake. In the ocean, they are bulges of water that lift the sea level as they move along the coast. They’re common during El Niño events, but this year’s super El Niño could intensify the impacts, experts say.
Over the next week, the 6-inch to foot-tall surge will move north along the California coast at about 6 miles per hour (9.6 kilometers per hour), or 150 miles per day (241 kilometers per day), bringing higher sea levels to Oregon and Washington state. Experts predict the waves will continue to pass through from October until February.
“It’s not that this Kelvin wave is going to come and flood anything on its own,” said Michael Jacox, a research oceanographer with National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration Fisheries’ Ecosystem Science Division.
Instead, it raises the baseline.
If you start with sea levels that are 6 inches higher than normal, when you have really high tides, big storms or storm surges, the water levels are now 6 inches higher, he said. “The effects can be amplified,” he said.
The waves also increase ocean temperatures and push cold, nutrient-rich waters deeper below the surface, which has an impact on marine life.
Here’s what to know about Kelvin waves.
How does a Kelvin wave form?
Kelvin waves are a “fact of life” during an El Niño, a naturally occurring climate pattern involving the warming ocean waters, said Dillon Amaya, an assistant professor in the Department of Marine, Earth, and Atmospheric Sciences at North Carolina State University.
They form when the trade winds along the equator change direction.
Winds blowing east to west along the equator push water in the Pacific Ocean west toward Asia, Jacox said. When those winds weaken or reverse direction, that bulge of water gets pushed back toward the east along the equator until it hits South America.
When the surge of water hits the coastline at the equator, it moves north and south along the North and South American coasts.
The wave isn’t visible to the naked eye and they won’t cause boats to go up and down, Amaya said. It’s more like a big pancake. It’s wider than it’s deep: The bulge extends 12 to 20 miles (19 to 32 kilometers) off the coast and about 200 meters deep, Amaya said.
What are the potential impacts of Kelvin waves?
Many coastal communities are already grappling with the impacts of rising sea levels, like the coastal erosion eating away at the beach in San Clemente, California. Waves are also getting bigger, experts say.
The higher sea levels could exacerbate those problems.
“People are on edge,” Amaya said. “They think about more flooding happening, more beach erosion so when you hear elevated sea states coastal inundation risk, I think that raises a lot of anxiety.”
The higher sea level combined with larger than average waves from North Pacific swell, which are expected during the El Niño, plus large spring tides from October to February, can cause exceptional erosion on the West Coast, said Sean Vitousek, a research oceanographer with the U.S. Geological Survey.
Generally, the largest El Niño events of 1982-83, 1997-98 and 2015-16 caused West Coast beaches to experience their worst erosion on record, Vitousek said.
“The loss of protective beaches also increases wave impacts and coastal flooding on property and infrastructure,” he said.
Things could intensify over time as more waves arrive over the winter.
Typically El Niños are associated with five or six of these waves, Amaya said. During the last major El Niño in 2015-2016 there were five Kelvin waves.
One already came through in May or June and there’s evidence of a third Kelvin wave forming, he said. Experts expect it to continue up the coast over the next month or so.
How are states responding to concerns about higher sea levels?
There’s concern the waves could worsen challenges along the Southern California coast, said Alyssa Napuri, deputy chief of staff for Orange County Supervisor Katrina Foley. Already, waves are approaching a seaside rail line and oceanfront homes were damaged during swells last month tied to Hurricane Marie.
Authorities are placing emergency sand on beaches as quickly as possible, Napuri said, adding that forecasts show the Kelvin Wave could send water levels between six to 12 inches higher.
“We’re already struggling as it is,” Napuri said.
California Gov. Gavin Newsom, a Democrat, proclaimed a state of emergency in late September to prepare the state for what will likely be a historic El Niño season. The proclamation will help the state “move faster to protect communities, stage critical resources, and strengthen readiness before severe weather intensifies,” the governor said in a statement.
Experts with the Washington state Department of Natural Resources are ready to respond to any disasters that might come with the Kelvin waves, said spokesperson Courtney James. They regularly coordinate through the state Emergency Management Division but they have not been asked to do any special preparation so far, she said.
Actual damages from the Kelvin waves will depend on the storms and tides magnified by El Niño, and if they’re stronger, the damage could be significant, Amaya said.
“It’s too too early to be sure whether this particular winter season will be a record breaker in terms of this El Niño, but this El Niño itself is certainly on that trajectory of being one of the largest if not the largest El Niño we’ve ever seen,” he said.
__
Associated Press reporter Amy Taxin contributed to this story from Santa Ana, California.

title: With two big defensive plays, Carter Moody helps Thornton football earn a big win
text:
SACO — There’s Carter Moody, stretched out to all of his 6-foot-3, practically horizontal to the Hill Stadium turf. The Thornton Academy junior is in the process of making the play of the game. Moody blocks Justin Bouchard’s try for a 33-yard field goal in the final minute of the first half, preserving his team’s one-point lead.
It’s the second time in the first half of this pivotal game against Portland that Moody makes the play of the game for the Golden Trojans. Late in the first quarter, with the Bulldogs threatening to turn a one-touchdown lead into a two-touchdown lead, Moody is there to fall on the ball inside his 5-yard line as Josiah Blain knocks it from Portland’s Alex Martin with a strong tackle.
This game between the teams that played in the last three Class A state championship games (won by Thornton in 2023, by Portland in 2024, and by the Trojans again last November) was a battle of two undefeated teams trying to reach another state final. For a half, it was as close as you’d expect. Eventually, Thornton wore down the Bulldogs. A one-point game at the half became a 43-13 blowout.
Moody was a big reason why his team clung to a one-point halftime lead. An all-SMAA defensive back last season as a sophomore, Moody is enjoying a bigger role this season.
“His role has increased. He’s on offense, defense, special teams. He made some great plays. He’s a great tackler,” Thornton coach Kevin Kezal said of Moody.
Portland scored quickly and with little resistance on the game’s first drive, with Martin leading the strong ground game. The Bulldogs were on the verge of putting the Trojans in a two-touchdown hole, a place with which they are unfamiliar, when Blain’s hit dislodged the ball in the final minute of the first quarter, inside Thornton’s 5-yard line.
Moody was there to pounce on the ball, evaporating the threat. He didn’t know who caused the fumble, only that it happened, and he needed to get the ball.
“It was right there in front of me and I just fell on it,” Moody said. “We battle. We stay strong. No matter where we are on the field.”
With Thornton up 14-13, the Bulldogs drove, and looked poised to take the lead just before the first half ended. Bouchard has the leg for the 33-yard field goal try. Before the play, Moody and teammate Brennan Tabor had a quick chat.
“(Tabor) was lined up next to me, and said ‘You go as tight as you can, and I’m going to try and take (the blockers) on so you’ve got a free shot,'” Moody said.
Then Moody described what happened in short, simple sentences, as if he was outlining a series of snapshots taken after the snap.
“It worked. I got around them. No one touched me. (I) put two hands up. Laid out. Blocked it. It felt amazing,” He said. “They were driving on us, but getting that stop right before halftime really helped us in the locker room.”
The Trojans spend a lot of time on special teams, both Moody and Kezal said. It’s something the team takes seriously and to heart. It was Moody’s first blocked kick, and it couldn’t have come at a better time. He held momentum in his outstretched body.
“Obviously, Carter is one of our best players, and he made a great play. It’s nice when the ball is on the hash because you have a better chance (to block it) with the angle,” Kezal said. “He took a good angle, and it was a huge play to get us into halftime with a lead.”
With two teams who have a recent history of playing big games against each other, don’t be surprised if Thornton and Portland meet again at Fitzpatrick Stadium on the Saturday before Thanksgiving.
“We knew somebody was going home with a loss,” Moody said.
With two big defensive plays in the first half, Moody helped ensure that wouldn’t be his team.

title: Calling for sanity from my sickbed in Maine
text:
Bill Hiss lives in Lewiston.
It does seem odd to be writing an op-ed from a hospital bed, with ninth-floor views to Mount Washington, and people bustling to and fro night and day. Being a healer here is like serving on a submarine: tiny spaces, machinery everywhere and staff maneuvering past each other.
But perhaps it’s a helpful time for a literal grayhead — I am 82 — to share three thoughts while attached to an IV pole.
First, seeing the staff at Maine Medical Center is a blunt reminder of how utterly insane, cruel and counterproductive for America is this federal administration’s hostility to immigrants. At least as I see them at work, perhaps 10%-20% of the doctors, 30%-40% of the RNs, 70% of the LPNs and the vast majority of the support staff of housekeepers, food staff, etc., are immigrants.
Hope to stay alive? Get meds at 2 a.m.? Need food brought to your bedside? Pay attention, folks: immigrants are doing much of the work we need to stay alive.
Within the last hour, I was seen by two infectious disease physicians, one an immigrant from Vietnam, the other from an Arab country, who will care for me over the six-week treatment for a spine infection. As a minister, I see the same pattern in hospitals, rehab centers and nursing homes: the immigrants are irreplaceable labor. The same is true of agricultural workers, meat packing, hospitality, restaurants, truck drivers and countless other fields.
Second, being caught in the tragic contractions of Central Maine Medical Center for nine weeks before being referred to Maine Medical Center has been a (literal) painful reminder that perhaps it is time to rethink our medical delivery system.
I have a fine education, can get information, can afford medical expenses and have a high-end Medicare Advantage policy. But all summer I was caught in one communication or insurance snafu after another. This federal administration and our for-profit insurance industry have their fingers around our throats. If I cannot figure it out with my advantages, what in God’s name are the 70%-80% of America’s lower economic bands to do when faced with a serious medical problem?
Third, seeing the barrage of negative TV ads reminds me that hopefully sooner — by
November — we will need to find common-sense, middle-ground spaces in our social contracts. Tragically for America, President Trump’s view of the world is based on his own mental illness of narcissism, hatreds, racism, insults, pathological incessant lying, policy ignorance and the instincts of a lifelong real estate con man. 
Equally tragic, the Republicans in Congress have been almost completely compliant with his daily whims, disrupting everything from fuel and food prices to international treaties to respect for our constitutional protections. Every day a new threat, a new distraction: masked and armed ICE officers at polling places, snipers on his garish monument to himself, threats to our closest allies, all while he and his family are raking in billions in illegal sweetheart deals.
Two of my fellow Lewiston citizens, running as Republicans for higher office, have yard signs that are purple, and one of these fellow citizens told me when she knocked on my door that this was deliberate, to try to send a signal that she hoped people would see her as a moderate. Well, I would like to believe so.
These two women are not MAGA cartoons spewing hate; they have worked faithfully in their current public offices. But how are we to interpret their candidacies in the light of Sen. Susan Collins claiming to be a moderate, while voting for what Trump wanted 95% of the time? My hope is that they will demonstrate clearly a rejection of MAGA cruelty and illegality.
And yes, if they are elected, I hope to offer thoughts on how we find more sensible middle ground for our country.

title: A quieter weekend weather wise with frosty conditions possible, rain possible Monday
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Two calm days with comfortable highs and some chilly lows but overall a really spectacular fall weekend for the entire region. More turbulent weather arrives Monday into the workweek with rain possible and gusty winds following it but enjoy this weekend while you can because fall colors are in full bloom and the temps will be very comfortable and sunshine will dominate.
Today: Chilly start then sunshine all around
After a chilly start it will be a picture perfect fall day out today. Highs will be in the upper 50s to low 60s for most with abundant sunshine. Winds will light out of the NW at 5-10 mph.
Tonight: Frosty to freeze conditions especially to the north.
Temps will drop into the 30s for most tonight and some cold spots way up north may see a few 20s on the thermometer. While growing season has ended if you do have any plants left out now is the time to bring them in.
Sunday: Very similar day with a colder start
The spots that see frost on Sunday morning will likely rebound quickly as the sun comes out quickly Sunday morning. Few clouds if any will be visible on Sunday across the state. As I mentioned, this is the weekend to get out and see the leaves or enjoy a fall festival or football game! Highs mainly in the low 60s with light winds.
Sunday night: Clouds arrive ahead of next system
It will cloud up and stay relatively warm on Sunday night ahead of our next system which will arrive on Monday. Winds will also pick up out of the SW at 10-15 mph overnight.
Monday and beyond: Rain possible on Monday followed by gusty winds.
Rain may arrive in the early on Monday but there is still a good amount of uncertainty in terms of when and how much rain we will get on Monday across the region as a cold front moves through. What is looking quite likely however is Tuesday is looking quite breezy and will knock a large number of leaves off the trees and being some colder temps as well.
Today: Sun all around, highs mostly in the low 60s. Winds NW at 5-10 mph
Tonight: Quite chilly with lows in the 30s and low 40s. Winds light.
Tomorrow: Another sun filled day. Highs near 60. Winds NW at 5-10 mph
Sunday night: Not as cold and clouds arrive. Lows near 50. Winds SW at 10-15 mph
Monday: Showers arrive with general cloudiness. Highs near 60. Winds SW at 10-15 mph.

title: Marine veteran to receive new home built on National Mall
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - A 76-year-old Marine Corps veteran is set to receive a brand new home built in just seven days on the National Mall.
The 480-square-foot modular home is being constructed piece by piece on America’s Front Lawn, in full public view of visitors to the nation’s capital.
“It’s been a great experience to be here on the National Mall and watching this home coming together and knowing that it’s going to be mine,” said Jim Taylor, the veteran receiving the home.
Taylor was nominated and chosen to receive the home from Purple Heart Homes, an organization dedicated to building safe, affordable housing for veterans. He said the decision came as a surprise.
“I was like, oh really? Why?” Taylor said.
The founders of Purple Heart Homes were on hand to walk Jim through the building process, explaining how the build symbolizes more than just a house.
“Every veteran just wants to be at home,” said John Gallina with Purple Heart Homes.
“They want to have a safe, accessible home that’s not going to cause them worries, that’s going to be affordable for them. And that’s what these homes represent,” Gallina said.
Taylor works with veterans in North Carolina on a daily basis and has seen firsthand the housing struggles of many.
“I work at a place called Fifth Street Ministries… and we have homeless veterans sleeping five beds to one room,” Taylor said. “People don’t realize that many veterans need help.”
The final unveiling of the finished home is Monday. The home will then be loaded up and sent to Glasgow, Va., where Taylor will move into his new neighborhood.

title: Woman accused of allowing doctor to sexually assault child at least 10 times in exchange for Adderall
text:
TYLER, Texas. (KLTV/Gray News) - A Texas woman allegedly took a child to a doctor, allowing him to sexually assault the child in exchange for Adderall, according to authorities.
Alicia Evonne Sanchez, 37, was arrested Wednesday and charged with continuous sexual assault of a child under 14.
Sanchez is accused of bringing the minor to Dr. Kenneth Donald Haygood’s office on numerous occasions.
She allegedly allowed Haygood to sexually assault the child, during which she remained in the room, on at least 10 occasions. The child would cry and plead for him to stop but was ignored or told, “this is what doctors do.”
After the alleged assaults took place, the child reported in their outcry to another adult and a counselor that Haygood would give Sanchez Adderall pills, which Sanchez would place in a clear baggie.
She allegedly told the child that they were “for people who couldn’t get them from their doctor” or that there was a medication shortage.
Sanchez is being held on a $3 million bond.
Haygood was sentenced in 2025 to eight years in prison after pleading guilty to other sexual assaults.

title: Family dog euthanized after attacking and killing 3-year-old child, authorities say
text:
SULLIGENT, Ala. (WTVA/Gray News) — Authorities say a dog attacked and killed a toddler this week in Alabama.
The reported attack occurred on Friday morning at a home on Walnut Street in Sulligent, according to the Lamar County coroner.
Authorities said the dog attacked a 3-year-old boy, who later died at the hospital.
Sulligent Police Chief Michael Franklin said the boy’s family owned the dog.
After the attack, the family surrendered the animal to police, who took the dog to a veterinarian in Russellville for euthanasia.
Franklin said the health department ordered the euthanasia and testing of the dog.
Sulligent authorities did not say if any charges were expected to be filed in the case. The family was not immediately identified.

title: Thieves steal almost entire field of pumpkins from first-year family farm
text:
CAPRON, Ill. (WIFR/Gray News) - A family farm has cut pumpkin season short after owners say a major theft wiped out the remainder of its unharvested crops.
Last week in a Facebook post, Meyers Family Farm in Illinois said thieves entered its field and stole almost all of its pumpkins. This included only regular orange ones, as other specialty pumpkins were already harvested.
The farm says after the recent theft, it will no longer be able to participate in pumpkin picking at this year’s Boone County Farm Stroll.
As a first-year farm, owners shared they did not carry crop insurance. Despite this, they plan to continue looking to the future.
“Financially, this is not a setback for our farm. We will continue to move forward, learn from this season, and prepare for the next. However, what hurts the most is thinking about the families and children who could have enjoyed these pumpkins, spent time outdoors, and made memories with us and their families,” the post said.
The farm also says these pumpkin thefts continue to affect multiple farms in the Poplar Grove and Capron area.
Owners say the best thing the community can do is to keep an eye out around area farms and report anything suspicious to police, as well as continue to support local farmers.

title: Shop clerk, son charged with selling illegal kratom amid probe into Ole Miss student deaths
text:
MEMPHIS, Tenn. (WMC/Gray News) - Authorities investigating the deaths of two University of Mississippi students have charged a store clerk and his son with selling an illegal kratom product.
A new federal filing says a toxicology report on Aidan Hamilton and Robert Strang found the substances mitragynine, MGM-15 and MGPI in their systems.
Those same substances were found in “Smax Mango Breeze” pills that investigators found in both students’ rooms after their deaths.
Investigators allege that Puffs Vape, Tobacco and Beer Store in Oxford sold Hamilton the pills twice in the days before his death. Bank records show Hamilton made multiple purchases in September from the store, according to a federal court filing.
The toxicology details come from a motion from federal prosecutors to keep Yahya Mosleh, the manager of Puffs, and his 18-year-old son, Islam Mosleh, in custody.
Mosleh, 51, and his son appeared in federal court on Thursday, where a judge ruled there was probable cause to hand down federal charges against the pair.
In the motion, prosecutors describe the men as posing a danger to the community.
Last week, Lafayette County Metro Narcotics agents sent a confidential informant into Puffs Vape, Tobacco and Beer Store in Oxford to investigate alleged sales of illegal substances, according to the arrest affidavit.
The informant asked if the store sold “7-OH kratom-based pills.”
Records show Yahya Mosleh allegedly said yes before warning the informant to “be careful taking the pills, because people are dying from them.”
Oxford police then executed a search warrant at the store, and 500 units of kratom and kratom-like products were seized. An assortment of “THC cartridges, gummies, pre-rolls and other suspected THC substances” was also recovered.
During the search, detectives found the same brand of Smax Mango Breeze MGM-15, with identical packaging, ingredients and a $39.99 price tag with a smudge on the 9, that had been found near Hamilton.
Prosecutors noted that Islam Mosleh, who attends Oxford High School, had previously drawn complaints from a school resource officer who suspected that Mosleh was selling THC vapes to students at the school. Similar vapes were found in Islam Mosleh’s pockets and backpack.
The Moslehs face federal charges of possession of a controlled substance with intent to distribute. Their attorneys told WMC they have no comment.
When WMC was at the scene of the vape shop on Friday night, four different people tried to walk in, only to be met with a note that the shop is closed until further notice.
Jimmy, who works at Heritage Wine & Liquor next door, said he came to work Thursday at 1 p.m. to a parking lot full of law enforcement and narcotics officers.
He said an employee told him a young man, assumed to be Islam Mosleh, tried to run when police arrived, though he didn’t see it himself.
“As a former college professor, it’s heartbreaking. They get to be not children, but kind of like surrogate children,” Jimmy said. “My bottom line is that I’m not going to say what they did. That’s none of my business. The law will determine that in time, but the loss of young people like that is a terrible tragedy.”
Angelica McKinney, who lives nearby, said she was shocked to learn the store at the center of the investigation was in her neighborhood.
“When I first heard that it was this store here, I was shocked because a lot of people do come here to buy what they need out of here,” McKinney said.
McKinney said she wasn’t necessarily surprised to hear an 18-year-old was accused of selling THC-type vapes.
“Nowadays, kids at the age of 18 think they know it all... Of course there’s something they’re gonna consider if it’s easy money, right?” she said.
She urged parents to have hard conversations about mental health and peer pressure:
“Kids are dealing with depression. So, right now, they’re literally trying to find any and everything to cope with whatever they have going on. So parents just be open to what’s going on with these children nowadays.”
While officials believe it was the Oxford store that sold Hamilton the narcotics found in his system, they say Strang bought his pills from a different store outside the county 20 miles away.
Investigators have not yet said if they’ve determined exactly what killed either student.
Hamilton was laid to rest in Denver on Friday.

title: Victoria Mansion kicks off Halloween season in Portland with ‘Bizarre Bazaar’
text:
PORTLAND —The Victoria Mansion isn’t haunted. At least, that’s what Stacia Hanscom, director of education and public programs, says.
But the mansion, a mid-19th century national historic landmark, welcomed spirits Saturday for a one-day fair to kick off the Halloween season. Featuring divination, a spooky poem performance, a visit from Dracula and more, visitors came to “A Bizarre Victorian Bazaar: An Exhibition of Oddities and the Obscure” to immerse themselves in the October mood and learn about a lesser known side of Victorian history — the gothic.
“It’s looking at the oddities and the things that we think are strange today, but that the Victorians believed in and tried,” Hanscom said. “They were experimenting.”
A costumed juggler paced around the mansion’s lawn, throwing pins. People lined up for tarot card readings and fortune telling under a tent. A mummy, which a party of Victorians would have been eager to unwrap, lay inside for viewing.
Bunny Rose, a tarot cart reader from Gorham, shuffled her deck of tarot cards and spread them out on the table.
She said the Victorians used tarot cards and other forms of divination to explore the rise of spiritualism. Some wanted to connect to people they had lost in the Civil War, and others were trying to bridge the gap between traditional religion and emerging science, Rose explained.
Katherine Doughty facilitated a divination reading called automatic drawing, where she placed a black cloth over a client’s hand and let them blindly draw on a paper underneath, letting their subconscious guide them. In the Victorian era, a medium would have done an automatic drawing themselves after connecting to a spirit.
“There’s a feeling the whole Halloween season, what we call ‘in between the worlds,'” Doughty said. “There’s more electricity and energy; there’s more opportunity for that in this time.”
A “cabinet of curiosities” stocked with keys, miniature mirrors, shells, dollhouse furniture, tiny shoes and other small treasures demonstrated “the hoarding nature of Victorian life” and a “mishmash of ideas,” said Anatole Brown from the Dyer Library and Saco Museum.
He said a few of the objects were “signs of death,” including a corvid skull, or a crow’s skull.
“A corvid skull is a definite form of occultism,” Brown said.
By the lawn’s edge, a basket of tiny “fire lighters” filled up as Andrew Harris repeatedly demonstrated how to fold the particularly flammable contraptions out of newspapers, which were “everywhere” and cheap in Victorian days.
Harris, who usually impersonates Charles Dickens, multitasked, also reading Penny Dreadfuls —cheap, serial literature produced in Great Britain — to interested passersby. The subjects of the stories were sensational, focused on crime or the supernatural. Since many Victorians were illiterate, people would read them out loud on the street for pennies.
Using the full range of his dynamic actor’s voice, Harris read a passage from the perspective of a dead man who had just been buried.
“If he (a Victorian) was a good reader, he could make a living at it,” Harris said. “A penny would have gone a long way.”
Not every part of the event was ominous. Sullivan House Bakery brought Victorian-themed treats, namely a “Victoria Sponge,” and costume designer Anna Halloran presented on Victorian fashion.
Nancy Noble, having just finished an oracle card reading, said it made her feel optimistic. She retired four months ago and is in a time of transition. Unlike a Victorian, she took a picture of her result with her phone to further study it later.
“I liked that it wasn’t like, here’s a death card,” Noble said.

title: Boston Bruins fall to Wild in Minnesota
text:
ST. PAUL, Minn. — Kirill Kaprizov scored twice, Jesper Wallstedt made 26 saves, and the Minnesota Wild beat the Boston Bruins 4-1 on Saturday night.
Quinn Hughes had a goal and assist, and Jared Spurgeon also scored.
With the win, Minnesota improved to 18-4-4 in home openers and its .769 points percentage in those games is second-best in the NHL to Vegas, which is at .850 while going 8-1-1.
Tanner Jeannot scored for Boston, which won 4-3 in overtime at Winnipeg Friday, and allowed just three goals in winning its first two games.
Michael DiPietro made 26 saves for the Bruins in his third career start and first since Jan. 23, 2022, with Vancouver. The 2025-26 American Hockey League MVP with Providence, he led the league with 34 wins, a 1.91 goals-against average and .930 save percentage.
Eight different Wild players had points on Saturday after nine did so in Thursday’s 3-1 season-opening win at Nashville.
Kaprizov tied the game 1-1 with a power-play goal six minutes into the second period, converting a feed from Maxim Shabanov.
He added an empty-net tally with 1:01 to play for his third goal of the season and 11th in eight career games against the Bruins.
Minnesota had a five-on-three power play for 1:52 midway through the second period. Hughes scored with one second left on the latter infraction with a wrist shot that went through Ryan Hartman’s screen for a 2-1 lead.
Boston was scoreless on four power-play chances. Minnesota has killed off all eight short-handed situations through two games after allowing none in the preseason.
Spurgeon added a goal early in the third period with a shot that changed direction off the skate off Nikita Zadorov.
Jeannot scored put the Bruins up 1-0 less than two minutes into the game, converting a touch pass from Mark Kastelic.
Up next
Bruins: Home against Ottawa on Monday night.
Wild: At Buffalo on Tuesday to begin a three-game road trip.

title: Maine men's basketball preps for season ahead
Two firefighters who died following Searsmont explosion among those honored at annual Firefighters Memorial
text:
Two firefighters who died following Searsmont explosion among those honored at annual Firefighters Memorial
The 29th annual Maine Firefighter Memorial Service was held in Augusta on Saturday and organizers say this year's event carried a heavy weight.
It comes after the fire and explosion at Robbins Lumber in Searsmont in May. It led to the deaths of Wayne Woodbury and Andrew Cross.
"9/11 was special. The 25th anniversary we had here of 25 years of 9/11 and today are the biggest three events we've had in 29 years," commented President of the Maine Federation of Firefighters Ken Desmond.
55 names of those who wore the firefighting uniform in the state and lost their lives in the past year were read, followed by the ringing of a bell.
The names of Cross and Woodbury came before four series of five ringings of the bell representing a death in the line of duty.
"Caring for those who still answer the call is one way that we can honor those who no longer can," commented Maine Fire Marshal Shawn Esler. "But today, above all, is about the people we miss. Let us remember how they lived, not how we lost them."
Many state fire leaders spoke at Saturday's event. At times, speakers highlighted who the two victims were as people, not just how they lived their lives.
"We remember Andrew and Wayne," said Liberty Fire Chief and President of the Maine Fire Chiefs Association Bill Gillespie. "A lot of us knew them personally. Knew their sense of humor. Knew how they acted on fires, knew their little quirks, and we were grateful for that opportunity to know them. But we're still dealing with the pain."
Several speakers also commented on the changes the state and fire departments can make in the future. Some pointed towards the upcoming session in Augusta and legislative changes they intend to advocate for, including further funding and training.

title: Trump urges calls to senator’s personal cellphone in push for permanent daylight saving time
text:
(AP) - President Donald Trump on Saturday pressured Republican Sen. Tom Cotton of Arkansas to support a bill to make daylight saving time permanent, posting the personal cellphone number of the chairman of Senate Intelligence Committee and urging Americans to call it.
The Sunshine Protection Act passed the House in July, but it faces roadblocks in the Senate where some Republicans are strongly opposed. Proponents, including the White House, argue that the change would provide more daylight during the times that Americans are most active. Detractors said permanent daylight saving time would lead to darker and potentially more hazardous winter mornings when children will be waiting for school buses and parents will be driving to work in darkness.
It was a remarkable escalation on Trump’s part of a longstanding fixation shared by both men — with Trump supporting making daylight saving time permanent, and Cotton vociferously opposed — at a time just weeks before the midterms, when Republicans would prefer that the president focus on talking about affordability issues and the party’s achievements. Cotton is also up for reelection this November, although that race is not expected to be competitive.
Trump calls daylight saving time ‘depressing’
Daylight saving time is that period between spring and fall when clocks in most parts of the United States are set one hour ahead of standard time. Not all states observe it — and under the bill, states can opt out of the change if their respective legislatures act to do so before the bill’s enactment.
“It’s a lot of work for a lot of people, running around for two days, changing all the clocks in the house,” Trump told reporters as his left the White House on Saturday for a rally in Vandalia, Ohio. “It discombobulates everybody,” he said.
Trump said the time change gives golfers less time on the greens and tennis players less time on the courts. He blamed Cotton for stopping the bill. “So, everyone in Arkansas, a State I love, and won 3 times, the last by by 34 points, tell Tom to, GET IT DONE! It will be appreciated by all,” Trump said on social media on Saturday morning, kicking off the fight.
Trump included a phone number with an Arkansas area code. The Associated Press called the number, but no one answered and the voicemail box was full.
Cotton, a member of Republican leadership, reiterated his opposition to permanent daylight saving time in a social media post of his own Saturday afternoon. He is not the only GOP senator who opposes the policy, though he has been among the most vocal opponents.
“No one likes changing the clock, me included, but Congress has enacted permanent Daylight Savings Time multiple times before and repealed it each time once Americans experienced absurdly late sunrises in the winter,” Cotton wrote. “Arkansans don’t want their kids going to school in the pitch dark, and I’ll always put Arkansas first.”
The fight over changing the clock went on all Saturday
Trump promptly fired back in another post. “If Tom Cotton were putting Arkansas first, he would give them an extra hour of daylight and, more importantly, they wouldn’t have to run all over their houses, farms, work places, and everywhere else, twice a year, having to change their Clocks, and often forgetting to do so,” Trump said, adding that “that is really putting Arkansas FIRST.”
As his motorcade was rolling back to the White House from his golf course, Trump added that “a table full of very distinguished people just told me that they HATE, immediately after a mandatory time change, going home at night – and it’s DARK.”
“It’s depressing!” Trump continued. “One of the gentleman stated that, ‘I just hate going home in darkness.’ It’s also, in Crime Ridden Blue States, a lot more dangerous to be walking home in the dark!”
A 2025 poll from The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research shows that if forced to choose, most Americans would prefer to keep that extra hour of daylight in the evening. Only 12% of U.S. adults favor the current system of daylight saving time, which requires people in most states to change their clocks twice a year, while 47% oppose it and 40% are neutral.
Members of Congress have long been interested in the potential benefits and costs of daylight saving time since it was first adopted as a wartime measure in 1942. The Senate passed a bill four years ago to make daylight saving time permanent, but it stalled in the House.
This is not the first time Trump has released personal information about a senator
While competing for the 2016 Republican presidential nomination, the late Sen. Lindsey Graham of South Carolina described Trump as “unfit for office” after Trump denigrated the military service of Sen. John McCain of Arizona. Trump then released Graham’s personal cellphone number. That prompted a viral video in which the senator dramatically destroyed a series of flip phones.
Graham later became a close ally of Trump. In contrast, although they share many of the same policy positions, Trump and Cotton are not known to be close.
Cotton, one of the Republican Party’s most prominent national security voices, has advocated for a more hawkish approach on Iran, particularly as Trump entertains pauses in military strikes amid the seven-month war. In Trump’s first term, Cotton was a critic of the president’s attempts at overhauling the nation’s sentencing laws, calling the proposal a “jailbreak.”
Earlier this year, Cotton had temporarily defied Trump’s attempts at stalling the confirmation process for his own nominee for director of national intelligence, Jay Clayton. The president had wanted to ensure his interim pick for the intelligence job, Bill Pulte, would be able to serve in that role at least briefly when the former director, Tulsi Gabbard, left the job.
But the appointment of Pulte, who had no known national security credentials, drew bipartisan condemnation from Capitol Hill and Cotton had tried to expedite Clayton’s confirmation process, which could have prevented Pulte from being installed as acting director.
But Trump ultimately ordered Clayton to not appear before Cotton’s committee for his confirmation hearing, and Pulte served in the job for several weeks this summer. Clayton was eventually confirmed by the Senate in late July.
___
Associated Press writer Mary Clare Jalonick in Washington contributed to this report.

title: Tennessee’s prisons chief is resigning after failed execution of Christa Pike, governor says
text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (AP) — The head of Tennessee’s prison system is resigning, Gov. Bill Lee announced Saturday, the first major staff shake-up since Christa Pike’s stunning failed execution left her unconscious and on a ventilator at a hospital.
Frank Strada, commissioner of the Department of Correction, will step down this month, Lee said. Some of the governor’s fellow Republicans and other elected officials had been urging a change in leadership.
It was the second time since May that Tennessee has not been able to execute a prisoner who was seemingly moments away from death.
The governor also announced that former U.S. Attorney Ed Stanton would lead a review of what happened in Pike’s death chamber. Stanton previously was named to conduct a review after Lee called off a different execution in 2022; he found in that case that Tennessee had not complied with its own lethal injection process.
Strada said in a statement that resigning was “in the best interest of Tennesseans” while Stanton’s review is conducted. The state failed to execute Pike despite administering two doses of a lethal drug, pentobarbital.
Pike, now 50, was 18 when she and her boyfriend tortured and killed a classmate, Colleen Slemmer, in a jealous rage in 1995. She became one of the youngest women to be sent to death row.
Strada defends execution protocol
There was no immediate response from Pike’s lawyers for an update Saturday on her condition at a hospital. They had disclosed Friday that she was on a ventilator and unconscious in the hours following the execution attempt and that hospital staff were trying to clear the two doses of pentobarbital.
The shocking failure has left both sides of the death penalty debate demanding answers. Lee has ordered an independent review and halted any new executions. Strada said he believes the state “carried out its responsibilities in accordance with the established protocol.”
Pike’s legal team welcomed Strada’s departure but said “it does nothing to help Christa now.”
“What happened to her Wednesday reflects a systemic failure that goes far beyond any one person,” the four-lawyer team said. “We hope the governor’s call for a full, independent review will expose the profound problems within Tennessee’s entire death penalty system.”
Second failed execution since May
Pike’s attorneys said they believed problems with the IV lines caused the pentobarbital to flow into her body instead of her bloodstream.
Pike was extraordinarily cooperative with the execution team, even instructing them to “please try here, please try here” as they tried to insert lines, lawyer Randy Spivey told reporters Thursday.
In May, Tennessee stopped the execution of Tony Carruthers after staff placed an IV into his right arm but couldn’t get a secondary IV line. The governor ordered officials to wait at least a year before trying to execute him again.
Strada took over the Correction Department in January 2023 after serving as deputy director of the Arizona Department of Corrections. In late 2024, he announced that Tennessee was changing its lethal injection protocol and would use only pentobarbital.
Four people have been executed in Tennessee since 2025, according to the Correction Department.
Some Arizona executions had snags
Court filings show that Strada’s job included overseeing executions in Arizona when they resumed in 2022 following an eight-year break.
Clarence Dixon was the first that year. The medical team had trouble finding a vein to administer the lethal drugs and finally made an incision in his groin area. The process took about 25 minutes.
That same year in Arizona, medical staff preparing Frank Atwood for execution initially could not locate a vein in his right arm but inserted the IV in his right hand — at Atwood’s suggestion, said Henry Brean, an Arizona Daily Star reporter who was a witness.
Strada announced Murray Hooper’s execution by lethal injection, the third in 2022. There was an unsuccessful attempt to insert an IV line in his right arm. The IV in Hooper’s leg was inserted into his femoral artery.
“When Governor Lee hired Strada to fix execution problems in Tennessee, his problematic history of executions in Arizona was well known,” said Kit Thomas, an attorney who has represented people on Tennessee’s death row.

title: Husson football gets first win of season
text:
Daniel Ruiz Cantu rushed for 65 yards and two touchdowns as Husson held on to beat Western New England College, 26-21, on Saturday in Bangor for its first win of the season
The Golden Bears (2-3, 1-1 Conference of New England) pulled within five points on Carey Kilroy’s 29-yard scoring pass to John De Camps with 2:17 left, but the Eagles (1-4, 1-1) were able to run out the clock to preserve the win.
Husson quarterback Brody Gibson was 16-of-26 passing for 143 yards and a score to Jacob Lenz (four catches, 55 yards).
AMHERST 22, BOWDOIN 13: The Mammoths (3-0, 3-0 NESCAC) overcame an early 10-point deficit and beat the Polar Bears (0-3, 0-3) in Amherst, Massachusetts.
Clinging to a 15-13 halftime lead, Amherst scored on a 2-yard rush by Demetrius Smith to extend its lead with the only points of the second half.
Bowdoin had a fourth-and-1 at the Amherst 9-yard line with 1:16 left, but was turned the ball over on downs. The Polar Bears got their only touchdown in the first quarter on an interception return by Ferris Collins. Quarterback Soren Hummell finished 23 of 39 for 171 yards.
ENDICOTT 55, UNIVERSITY OF NEW ENGLAND 27: Quarterback Shea Lynch completed 20 of 34 passes for 369 yards and two touchdowns, and also rushed for 75 yards and a pair of scores, as the Gulls (5-0, 2-0 Conference of New England) beat the Nor’easters (0-5, 0-2) in Biddeford.
Bryan Ferreira rushed for 196 yards on 20 carries and had two touchdowns for the Gulls.
For UNE, Damien Jones rushed for 78 yards on 14 carries and scored a touchdown. He also had two receptions for 104 yards, including a 73-yard score. Javin Willis added a 9-yard scoring run and CJ Cooper returned an interception for a touchdown.
MIDDLEBURY 32, COLBY 2: Connor McClennan rushed for 121 yards and four touchdowns as the Panthers (2-1, 2-1 NESCAC) beat the Mules (0-3, 0-3) in Middlebury, Vermont.
Aidan Moss was 15-for-29 passing for 163 yards, including a 13-yard scoring pass to Luis Kuehberger.
The Mules scores on a safety in the third quarter.
TUFTS 22, BATES 21: With three seconds left, the Bobcats (0-3) lined up for a field goal with a chance to earn their first win of the season, but Marcos Ruiz’s kick was blocked by the Jumbos (2-1), who held on for a road victory Saturday night in Lewiston.
Tufts led 14-7 at halftime, backed by two touchdowns from Christian Shapiro, but Bates battled back in the second half to jump ahead by a score, 21-14, with just over three minutes to go in the third quarter.
Shapiro caught a touchdown pass for his third score of the game with 51 seconds left in the game. Tufts then converted its 2-point conversion to go ahead by one point before stopping Bates on its near game-winning drive.

title: Car drives into large crowd of rugby fans in Australia
text:
Car drives into large crowd of Australian rugby fans, injuring 10 people north of Sydney
A vehicle drove into a crowd standing on a road to cheer on the Newcastle Knights rugby team north of Sydney on Saturday, injuring 10 people, including several children, Australian officials said.
Two of the injured — a 5-year-old girl and a 67-year-old man — were in critical condition, and the other eight were in stable condition at a hospital, according to New South Wales police. Those in stable condition included another 5-year-old girl and a 2-year-old girl.
Police said they arrested the 18-year-old man driving the vehicle and were investigating what happened. They said the crash was not believed to be related to terrorism.
Thousands had been cheering the team on this week as they trained, the Australian Associated Press reported. Another large crowd was on the street Saturday morning to see the team bus off ahead of the rugby league finals match on Sunday.

title: ‘I just want to be a child again’: Boy overcomes rare condition through stem cell transplant
text:
NEW ORLEANS (WVUE/Gray News) - A boy from Gulfport, Mississippi, is dreaming big after receiving what doctors call a lifesaving stem cell transplant.
Peyton Stewart is an 11-year-old with big dreams. One of them is to play in the NBA. It’s a dream the staff at Manning Family Children’s hospital quickly learned about when Stewart arrived there in 2024 suffering from a rare mutation called STAT1 gain-of-function.
“At that time, we didn’t know the cause of it. We knew his red blood cells were getting destroyed, but we didn’t know why,” said Dr. Benjamin Watkins, pediatric hematology oncologist at Manning Family Children’s Hospital.
Stewart’s doctor said the condition caused his immune system to attack his own red blood cells, and his only hope for a cure was a bone marrow transplant. Stewart’s older brother, Acie, was a match for the procedure. Their mom worried.
“It touched my heart to see the siblings pull together like that, and I was nervous during the process because I had two children going through something at the same time,” said Laurie Stewart, Peyton Stewart’s mother.
During the six months Peyton Stewart spent at the hospital, he seemingly won over everybody, including its CEO, who found himself going one-on-one with the aspiring hooper.
“Somewhere along the way, he stopped being a kiddo I visited in the hospital, and he became my buddy. We played basketball, me not very well, so he taught me a lot,” said Lucio Fragoso, president and CEO of Manning Family Children’s Hospital.
On Thursday (Oct. 1), the hospital held a special bell ringing ceremony exactly one year after Peyton underwent the life-changing transplant. With a basketball hoop, brass band and a room full of hospital staff, Peyton rang the bell celebrating his so-called “re-birthday.”
Sitting just a few feet from the second line, Stewart’s grandmother Yvonne Hill thought of just how far he has come and what he said when he was sick.
“He said, ‘I just want to be a child again...I want to go to school,’” said Hill.
When Peyton took the podium during the ceremony, he thanked the brother that made the moment possible.
“Acie, thank you for being brave and helping me get better. I love you,” he said.
There weren’t many dry eyes among the people who took care of him.
“Thank you for helping me through the hard days and giving me reasons to smile. You held my mom too and made us feel like family,” Peyton told the hospital staff.
Peyton’s doctor said his immune system is now healthy, and there’s not much holding him back. He told the crowd he’s ready to take a shot at his new life.
“Today, ringing this bell means I get to look forward to being home, playing basketball and following my dreams, including becoming the future CEO of Manning Family Children’s Hospital, only after my NBA career, of course,” he said.
Stewart’s father, Christopher Stewart, said he feels fortunate his son now has the possibility of pursuing dreams.
“He’s obsessed with the NBA. I’m hoping for a CEO, but chances are it’s going to be the NBA,” he said.
Whatever path Peyton chooses, he’ll have support from the home team.
“He’s just full of life, and I just love to see him just be him. I just love it,” said Stewart’s grandmother.

title: Victoria Mansion kicks off Halloween season in Portland with ‘Bizarre Bazaar’
text:
PORTLAND —The Victoria Mansion isn’t haunted. At least, that’s what Stacia Hanscom, director of education and public programs, says.
But the mansion, a mid-19th century national historic landmark, welcomed spirits Saturday for a one-day fair to kick off the Halloween season. Featuring divination, a spooky poem performance, a visit from Dracula and more, visitors came to “A Bizarre Victorian Bazaar: An Exhibition of Oddities and the Obscure” to immerse themselves in the October mood and learn about a lesser known side of Victorian history — the gothic.
“It’s looking at the oddities and the things that we think are strange today, but that the Victorians believed in and tried,” Hanscom said. “They were experimenting.”
A costumed juggler paced around the mansion’s lawn, throwing pins. People lined up for tarot card readings and fortune telling under a tent. A mummy, which a party of Victorians would have been eager to unwrap, lay inside for viewing.
Bunny Rose, a tarot cart reader from Gorham, shuffled her deck of tarot cards and spread them out on the table.
She said the Victorians used tarot cards and other forms of divination to explore the rise of spiritualism. Some wanted to connect to people they had lost in the Civil War, and others were trying to bridge the gap between traditional religion and emerging science, Rose explained.
Katherine Doughty facilitated a divination reading called automatic drawing, where she placed a black cloth over a client’s hand and let them blindly draw on a paper underneath, letting their subconscious guide them. In the Victorian era, a medium would have done an automatic drawing themselves after connecting to a spirit.
“There’s a feeling the whole Halloween season, what we call ‘in between the worlds,'” Doughty said. “There’s more electricity and energy; there’s more opportunity for that in this time.”
A “cabinet of curiosities” stocked with keys, miniature mirrors, shells, dollhouse furniture, tiny shoes and other small treasures demonstrated “the hoarding nature of Victorian life” and a “mishmash of ideas,” said Anatole Brown from the Dyer Library and Saco Museum.
He said a few of the objects were “signs of death,” including a corvid skull, or a crow’s skull.
“A corvid skull is a definite form of occultism,” Brown said.
By the lawn’s edge, a basket of tiny “fire lighters” filled up as Andrew Harris repeatedly demonstrated how to fold the particularly flammable contraptions out of newspapers, which were “everywhere” and cheap in Victorian days.
Harris, who usually impersonates Charles Dickens, multitasked, also reading Penny Dreadfuls —cheap, serial literature produced in Great Britain — to interested passersby. The subjects of the stories were sensational, focused on crime or the supernatural. Since many Victorians were illiterate, people would read them out loud on the street for pennies.
Using the full range of his dynamic actor’s voice, Harris read a passage from the perspective of a dead man who had just been buried.
“If he (a Victorian) was a good reader, he could make a living at it,” Harris said. “A penny would have gone a long way.”
Not every part of the event was ominous. Sullivan House Bakery brought Victorian-themed treats, namely a “Victoria Sponge,” and costume designer Anna Halloran presented on Victorian fashion.
Nancy Noble, having just finished an oracle card reading, said it made her feel optimistic. She retired four months ago and is in a time of transition. Unlike a Victorian, she took a picture of her result with her phone to further study it later.
“I liked that it wasn’t like, here’s a death card,” Noble said.

title: Maine honors two firefighters killed in line of duty among others at memorial service
text:
AUGUSTA, Maine (WABI) - The ceremonial bell echoed across the Capitol grounds Saturday at the annual Firefighter Memorial Service, honoring the 42 Maine firefighters lost this year.
The Firefighters Memorial, across from Capitol Park, was dedicated in 1997 by then-Gov. Angus King, said Ken Desmond, president of the Maine State Federation of Firefighters.
Desmond has attended every year since, and said Saturday’s turnout was reminiscent of the service in 2001 after the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks.
“Obviously I’m old enough to remember the ceremony around 9/11 and just how the communities came together to support the fire service. This year has been pretty much the same,” echoed Bill Gillespie, Liberty Fire Chief and President of the Maine Fire Chiefs Assocation. “Maine has suffered a lot of tragedy this year, including myself and Waldo County.”
Montville firefighter Jacob Spaulding and Lt. Katherine Paige of Belmont Fire laid the wreath at the memorial. Both suffered major injuries in the Searsmont explosion.
Among those in attendance was Sen. Susan Collins, who said during her remarks: “This annual memorial service is always powerful and inspiring, but it has a special significance this year. As we honor 2 firefighters who made the ultimate sacrifice battling the horrific explosion at Robbins Lumber in Searsmont last May.”
Searsmont Assistant Fire Chief Wayne Woodbury and Morrill firefighter Andrew Cross were each honored with 20 bell tolls, signifying their line-of-duty deaths.
“As far as line of duty deaths, having two at the same incident is significant for Maine in the last decade or so,” explained Maine State Fire Marshal Shawn Esler. “But to be honest with you, one firefighter death in the line of duty is too many.”
Saturday’s service not only served as a commemoration of the lives lost, but as a call to action to address the challenges and future of the Maine fire service.
Gillespie said Maine’s fire service remains among the least expensive because of its reliance on volunteers. With volunteerism down and departments statewide facing critical staffing shortages, he said changes must be made.
“We need to figure out a way to create more volunteer opportunities for firefighters. We need to figure out a way to get them trained. We need to figure out a way for them to have time off from work so they can get trained. So all these initiatives are things that we’re looking at to try to better the fire service in the future,” described Gillespie.
Esler went on to explain those changes come through collaboration among the Fire Marshal’s Office, Fire Commission and legislators at the State House.

title: Coast Guard searching for plane with 6 aboard that lost contact on a trip from Bermuda to Boston
text:
NANTUCKET, Mass. (AP) — An air ambulance vanished over the Atlantic early Saturday with six people aboard while flying from Bermuda to Boston, triggering a search by air and sea in the waters off Nantucket.
Air traffic control audio posted by LiveATC.net offered a fragmentary and troubling glimpse of the flight’s final communications. “Roger, you said you’re coming in blind. Is that what you said?” a controller can be heard asking the pilot. The pilot’s transmission could not be heard in the recording. The controller later confirmed the pilot was declaring an emergency just before losing contact with the plane.
The controller then asked other aircraft in the area if they showed the Gulfstream jet on their collision avoidance systems or whether they could reach them on the radio, but the medevac plane with the call sign “Heartbeat 104” was never heard from again.
The Canadian-registered air ambulance jet had four crew members and two passengers aboard when it departed Bermuda’s L.F. Wade International Airport overnight for the flight to Massachusetts, according to a statement from the Bermuda airport’s operator, Skyport.
Four of the six people on board the flight that went missing early Saturday were Canadian nationals, the country’s Minister of Transport Steven MacKinnon said on X. Transport Canada is closely monitoring and working with authorities on search and rescue efforts, he said.
The Coast Guard said the Federal Aviation Administration reported that the Gulfstream G100 had lost contact very early Saturday morning. The search for the jet included crews in the air and on the water, the Coast Guard said.
The National Transportation Safety Board said it was gathering information about the situation Saturday morning but had no further update to share.

title: Husson football gets first win of season
text:
Daniel Ruiz Cantu rushed for 65 yards and two touchdowns as Husson held on to beat Western New England College, 26-21, on Saturday in Bangor for its first win of the season
The Golden Bears (2-3, 1-1 Conference of New England) pulled within five points on Carey Kilroy’s 29-yard scoring pass to John De Camps with 2:17 left, but the Eagles (1-4, 1-1) were able to run out the clock to preserve the win.
Husson quarterback Brody Gibson was 16-of-26 passing for 143 yards and a score to Jacob Lenz (four catches, 55 yards).
AMHERST 22, BOWDOIN 13: The Mammoths (3-0, 3-0 NESCAC) overcame an early 10-point deficit and beat the Polar Bears (0-3, 0-3) in Amherst, Massachusetts.
Clinging to a 15-13 halftime lead, Amherst scored on a 2-yard rush by Demetrius Smith to extend its lead with the only points of the second half.
Bowdoin had a fourth-and-1 at the Amherst 9-yard line with 1:16 left, but was turned the ball over on downs. The Polar Bears got their only touchdown in the first quarter on an interception return by Ferris Collins. Quarterback Soren Hummell finished 23 of 39 for 171 yards.
ENDICOTT 55, UNIVERSITY OF NEW ENGLAND 27: Quarterback Shea Lynch completed 20 of 34 passes for 369 yards and two touchdowns, and also rushed for 75 yards and a pair of scores, as the Gulls (5-0, 2-0 Conference of New England) beat the Nor’easters (0-5, 0-2) in Biddeford.
Bryan Ferreira rushed for 196 yards on 20 carries and had two touchdowns for the Gulls.
For UNE, Damien Jones rushed for 78 yards on 14 carries and scored a touchdown. He also had two receptions for 104 yards, including a 73-yard score. Javin Willis added a 9-yard scoring run and CJ Cooper returned an interception for a touchdown.
MIDDLEBURY 32, COLBY 2: Connor McClennan rushed for 121 yards and four touchdowns as the Panthers (2-1, 2-1 NESCAC) beat the Mules (0-3, 0-3) in Middlebury, Vermont.
Aidan Moss was 15-for-29 passing for 163 yards, including a 13-yard scoring pass to Luis Kuehberger.
The Mules scores on a safety in the third quarter.
TUFTS 22, BATES 21: With three seconds left, the Bobcats (0-3) lined up for a field goal with a chance to earn their first win of the season, but Marcos Ruiz’s kick was blocked by the Jumbos (2-1), who held on for a road victory Saturday night in Lewiston.
Tufts led 14-7 at halftime, backed by two touchdowns from Christian Shapiro, but Bates battled back in the second half to jump ahead by a score, 21-14, with just over three minutes to go in the third quarter.
Shapiro caught a touchdown pass for his third score of the game with 51 seconds left in the game. Tufts then converted its 2-point conversion to go ahead by one point before stopping Bates on its near game-winning drive.

title: Gorneault, Graves Lead County At Festival Of Champions
text:
Gorneault, Graves Crack Top 10 At Festival Of Champions; Houlton Boys Finish Ninth
Aroostook County runners held their own against one of the largest fields they will see this fall Saturday at the Maine Cross Country Festival of Champions in Belfast.
The complete results included 940 boys and 611 girls, with schools from throughout Maine and New England taking part. Caribou’s Pierce Gorneault led the County boys with a seventh-place finish in 16:01.17, while fellow Viking Emma Graves placed eighth overall in the girls race in 19:06.96.
The County also had strong team showings. Houlton/GHCA placed ninth overall in the boys standings with 425 points, while Presque Isle was the top County girls team, finishing 12th with 401 points.
Gorneault Runs To Seventh
Gorneault stayed with the leaders and crossed the line seventh overall in 16:01.17.
Scarborough’s Atticus Merriam won an incredibly tight boys race in 15:21.18, just .15 seconds ahead of Dirigo’s William Morris at 15:21.33.
Houlton/GHCA also packed several runners high in the standings. Malachi Witmer finished 46th in 17:00.21, Brayden Drake was 50th in 17:01.89, Wyatt Quint placed 62nd in 17:09.53 and Logan Witmer was 66th in 17:12.16.
That depth helped Houlton/GHCA finish ninth out of 79 scoring boys teams with 425 points.
Presque Isle’s Paxton Darrell also broke into the top 100, finishing 78th in 17:20.05, while Caribou’s Peyton Gorneault was 91st in 17:33.39.
Graves Finishes Eighth In Girls Race
Graves produced another top-10 performance against a deep field, finishing eighth in 19:06.96.
Falmouth’s Georgia Moon won the girls race in 17:24.31, followed by Glastonbury’s Lauren Parrett and Portland’s Nora Schmidt.
Presque Isle had two more County runners near the front. Lillian Johnson placed 19th in 19:37.19 and Aleah Rideout followed in 23rd at 19:45.74.
Taylor York finished 64th for Presque Isle in 20:43.37, with Caribou’s Jenna Strid immediately behind her in 65th at 20:47.69.
Those performances helped Presque Isle take 12th in the girls team standings with 401 points. Caribou finished 18th with 595.

title: Obituary: Ruth E. Bridges
text:
SCARBOROUGH – Ruth E. Bridges, 81, passed away peacefully on Sept. 26, 2026, at the Enclave, where she was cared for with compassion and dignity.
Born September 1945 in Portland to the late Martin and Hazel (Henderson) Casey, Ruth graduated from Portland High School in 1963 and built a meaningful career in service and finance. She began as a telephone operator, then transitioned to banking, where she spent decades as a mortgage underwriter before moving into auditing and quality control.
In 1972, Ruth married David, and together they created a life full of joy and adventure. They were boating enthusiasts, spending countless weekends aboard their beloved Sandpiper, exploring the Boothbay region with friends and family. Their shared love of travel took them to Florida, where they made new memories over two decades before David’s passing in 2006.
Life had a beautiful gift in store. During a visit to Maine years later, Ruth attended her 50th high school reunion and reconnected with her high school sweetheart, Louie. What followed was a second chance at companionship and love; enjoying life’s simple pleasures, traveling to St. Petersburg, Fla., and spending summers at Highland Lake.
Ruth was predeceased by her husband, David Bridges; and sister, Barbara Fortier.
She is survived by her special partner of 12 years, Louis Savard; and her beloved cat, Casey; daughter, Cindy Bridges; grand-kitty, Rosie; cousin, Linda Henderson; as well as many extended family members.
The family expresses deep gratitude to The Enclave and Gentiva Hospice for their exceptional care.
Visiting hours will be held from 4 p.m. to 6 p.m. on Tuesday, Oct. 6, at the new Conroy-Tully Walker Cremation, Funeral, and Gathering Center, 300 Allen Ave., Portland. Prayers will be recited at the funeral home at 10 a.m. on Wednesday, Oct. 7; a Mass of Christian Burial will be celebrated at 11 a.m. at St. Pius X Church, 492 Ocean Ave., Portland. Graveside services will be rendered at 11 a.m. on Friday, Oct. 9, at Laurel Hill Cemetery, Saco.
To view Ruth’s memorial page or to leave an online condolence, please visit http://www.ConroyTullyWalker.com.

title: Former UMaine 2-sport star Jack Leggett earns prestigious Clemson honor
text:
Jack Leggett is enshrined in a Hall of Fame everywhere he has been.
But the former University of Maine two-sport all-conference selection will be honored for a unique award at Saturday night’s Miami-Clemson football game in South Carolina.
He has become just the third person to be inducted in the Clemson Baseball Ring of Honor, joining legendary coach Bill Wilhelm and three-time All-American second baseman Rusty Adkins.
It is the highest honor awarded by the Clemson athletic department and the inductee must have made a significant contribution to Clemson athletics, be a member of the Clemson Hall of Fame and be a graduate of a four-year institution.
Leggett was a three-time All-Yankee Conference infielder at UMaine and he was also a three-time All-Yankee Conference defensive back and placekicker in football.
He captained the 1976 UMaine baseball team to a fourth place finish in the College World Series.
The Bangor-born and South Burlington, Vermont-raised Leggett became the youngest Division I head baseball coach at age 23 when he landed the job at the University of Vermont in 1978.
In 36 years as a head coach at three schools — Vermont (5 years), Western Carolina (9 years) and Clemson (22 years) – he compiled a record of 1,332-770-1 and had only two losing seasons, one at Vermont and the other at Western Carolina.
Entering the 2026 season, his 1,332 wins were tied for 13th in Division I history.
As the head coach at Clemson, he guided the Tigers to 21 NCAA Tournament appearances in his 22 seasons and six College World Series berths between 1994 and 2015. They reached the final four on three occasions.
He was named the Atlantic Coach Conference Coach of the Year in 1994, 1995 and 2006.
He posted a record of 955-480-1 at Clemson, second in career wins behind Wilhelm’s 1,161 in 36 years, and Leggett averaged 43.4 wins per year, which is first in Clemson’s history and seventh in the country during that time period.
He spent two seasons as Wilhelm’s assistant before taking over for him after he retired.
The 72-year-old Leggett had his number 7 retired at Clemson.
He led Western Carolina to five NCAA Tournament appearances and has been inducted into its Hall of Fame. He has also been inducted into the Vermont Hall of Fame and the American Baseball Coaches Association Hall of Fame, among others.
The UMaine Sports Hall of Famer said in a news release from Clemson that being inducted into the Ring of Honor is a “tremendous honor for me and my family.”
“It is a true reflection of the support of my family, the many hard-working and competitive players, loyal assistant coaches, passionate fans and the many supportive administrators, staff and friends and great coaches in the department that I was lucky enough to work alongside,” Leggett said.
He also said it was an honor to be “representing the Clemson athletic department and our storied baseball program. This is one more of the many great moments and memories that we’ve shared together.”
