title: Calling for sanity from my sickbed in Maine
text:
Bill Hiss lives in Lewiston.
It does seem odd to be writing an op-ed from a hospital bed, with ninth-floor views to Mount Washington, and people bustling to and fro night and day. Being a healer here is like serving on a submarine: tiny spaces, machinery everywhere and staff maneuvering past each other.
But perhaps it’s a helpful time for a literal grayhead — I am 82 — to share three thoughts while attached to an IV pole.
First, seeing the staff at Maine Medical Center is a blunt reminder of how utterly insane, cruel and counterproductive for America is this federal administration’s hostility to immigrants. At least as I see them at work, perhaps 10%-20% of the doctors, 30%-40% of the RNs, 70% of the LPNs and the vast majority of the support staff of housekeepers, food staff, etc., are immigrants.
Hope to stay alive? Get meds at 2 a.m.? Need food brought to your bedside? Pay attention, folks: immigrants are doing much of the work we need to stay alive.
Within the last hour, I was seen by two infectious disease physicians, one an immigrant from Vietnam, the other from an Arab country, who will care for me over the six-week treatment for a spine infection. As a minister, I see the same pattern in hospitals, rehab centers and nursing homes: the immigrants are irreplaceable labor. The same is true of agricultural workers, meat packing, hospitality, restaurants, truck drivers and countless other fields.
Second, being caught in the tragic contractions of Central Maine Medical Center for nine weeks before being referred to Maine Medical Center has been a (literal) painful reminder that perhaps it is time to rethink our medical delivery system.
I have a fine education, can get information, can afford medical expenses and have a high-end Medicare Advantage policy. But all summer I was caught in one communication or insurance snafu after another. This federal administration and our for-profit insurance industry have their fingers around our throats. If I cannot figure it out with my advantages, what in God’s name are the 70%-80% of America’s lower economic bands to do when faced with a serious medical problem?
Third, seeing the barrage of negative TV ads reminds me that hopefully sooner — by
November — we will need to find common-sense, middle-ground spaces in our social contracts. Tragically for America, President Trump’s view of the world is based on his own mental illness of narcissism, hatreds, racism, insults, pathological incessant lying, policy ignorance and the instincts of a lifelong real estate con man. 
Equally tragic, the Republicans in Congress have been almost completely compliant with his daily whims, disrupting everything from fuel and food prices to international treaties to respect for our constitutional protections. Every day a new threat, a new distraction: masked and armed ICE officers at polling places, snipers on his garish monument to himself, threats to our closest allies, all while he and his family are raking in billions in illegal sweetheart deals.
Two of my fellow Lewiston citizens, running as Republicans for higher office, have yard signs that are purple, and one of these fellow citizens told me when she knocked on my door that this was deliberate, to try to send a signal that she hoped people would see her as a moderate. Well, I would like to believe so.
These two women are not MAGA cartoons spewing hate; they have worked faithfully in their current public offices. But how are we to interpret their candidacies in the light of Sen. Susan Collins claiming to be a moderate, while voting for what Trump wanted 95% of the time? My hope is that they will demonstrate clearly a rejection of MAGA cruelty and illegality.
And yes, if they are elected, I hope to offer thoughts on how we find more sensible middle ground for our country.

title: Governor says Tennessee's prisons chief is resigning after failed execution of Christa Pike
text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (AP) — The head of Tennessee’s prison system is resigning after the failed execution of Christa Pike, Gov. Bill Lee announced Saturday.
Lee said that Department of Correction Commissioner Frank Strada will step down this month.
Strada said in a statement that stepping aside “is in the best interests” of the state as an independent review is carried out to determine why Pike’s execution failed Wednesday.
Pike was placed on a ventilator and remained unconscious in a hospital, her attorneys said in a court filing Friday.
Hospital staff, her lawyers said, were working to save Pike’s life and as of late Thursday were trying to clear the two doses of the drug that the state uses to execute prisoners.
The stunning failure in Tennessee’s execution chamber on Wednesday has left both sides of the death penalty debate demanding answers. Lee has ordered an independent review.
Pike’s attorneys said they believed problems with the IV lines caused the pentobarbital to flow into her body instead of her bloodstream.
“Apparently at no point did any member of the execution team realize that the IV lines were not correctly placed or that the veins had blown and that the pentobarbital was, in whole or in part, entering Ms. Pike’s body,” they wrote in the court filing.
Pike was 18 when she and her boyfriend tortured and killed a classmate, Colleen Slemmer, in a jealous rage. She later became one of the youngest women to be sent to death row.

title: Fact checking claims from Maine's Total Coverage Congressional debate
text:
Fact checking claims from Maine's Total Coverage CD-2 debate
Democrat Matt Dunlap and Republican Paul LePage faced off in a debate in the WMTW studio on Thursday night. We're checking some of their claims.
Fact checking claims from Maine's Total Coverage CD-2 debate
Democrat Matt Dunlap and Republican Paul LePage faced off in a debate in the WMTW studio on Thursday night. We're checking some of their claims.
On Thursday night on Maine's Total Coverage, candidates for Maine's Second Congressional District debated for the first time.
During a fiery exchange, former two-term Republican Governor Paul LePage called Democratic State Auditor Matt Dunlap a liar as it relates to something LePage wrote in a press release when he was governor.
"My opponent here has said on the record that Social Security and Medicare were welfare programs. Plain and simple, and I disagree," Dunlap said.
"That's a lie," LePage responded.
The press release Dunlap mentioned was from 2014. At the time LePage was governor and Dunlap was secretary of state.
The press release from the LePage Administration Archives said, "The U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis conceals welfare benefits by calling them Personal Current Transfer Receipts. These Transfer Receipts include: Social Security benefits; Medicare payments; Medicaid; and state unemployment insurance benefits."
The release continues with a quote from LePage, "It doesn't matter what liberals call these payments, it is welfare, pure and simple."
Another exchange involving the state gas tax and Maine's roads and bridges.
Dunlap was responding to debate moderator Jon Chrisos, who asked about Dunlap's vote to increase the gas tax in 1999. Dunlap said that by increasing the gas tax, it put about $400 million into the state highway fund.
"Absolutely. It was the right vote. The idea was to index the gas tax so that we could maintain our roads and bridges," Dunlap said.
LePage said the gas tax is not needed for this work.
"What he just said is absolutely wrong. In my eight years as governor, we did. We stopped the gas tax increase, and we did more road construction in the history of the state of Maine. In fact, one year in [20]17, I believe it was we did over 1000 miles," LePage responded.
According to the Maine Department of Transportation's year-end report in 2017, there were 994 miles paved, 14.5 miles of highway reconstruction and 48.3 miles of highway rehabilitation.
According to Maine Revenue Services, the gas tax has remained at 30 cents a gallon since 2011, so it did not increase under the LePage Administration, and the DOT did improve more than 1,000 roads.
DOT year-end reports are not available prior to LePage taking office, so it is not clear whether or not 2017 was the year with the most road construction up until that point. Since Gov. Janet Mills took office in 2019, there have been almost 8,000 miles of roads repaved, averaging more than 1,100 miles a year.

title: With two big defensive plays, Carter Moody helps Thornton football earn a big win
text:
SACO — There’s Carter Moody, stretched out to all of his 6-foot-3, practically horizontal to the Hill Stadium turf. The Thornton Academy junior is in the process of making the play of the game. Moody blocks Justin Bouchard’s try for a 33-yard field goal in the final minute of the first half, preserving his team’s one-point lead.
It’s the second time in the first half of this pivotal game against Portland that Moody makes the play of the game for the Golden Trojans. Late in the first quarter, with the Bulldogs threatening to turn a one-touchdown lead into a two-touchdown lead, Moody is there to fall on the ball inside his 5-yard line as Josiah Blain knocks it from Portland’s Alex Martin with a strong tackle.
This game between the teams that played in the last three Class A state championship games (won by Thornton in 2023, by Portland in 2024, and by the Trojans again last November) was a battle of two undefeated teams trying to reach another state final. For a half, it was as close as you’d expect. Eventually, Thornton wore down the Bulldogs. A one-point game at the half became a 43-13 blowout.
Moody was a big reason why his team clung to a one-point halftime lead. An all-SMAA defensive back last season as a sophomore, Moody is enjoying a bigger role this season.
“His role has increased. He’s on offense, defense, special teams. He made some great plays. He’s a great tackler,” Thornton coach Kevin Kezal said of Moody.
Portland scored quickly and with little resistance on the game’s first drive, with Martin leading the strong ground game. The Bulldogs were on the verge of putting the Trojans in a two-touchdown hole, a place with which they are unfamiliar, when Blain’s hit dislodged the ball in the final minute of the first quarter, inside Thornton’s 5-yard line.
Moody was there to pounce on the ball, evaporating the threat. He didn’t know who caused the fumble, only that it happened, and he needed to get the ball.
“It was right there in front of me and I just fell on it,” Moody said. “We battle. We stay strong. No matter where we are on the field.”
With Thornton up 14-13, the Bulldogs drove, and looked poised to take the lead just before the first half ended. Bouchard has the leg for the 33-yard field goal try. Before the play, Moody and teammate Brennan Tabor had a quick chat.
“(Tabor) was lined up next to me, and said ‘You go as tight as you can, and I’m going to try and take (the blockers) on so you’ve got a free shot,'” Moody said.
Then Moody described what happened in short, simple sentences, as if he was outlining a series of snapshots taken after the snap.
“It worked. I got around them. No one touched me. (I) put two hands up. Laid out. Blocked it. It felt amazing,” He said. “They were driving on us, but getting that stop right before halftime really helped us in the locker room.”
The Trojans spend a lot of time on special teams, both Moody and Kezal said. It’s something the team takes seriously and to heart. It was Moody’s first blocked kick, and it couldn’t have come at a better time. He held momentum in his outstretched body.
“Obviously, Carter is one of our best players, and he made a great play. It’s nice when the ball is on the hash because you have a better chance (to block it) with the angle,” Kezal said. “He took a good angle, and it was a huge play to get us into halftime with a lead.”
With two teams who have a recent history of playing big games against each other, don’t be surprised if Thornton and Portland meet again at Fitzpatrick Stadium on the Saturday before Thanksgiving.
“We knew somebody was going home with a loss,” Moody said.
With two big defensive plays in the first half, Moody helped ensure that wouldn’t be his team.

title: Why I’m choosing Jackson over Collins
text:
At age 54, with several years of service in public safety, many as a firefighter/EMT, my life’s work has been rooted in keeping our communities safe, secure and supported. I know what it means to answer the call when families are facing their worst moments.
Sen. Susan Collins’ commercial showcasing the firehouses that received federal funding are grinding my gears. The much-needed funding was coming, no matter who put the requests through. Many firefighters are sitting around their kitchen tables trying to figure out how to pay their bills because of Collins’ negligence in the U.S. Senate.
Federal firehouse funding relies on the state delegation’s collaborative effort. The senators submit parallel requests for municipal projects, while the representatives submit matching House earmarks to ensure budget parity. Meanwhile, operational equipment, turnout gear and staffing funds flow through FEMA programs.
By contrast, Troy Jackson has tirelessly supported first responders. His high-profile advocacy for emergency services throughout his Maine legislative career makes his seat on the Congressional Fire Services Caucus a given — potentially it could even lead to a chairmanship.
Here’s just a couple examples:
- 2010 (LD 1558): Jackson sponsored accidental death benefits to close MainePERS loopholes for families of firefighters lost to job-related cardiovascular or respiratory events.
- 2021 (LD 213): Jackson championed the expanded firefighter cancer presumption, updating worker protections to cover female firefighters facing gynecologic cancers tied to PFAS and toxic exposure.
That is why I am proudly supporting Troy Jackson for the U.S. Senate and I hope others will also.
Jeffrey Stanley
Arrowsic

title: Coast Guard searching for missing jet heading to Boston from Bermuda with 6 on board
text:
(Gray News) - The U.S. Coast Guard has launched a search for a missing jet after the FAA reported losing contact with the aircraft.
The U.S. Coast Guard Northeast reported at 6:15 a.m. Saturday that a Gulfstream G100 jet with the tail number CGRJP was heading to Boston from Bermuda when it disappeared.
Six people were on board.
According to Boston 25 News, the jet was a medical transfer aircraft. The Nantucket Current reported that the aircraft is registered to Latitude Air Ambulance, which is based in Ontario, Canada.
Boston 25 News obtained audio transmissions from air traffic controllers in Boston in the moments before they lost contact. In the transmissions, the air traffic controllers asked the aircraft if it was “coming in blind.” According to the Nantucket Current, the Nantucket Memorial Airport reported the pilot declared an emergency before the jet disappeared.
The Coast Guard said it is currently searching for the plane in the area surrounding Nantucket. Both air and surface crews have been launched to assist with the search.
The Coast Guard said the HC-144 Ocean Sentry airplane crew and MH-60 Jayhawk helicopter crew from AirSta Cape Cod, the HC-130 Hercules crew from AirSta Elizabeth City, the 7-foot MLB crew from Station Brant Point and FRC William Sparling (WPC-1154) are assisting in the search.
In an update posted at 11:46 a.m. Saturday, the Coast Guard said its search remains ongoing.
By that evening, Coast Guard crews found a debris field associated with the plane, but no passengers had been found.
No further information has been provided at this time.

title: Mormon leader decries explosion in sports betting, prediction markets
text:
Mormon leader decries explosion in sports betting, prediction markets
A leader of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints warned Saturday that an explosion in gambling driven by online prediction markets and sports betting is fostering greed, particularly among youths, while producing “nothing of value.”
D. Todd Christofferson, one of the top three leaders of what is known widely as the Mormon church, said rampant betting among teenagers and young adults is robbing time from their studies and relationships as smartphones make gambling possible anywhere.
“For us as Latter-day Saints, overarching all other concerns is the fact that gambling is morally wrong. Gambling is built on the desire to obtain something for nothing,” Christofferson said at the faith’s twice-annual general conference.
Related video above: DraftKings faces proposed class-action lawsuit over alleged AI-driven gambling promotions
The declaration that prediction markets are gambling puts the conservative church at odds with President Donald Trump. The Republican's administration has argued platforms such as Kalshi and Polymarket don’t constitute gambling and therefore shouldn’t be subjected to restrictions in states such as Utah, where the church is based.
Utah has been at the forefront of the legal dispute over who regulates the markets and whether they should be considered finance or gambling. A federal judge ruled in August that Utah officials can enforce its strict-anti-gambling laws on prediction markets.
Legislation was enacted this year to make Utah’s gambling laws stricter and amend some of the language so that they’d almost certainly apply to prediction markets.
Prediction markets allow wagers on anything from whether it will rain in Los Angeles, to if the United States will go to war.
“Or even, if you can imagine, the timing of the Second Coming,” Christofferson said Saturday. “Where do you go to collect on that bet?”
Opposition to gambling is common among religious organizations. The United Methodist Church refers to it as “a menace to society.” The Southern Baptist Convention, the largest Protestant denomination in America, has condemned gambling several times and in 2025 declared sports gambling inconsistent with biblical principle.
Gambling is forbidden in Islam and considered a vice among Hindus. In the Catholic Church, gambling is not in itself a sin, but is considered potentially problematic.
For more than a century, Utah kept gambling almost entirely out of the state. There are no casinos, no lotteries and no racetracks that allow bets. The prohibition is rooted in the ideals of members of the Latter-day Saints church who view gambling as a path to selfishness and addiction.
“The rise of predictive markets, and the legalization of sports gambling, this is just really taking off all across the country,” said Matthew Bowman, a professor of religion and history at Claremont Graduate University in California. “And a lot of institutions — religious, state and otherwise — are grappling with this problem.”
Saturday’s speech comes as the church has been wading into political issues under President Dallin Oaks, a former Utah Supreme Court justice who became the faith’s top leader last October. Church leaders this year have opposed state ballot measures that would establish rights to abortion in Idaho and Nevada.
Yet the institution's approach to political issues — using public statements and behind-the-scenes lobbying to convey its message — has become more calculated in recent years, Bowman said.
The shift followed public blowback to the church’s stance against California’s Proposition 8, a 2008 ballot measure that sought to ban gay marriage. In that case, Bowman said church leaders encouraged its members to get directly involved.
___
Brown reported from Billings, Montana. Holly Meyer contributed to this story from Nashville, Tennessee.

title: Heisman Trophy makes its way to Bates
text:
LEWISTON — Jeff Price may not have won the Heisman Trophy as a football player at Bates College, but on Saturday brought college football’s most coveted award to his alma mater.
Price, who graduated in 1987, currently serves as the CEO of the Heisman Trophy Trust. He had the trophy near Garcelon Field where people could pose and take photos ahead of Bates’ football game against Tufts.
The Heisman Trophy is awarded annually to the top player in college football.
“As a proud Bobcat and someone who’s spent 35 years in the sports industry, now at Heisman, to have the opportunity to bring the Heisman here, it represents excellence, certainly something Bates represents,” said Price. “Empowerment, which is certainly core to who Bates is. And we at the Heisman want to create enduring impact and I know that’s what Bates wants to do.”
In leading the Heisman Trophy Trust, Price has had a chance to cross paths with many of the award’s former recipients.
“The Heisman winners have been incredible,” Price said. “Just 61 living Heisman winners and so many of them, since I’ve started, have given us hours and hours of their time. Because, as we’re creating the Heisman Club, it’s something that they care about deeply. It’s their club.
“Only one person a year gets into it. And so, we’re co-creating that and building it together so that we can drive charitable impact, we can do better storytelling around the Heisman winners and ultimately make a difference.”
One memorable occurrence with a former recipient was with last year’s winner, Fernando Mendoza, who led Indiana to the national championship and was selected with the top pick in the NFL Draft by the Las Vegas Raiders. Price said Mendoza asked for his phone number at the culmination of the Heisman Trophy ceremony weekend.
“I’ve been in sports for a long time, dealt with a lot of high-profile athletes,” said Price. “(Mendoza’s) the only athlete who at the end of a weekend, asked if he could get my cell phone number so that we could stay connected.”
The trophy display drew a crowd of students, alumni, parents and community members, many mimicking the pose of the player sculpted in the award.
Sheila and James McKinnon were on campus to watch their nephew, Bates offensive lineman Ryder Smith. They were just two of the many who stopped by the Bobcat Fan Zone and took a picture with the trophy.
“It’s kind of like the Stanley Cup, you don’t really see it a lot,” James said.
They had already planned to come for the game, so the trophy being on campus was an added bonus.
“It was fun watching everybody do the (pose),” Sheila said, miming the motion. “Everybody’s going to do the pose.”
The Heisman Trophy is the latest major award to make its way to Maine in the last couple months. The Boston Celtics’ 2024 NBA Finals trophy was displayed at a Jr. Celtics Academy basketball camp session at the Lewiston Armory in August and the Stanley Cup was at a Portland Sea Dogs game in September.
For Price, bringing it to Bates was a way to merge both of his worlds.
“Meeting of kind of two assets and two institutions of a long-standing stature and excellence, and just thrilled to be here,” Price said.

title: Maine runners from Scarborough, Falmouth win titles at Festival of Champions
text:
BELFAST — Scarborough’s Atticus Merriam knew he had a challenge on his hands in the boys race of the 25th Festival of Champions.
And Dirigo William Morris pushed him to the brink.
Merriam finished in 15:21.18 to beat Morris, who finished in 15:21.33 to win the annual cross country race at Troy Howard Middle School on Saturday. The meet included a record 100 schools and 1,800 runners from Maine, Massachusetts, Rhode Island, Vermont and Nova Scotia.
“I’m a little tired, but I feel good,” Merriam said. “(My thought was), ‘I just have to hold him off,’ because this is a bit of a state (championship) preview,” Merriam said. “It worked out today … I knew there was about six guys (to beat), but he was the one I had in my mind that was probably going to give me the most trouble.”
Falmouth senior Georgia Moon won the girls race by more than five seconds in 17:24.51, holding off Glastonbury (Conn.) junior Lauren Parrett (17:29.42). Last year’s girls winner, Portland sophomore Nora Schmidt, finished third with a time of 17:41.62.
Merriam and Morris kept pace with each other throughout the final mile of the race. The pair sprinted toward the finish line in the final 100 yards, gasping for air while trying to get ahead. Both runners collapsed to the ground, congratulating the other on a good race.
“I feel a little let down,” Morris said. “It came down to the wire, and it just wasn’t quite there. I’m happy with the time, but I was really shooting for that win and I was a little bummed I didn’t get it.”
Moon secured the victory with a strong finishing kick, using her prior success and knowledge of the course.
“Lauren and Nora, we ran together for a while,” Moon said. “I’m just really happy to finally make that jump. It means a lot. I didn’t want to burn out too soon. I sat for a bit until I knew I could kick it in and have (momentum) all the way through, because I think that’s something I’m really strong at.”
Parrett was pleased with her time and effort against Moon.
“This is a pretty flat course, so I was extremely excited about possibly beating my top time,” Parrett said. “I was definitely trying to push and catch up (to Moon), but my legs were starting to let up.”
Yarmouth High School won the boys team title with 114 points, followed by East Greenwich (Conn.) High School (139) and Portland (156). The Clippers were led by junior Bowen Mitchell, who finished sixth in 15:59.43.
Glastonbury dominated the field for the girls team title with 76 points, followed by Hampden Academy (196) and Mercy (Conn.) High School (236).
Temperatures were in the low 60s, slightly warm, but otherwise ideal for the relatively flat track at Troy Howard, allowing runners to post strong times.
“The full sun made it warm, but I would take weather like this any day,” Merriam said.
The girls course and race record still belong to Orono graduate Ruth White, who ran a time of 16:56.92 in 2023. The boys course and meet record is held by Sean Gray of Portsmouth (N.H.) High School, who ran a time of 14:55.56 in 2024.

title: Police bodycam footage of Luigi Mangione’s arrest released
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — Police bodycam footage released Friday shows the moment officers located and arrested Luigi Mangione at a Pennsylvania McDonald’s in connection with the shooting death of United Healthcare CEO Brian Thompson in Manhattan.
In one video, officers ask Mangione to lower the face mask he was wearing to hide his identity.
“That’s 100% him,” one officer says eagerly as they step outside to speak out of Mangione’s earshot.
“I told you, man,” another responds off camera.
Later, an officer searches Mangione’s belongings and smiles widely as she pulls out a gun cartridge, seemingly confirming they’d found their suspect.
The trove of videos comes from Mangione’s Dec. 9, 2024, arrest in Altoona, five days after Thompson, a 50-year-old Minnesota executive, was gunned down as he walked to a midtown Manhattan hotel for his company’s annual investor conference.
A Manhattan judge unsealed the recordings Friday after CNN petitioned for their release. Parts of the videos were shown during a December court hearing as Mangione’s lawyers unsuccessfully sought to get key evidence thrown out, including his initial statements to police and items seized at the time of his arrest.
Mangione pleaded guilty in August to federal stalking charges and faces life in prison when he’s sentenced in December. He also faces murder charges in New York state court, though those proceedings have been postponed indefinitely as his lawyers seek to have the case thrown out.
The videos released Friday begin as officers descend on the McDonald’s in central Pennsylvania, nearly 300 miles (483 kilometers) from Manhattan.
They find Mangione, the Ivy League-educated scion of a wealthy Maryland family, seated at a table wearing a ski hat, surgical face mask and winter coat. The officers say they’re responding to a call about a suspicious person and ask for his name and identification.
“You’re a little nervous right now. Why are you nervous?” an officer asks at one point.
They order him to put his hands on his head and ask him if he’s been in New York recently. They confront him about a phony New Jersey driver’s license he offers up bearing the name Mark Rosario.
“You’re under official police investigation right now,” one officer warns. “You give a false name to us again, you’re gonna be arrested for false ID.”
When Mangione finally comes clean, they ask why he had lied.
“I clearly shouldn’t have,” he responds as he’s asked to write his real name and spell it aloud.
Other videos show officers patting Mangione down, reading him his rights, placing him in cuffs and taking him to the police station.
As an officer searches him more thoroughly at the station, another officer goes through his backpack.
The officer finds the 9 mm handgun authorities would later confirm was used in the killing, as well as a silencer and another ammo magazine. They also recover the journal that prosecutors would later say revealed Mangione’s intent to “wack” a health insurance executive, as well as his other handwritten notes.
“He has a checklist for today,” another officer says, ticking off the seized items to someone on the phone. “Tomorrow he’s supposed to do an intel check-in and get a survival kit.”

title: UMaine football drops 5th straight game
text:
Nick Laughlin of Cape Elizabeth scored early in the fourth quarter to pull Maine within six, but the Black Bears couldn’t get any closer and suffered their fifth straight loss, falling to Sacred Heart 24-16 on Saturday in Orono.
Maine falls to 1-5 overall and 1-2 in the Coastal Athletic Conference. The Black Bears have not won since beating Towson in their season opener on Aug. 27.
Sacred Heart improves to 2-3 overall and 2-2 in the conference.
Laughlin scored on a 2-yard rush with 12:03 left to make it 21-15. Maine gave up a 40-yard field goal to Ryan Bocklet on the ensuing Sacred Heart possession, then drove to the Pioneers’ 37-yard line before turning the ball over on downs with 1:40 left.
Maine forced a Sacred Heart punt and started a drive at its own 43 with 1:16 left. The Black Bears gained one first down, but quarterback Caden Drezek threw four straight incomplete passes from the Sacred Heart 47 to end Maine’s hopes.
Drezek, who saw the bulk of the snaps after starting the season as the backup, went 12 for 28 passing for 141 yards. Eddie Buehler completed 1 of 5 passes for 13 yards and was sacked twice.
Maine took a 9-0 lead early in the second quarter on three field goals by Samuel Tremblay (42, 45 and 37 yards). Sacred Heart took the lead on an 11-yard pass from Poochie Snyder to Jason Palmieri with 19 seconds left in the first half.
Snyder completed 21 of 27 passes for 207 yards and two touchdowns.
Maine is off next week and returns to action on Oct. 17 when it host Bryant.

title: Letter: Vote to change our course
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Since taking office, President Donald Trump has had all three branches of government on his side, so he could have gotten anything he wanted done. He promised a “Great Healthcare Plan” that would lower drug prices and lower insurance premiums, and promised to bring down the cost of living. Apparently, a military war with Iran, and trade wars with the rest of the world, were more important to him, and the Republican-controlled Congress did nothing to change his mind.
The Iran war has cost us, the U.S. taxpayers, $44 billion, so far, and despite estimates the war would be over in weeks, there is still no end in sight. Thanks to all these wars, the cost of heating oil has nearly doubled, gas and coffee are up by more than 30%, and beef by more than 20%.
As for making health care more affordable, rather than The Great Healthcare Plan, the Republicans passed a Big Beautiful Bill while medical insurance premiums, for those without employer-sponsored coverage, will rise more than 20%, while those with employer-sponsored insurance experienced the largest premium increases in 15 years.
Are you better off now than you were two years ago? Between now and Nov. 3, vote for Troy Jackson for U.S. Senate and Matt Dunlap for U.S. House of Representatives. I believe we need to change our course, away from chaotic self destruction, and toward a vibrant, compassionate economy that makes all of us better off, not just the rich. You can vote, in person, from Oct. 5 to Oct. 29.

title: Restaurants on this Maine peninsula close often and earlier in fall without workers
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
El El Frijoles was busier than ever this year — but closed for the season earlier than ever.
When Michael Rossney and Michele Levesque opened the taqueria in Sargentville almost 20 years ago, “it was a whole different peninsula,” Levesque said of the Blue Hill area.
As their business grew, staffed mostly by students with a few local adults, they operated some years into October and even through the winter. But this season, they closed their doors before Labor Day for the first time when no additional employees were available for the shoulder season, focusing instead on selling premade food at their neighboring year-round shop.
The couple said that, anecdotally, they’ve observed serious cultural shifts on the peninsula since the pandemic that seem to have reduced the local adult workforce and raise questions for them about the area’s future.
“It is a real problem. And I think what we’ve started talking to other businesses about is, it’s like, what happens to our society when there’s nobody to work at any of these, this whole type of job?” Rossney said, also referring to trades workers. “And it’s not like menial work. I mean, the people that work for us are highly skilled professionals.”
El El Frijoles is just one of the restaurants on the Blue Hill peninsula and in Deer Isle-Stonington that shorten their weekly hours and the length of their seasons because of a lack of employees. That’s been a long-running challenge in an area with limited affordable housing, but it seems to some to have intensified amid the complex changes brought on by the pandemic, and has some local business owners seeing more need to bring in outside seasonal workers.
Nearby Mount Desert Island and its major tourist draw of Acadia National Park has an established system of housing for seasonal employees, often arriving from other countries on work visas. But employers on the comparatively much quieter Blue Hill peninsula generally don’t have such resources.
In 2019, when five new restaurants had recently opened in Blue Hill, the owners of four of them told the Bangor Daily News that operations were limited by a “desperate” shortage of workers and largely attributed that to a lack of affordable housing. All four establishments have since closed.
Since the pandemic, a number of people who work from home for employers based elsewhere seem to have stayed, Rossney said, and he sees the peninsula trending toward being home to mostly retirees and remote workers.
It’s not just restaurant workers in demand: it’s difficult to get on the schedules of tradespeople in the area now, and the couple wonder whether that’s related to newcomers or seasonal residents building with pockets deep enough to pay any cost. It’s a contrast to the peninsula of a decade ago, when they remember many more vacant buildings and small apartments before the rise of short term rentals.
Rossney, who grew up spending summers in the area, said the peninsula has always been made up of distinct groups. But he thinks the separation is becoming more stark, and sees some early signs here of the social media-fueled, short term tourism that has crowded Bar Harbor — though he emphasized appreciation for El El Frijoles’ employees and customers.
Pandemic fallout hasn’t seemed as stark to Ron Watson, who has done business in Stonington for decades, but he, too, sees a problem. He opened Stonington Ice Cream Company on Main Street in 2008, adding the Stonington Food Company restaurant three years ago in the neighboring building he owns, and is closed more often than he’d like because of a lack of staff.
“Everyone is in this boat, where they could do more business if there were workers, and there just aren’t,” he said.
Watson wants to be open from early May through late October, but closed before the end of September this year because he had only one employee when the rest of his workforce went back to school.
He thinks seasonal housing for workers is needed on the island, but suspects it may be a harder sell for donors than existing local efforts to build housing for the year-round workforce.
“I get frustrated that there’s no emphasis on seasonal [worker] housing, and this community is rapidly becoming a tourist community, except for the lobster industry, and it’s not going to change,” Watson said, citing factors like the island’s limited industrial infrastructure and fresh water supply that he thinks limits its options for growth.
He doesn’t know how much the unfilled positions have to do with housing availability for locals, he said, noting that seasonal work isn’t appealing for everybody. Watson’s interest in more seasonal housing stems from local lobster dealers’ successes bringing in workers from Puerto Rico, who are U.S. citizens and thus simpler to hire than those requiring visas.
He would have been there himself this spring recruiting, Watson said, if he had housing here to offer. But restaurant owners don’t generally have the margins to take on such a project alone, according to Watson.
“[Stonington] is going to be a tourist community, and like any tourist community where real estate values are increasing, it’s hard to find accommodations for workers, for seasonal workers,” he said.
He, Rossney and Levesque said numerous other local restaurants face similar staffing challenges that limit their hours.
Earlier this year, area establishments such as pizza restaurant and cafe Tinder Hearth in Brooksville and The Ark inn and restaurant in Deer Isle advertised for employee housing.
“It’s a rough go out there,” Tinder Hearth posted on social media in May, asking for leads for seasonal staff whose accommodations fell through.
It’s also hard for seasonal restaurants to find local adult workers because people who want to work in restaurants prefer to be employed year-round and get health benefits, according to Watson.
Bringing in workers through visas also requires housing, which most area restaurants don’t have, Rossney and Levesque said.
They see the economy here as booming but not necessarily healthy, and wonder if at some point a bubble will burst amid national trends of wealth consolidation.
Overall, the labor shortage appears to be one symptom of a web of complex challenges facing communities across coastal Maine, and quick fixes aren’t easy to find.
“I don’t have any real solutions. I think it’s a difficult issue, even more difficult than long term housing,” said Watson. “But … it contributes to the life of the community, and I think there are people who come seasonally who stay and contribute to the life of the community.”

A Windham woman is asking for the public's help finding her dog, Boomer, who has been missing for several days.
According to the owner, Boomer was last seen on Vance Drive in Windham on Sept. 25 between 5 p.m. and 6 p.m. He is an 8-year-old brown Lab-pit mix weighing about 90 pounds and was not wearing a collar or other identifying gear when he disappeared.

A New Hampshire-based drone search team, 2A TAC Air OPS Drone Services, joined the search for Boomer using thermal imaging drones.

title: Bride’s sheepadoodle steals the show in viral wedding video
text:
DOOR COUNTY, Wis. (WBAY/Gray News) - When a bride decided to have her dog be part of her wedding, she couldn’t have expected that he’d end up being the star of the show.
Emily Cowles and her husband, Josh, married Aug. 22 in Door County, Wisconsin.
“Door County is just like heaven. It’s my happy place. So, we go back frequently. And yeah, that’s where we wanted to get married,” Cowles said.
The couple had decided that Cowles’s 5-year-old sheepadoodle, Swayze, needed to be part of their celebration.
“He is just a bright light to anybody who meets him. He’s so goofy and a great snuggler. Everybody calls him a Muppet. He’s just the best,” Cowles said.
Cowles had the idea to strap a GoPro onto Swayze and capture the celebration from the dog’s point of view.
Cowles posted the video of Swayze’s perspective of the wedding online. It has since gone viral, drawing millions of views.
“All of a sudden, the shares started going up. I’m like, what is going on? Then suddenly The Dodo’s reaching out, we got published in People, and then we woke up to being on Good Morning America. I’m like, what is going on?” Cowles said.
Cowles said the best part isn’t the attention the video received but the moments she didn’t know were caught on camera, including one between Swayze and her 91-year-old grandmother.
“He, like, took refuge in spending time with her for like 20 minutes. It was so sweet. And you can just hear him talk or her talking to him. And it was just so, so sweet to watch back,” Cowles said.
Cowles said she and Josh will keep those unscripted moments for years to come.
“There’s going to be a day when not all those people are going to be around. And especially Swayze. Um, so we’re going to be able to look back and it’s just going to bring a smile to our face for the rest of our lives,” Cowles said.
Cowles said Swayze has taken the newfound attention in stride.
“He’s so humble. We’re trying not to let it go to his head,” Cowles said.

title: Why I’m choosing Jackson over Collins
text:
At age 54, with several years of service in public safety, many as a firefighter/EMT, my life’s work has been rooted in keeping our communities safe, secure and supported. I know what it means to answer the call when families are facing their worst moments.
Sen. Susan Collins’ commercial showcasing the firehouses that received federal funding are grinding my gears. The much-needed funding was coming, no matter who put the requests through. Many firefighters are sitting around their kitchen tables trying to figure out how to pay their bills because of Collins’ negligence in the U.S. Senate.
Federal firehouse funding relies on the state delegation’s collaborative effort. The senators submit parallel requests for municipal projects, while the representatives submit matching House earmarks to ensure budget parity. Meanwhile, operational equipment, turnout gear and staffing funds flow through FEMA programs.
By contrast, Troy Jackson has tirelessly supported first responders. His high-profile advocacy for emergency services throughout his Maine legislative career makes his seat on the Congressional Fire Services Caucus a given — potentially it could even lead to a chairmanship.
Here’s just a couple examples:
- 2010 (LD 1558): Jackson sponsored accidental death benefits to close MainePERS loopholes for families of firefighters lost to job-related cardiovascular or respiratory events.
- 2021 (LD 213): Jackson championed the expanded firefighter cancer presumption, updating worker protections to cover female firefighters facing gynecologic cancers tied to PFAS and toxic exposure.
That is why I am proudly supporting Troy Jackson for the U.S. Senate and I hope others will also.

title: Nolo becomes a Category 3 Hurricane in the remote Pacific Ocean
text:
Nolo strengthened into a major hurricane Saturday in the remote Pacific Ocean, far to the west of Hawaii’s main islands and population centers.
The storm’s maximum sustained winds rapidly intensified to 115 mph (185 kph), the Miami-based National Hurricane Center reported, meaning it was a Category 3 hurricane.
Nolo was located about 210 miles (335 kilometers) south-southwest of Maro Reef and moving westward at 17 mph (28 kph).
A tropical storm warning was issued for the Papahanaumokuakea Marine National Monument — a massive and remote federally protected area with islands, atolls, seamounts, shoals and coral reefs — from Maro Reef to Lisianski Island.
The hurricane center said large surf associated with Nolo “will likely inundate some of the low-lying atolls.”
No threat was in the forecast for any populated islands, however.
The hurricane center said Nolo was expected to cross the international date line Sunday.
Nolo skirted Hawaii as a hurricane a week ago. It then lost some of its punch and became a tropical storm, before regaining hurricane strength Friday.
Meanwhile another Pacific hurricane, Category 1 Rachel, continued heading westward on a path away from the west coast of Mexico.
Dangerous swells were forecast through the weekend for the coast of west-central Mexico and through Monday for the Baja California Peninsula, according to the hurricane center.

title: Coast Guard searching for missing jet heading to Boston from Bermuda with 6 on board
text:
(Gray News) - The U.S. Coast Guard has launched a search for a missing jet after the FAA reported losing contact with the aircraft.
The U.S. Coast Guard Northeast reported at 6:15 a.m. Saturday that a Gulfstream G100 jet with the tail number CGRJP was heading to Boston from Bermuda when it disappeared.
Six people were on board.
According to Boston 25 News, the jet was a medical transfer aircraft. The Nantucket Current reported that the aircraft is registered to Latitude Air Ambulance, which is based in Ontario, Canada.
Boston 25 News obtained audio transmissions from air traffic controllers in Boston in the moments before they lost contact. In the transmissions, the air traffic controllers asked the aircraft if it was “coming in blind.” According to the Nantucket Current, the Nantucket Memorial Airport reported the pilot declared an emergency before the jet disappeared.
The Coast Guard said it is currently searching for the plane in the area surrounding Nantucket. Both air and surface crews have been launched to assist with the search.
The Coast Guard said the HC-144 Ocean Sentry airplane crew and MH-60 Jayhawk helicopter crew from AirSta Cape Cod, the HC-130 Hercules crew from AirSta Elizabeth City, the 7-foot MLB crew from Station Brant Point and FRC William Sparling (WPC-1154) are assisting in the search.
In an update posted at 11:46 a.m. Saturday, the Coast Guard said its search remains ongoing.
By that evening, Coast Guard crews found a debris field associated with the plane, but no passengers had been found.
No further information has been provided at this time.

title: Divide over vote to strip George Mitchell's name at UMaine shows how deep his legacy extends
text:
While former U.S. Senator George Mitchell’s name will soon be removed from a University of Maine building, those who know him say his legacy will continue — with some scarring.
The University of Maine System Board of Trustees voted 9-5 to remove Mitchell’s name from a building, fund and scholarship Monday. The renaming was brought to a vote after a taskforce found that using Mitchell’s name would “compromise the public trust and reflect adversely upon” UMaine or the system.
The half hour of discussion before the vote showed a divide between Mainers who think Mitchell’s association with convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, and allegations of him knowing about Epstein’s illegal actions, warranted his name being stripped from programs and buildings and those who say the allegations shouldn’t affect Mitchell’s legacy in the state.
Mitchell, who served as a U.S. Senator from 1980 to 1995 and created multiple charitable organizations and programs including the Mitchell Institute, is a renowned Maine politician and statesman. His work has been met with awards and recognition, but he has faced an ongoing reckoning for his relationship with Epstein after his name was found in more than 300 documents released by the Department of Justice earlier this year.
Despite Mitchell, 93, denying any knowledge of Epstein’s illegal actions, his name has been stripped from buildings and programs in Maine and Ireland. He also stepped down as honorary chairman of the Mitchell Institute.
Nevertheless, his defenders have said his legacy of philanthropy that has helped Mainers afford college and brought peace to Northern Ireland will remain but may require more explaining.
Former U.S. Rep. Tom Allen can remember meeting Mitchell for what may have been the first time in 1970 when both of them worked for U.S. Senator Edmund Muskie’s re-election campaign. In the decades that followed, Allen and Mitchell talked and occasionally played tennis together. Despite taking lessons, Allen said he may have only won one set because Mitchell would always rally without mistakes.
When reflecting on Mitchell’s achievements in the past half century, which include being awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom for his work in Northern Ireland, Allen, 81, said it would be a discredit to Mitchell’s work if his name were absent from Maine. If he were part of the discussion at UMaine, Allen would have told the board of trustees to “soldier through” any negative feedback Mitchell’s name would have incurred.
“I just think it’s wrong because it feels as if the people who are making those decisions may be anticipating some negative impact on the board or the group that they’re representing, and I think they ought to filter through it because this is one of Maine’s greatest political figures, and in my experience, one of the finest human beings I’ve ever known,” Allen said.
Although he admits he doesn’t know details about the Epstein allegations or files, Allen said Mitchell was an influential figure as the senate majority leader and would have built connections with the people in Epstein’s circle. Knowing those figures doesn’t mean the allegations are true, Allen said.
“In five years, this will be a non-issue,” Allen said. “The Epstein files will be buried, and Mitchell’s legacy will be, you know, there’s a scar there because he went to those gatherings, but it’s basically, in my opinion, guilt by association.”
One of the five trustees who voted against the renaming, Donna Loring, said her vote was based on Mitchel’s legacy, she wrote in a Bangor Daily News op-ed.
Mitchell’s work in congress, peace negotiations in Ireland and the more than 4,000 scholarships awarded to Mainers from his institute are all part of his legacy, she wrote. By keeping his name in place, Maine can “tell the whole story” of his career and let people ask questions about the allegations.
“We should not ignore the questions raised about Mitchell’s association with Epstein. We should not minimize them, and we should certainly not prevent students from examining them. But neither should those questions cause us to diminish everything else,” Loring wrote.
Loring went on to say she “could not vote to diminish a lifetime of documented public service based on allegations for which there has been no finding of wrongdoing.”
Echoing Loring’s statement, trustee Roger Katz, who voted to accept the renaming, said at the board meeting that while he agreed with the task force’s finding that keeping Mitchell’s name related to the university may reflect poorly, he hoped “the next generations appreciate what a giant this person has been in so many areas, and what a credit to Maine.”
The board’s vote was “an appropriate action to protect the reputation” of UMaine, State Sen. Joe Baldacci, D-Bangor, Mitchell’s cousin, said. It’s “wise advice” to not name buildings or monuments after living figures and let history make a judgment, he said.
It’s hard to know if any of the discussions and choices to rename programs and buildings will actually affect Mitchell’s legacy, Allen said.
“It’s hard to say. I mean, your name on a building when you’ve had a career like that is a trigger for people to remember. How much it changes [a person’s legacy], I’m not sure,” Allen said.

title: Axe-wielding FlyDubai co-pilot had been flagged over extremism concerns, sources say
text:
Axe-wielding FlyDubai co-pilot had been flagged over concerns about extremist views, sources say
The co-pilot accused of attacking the captain on an Israel-bound flight with an axe and trying to seize the controls was an Omani national who had been barred from flying on his country’s airline because of concerns about extremist views, officials said Saturday.
Related video above: Co-pilot of an Israel-bound FlyDubai flight tried to hijack the plane after stabbing the captain
The co-pilot has been identified as Hamam al-Hammami, according to three people with knowledge of the situation, including a Gulf and Western diplomat, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to the media.
The United Arab Emirates, which is leading the investigation, said the co-pilot attacked with the cockpit’s crash axe and tried to take control of the sharply plummeting plane in a "terrorist attack" Wednesday. His actions nearly crashed the plane with 182 people on board before passengers and others rushed in and subdued him.
The new details raised questions about how thoroughly FlyDubai vets potential employees, and how the co-pilot's presence on a flight filled with Israeli passengers got past Israel's strict security protocols.
Israel’s government has said it has agreements with foreign carriers to keep pilots from nations without diplomatic ties from flying there. Israel and Oman do not have formal diplomatic relations. The UAE government has earned a reputation for effective measures against extremist activities but has bristled in the past over criticism of security lapses.
The incident occurred at a sensitive time for Israel, a week before the anniversary of the Hamas-led attack on Oct. 7, 2023, that sparked the war in Gaza. It also came weeks before a highly contentious election in which security and Oct. 7 security failures have been central issues.
FlyDubai hired the co-pilot after Oman Air barred him
Separately, a regional official and a person familiar with the matter said the co-pilot had been barred from flying by Oman over concerns he had adopted extremist views. The official said he was moved to an administrative job at Oman Air. Both spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss the ongoing investigation. They gave no details about the alleged extremist views.
The co-pilot was later hired by UAE-based airline FlyDubai, the person said. It was not immediately clear to what extent the co-pilot was vetted. The Gulf diplomat said he had undergone standard security checks before being hired, but it appears that the checks focused on whether he had been convicted of criminal charges and did not go deeper into examining his background for potential signs of radicalization.
The regional official also said security agencies from four regional countries were working to establish the co-pilot’s motives, aided by the United States and other Western governments. The Gulf diplomat said investigations were trying to establish whether the co-pilot acted alone or "has any connection with any extremist groups."
The regional official said the co-pilot was born in the UAE and his mother is Syrian. He obtained Omani nationality from his father, also an Omani national. The regional official also said the co-pilot had traveled to Syria, with no details.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Friday said the co-pilot had undergone “Islamist radicalization,” but provided no evidence. There was no immediate comment Saturday from Israel’s government.
A social media account was deleted the day of the flight
A FlyDubai spokesperson said in an email that the airline could not comment beyond its official statements and acknowledged “there are many questions at this stage.” There was no immediate comment from Oman Air, and Oman’s government has said nothing publicly in response to repeated questions since the incident.
In a statement to the AP, Royal Air Maroc, Morocco's national carrier, said the co-pilot "completed a three-month theoretical training period with the airline in 2025, as part of the pre-employment process. At the end of this training period, his application was not selected for employment.” There were no details.
Keith Coles, a spokesperson for Buckinghamshire New University in England, told the AP that al-Hammami previously completed a distance-learning course in aviation management there but “did not undertake any pilot training.” There were no details on the timing.
Little else was immediately known about the co-pilot’s background. His Instagram account was active until the day of the flight and then deleted.
Captain and passengers have described a drama set to screams
Airlines are generally required to carry crash axes in the cockpit that could be used in an emergency to break open a window to escape or break open a panel to access a fire.
The captain, who was badly wounded in the axe attack, has said he used his remaining energy while being attacked to unlock the cockpit door, allowing people who had noticed alarmingly unusual sounds to come in, tackle the co-pilot and stabilize the flight while passengers screamed.
The plane made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia after a descent so extreme that part of the rudder was torn away, and aviation experts have marveled that it did not crash. FlyDubai has said a crew traveling on the plane helped stabilize the plane and land. They have not yet been publicly identified.
Both the captain and co-pilot were later taken to the UAE. The passengers, most of them Israeli, flew home later Wednesday on a separate plane, to cheers.
___
Mednick reported from Tel Aviv, Israel, and Anna from Jerusalem. AP Washington bureau chief Anna Johnson in Washington, aviation writer Josh Funk and Sam Metz in Jerusalem contributed.

title: UMaine football drops 5th straight game
text:
Nick Laughlin of Cape Elizabeth scored early in the fourth quarter to pull Maine within six, but the Black Bears couldn’t get any closer and suffered their fifth straight loss, falling to Sacred Heart 24-16 on Saturday in Orono.
Maine falls to 1-5 overall and 1-2 in the Coastal Athletic Conference. The Black Bears have not won since beating Towson in their season opener on Aug. 27.
Sacred Heart improves to 2-3 overall and 2-2 in the conference.
Laughlin scored on a 2-yard rush with 12:03 left to make it 21-15. Maine gave up a 40-yard field goal to Ryan Bocklet on the ensuing Sacred Heart possession, then drove to the Pioneers’ 37-yard line before turning the ball over on downs with 1:40 left.
Maine forced a Sacred Heart punt and started a drive at its own 43 with 1:16 left. The Black Bears gained one first down, but quarterback Caden Drezek threw four straight incomplete passes from the Sacred Heart 47 to end Maine’s hopes.
Drezek, who saw the bulk of the snaps after starting the season as the backup, went 12 for 28 passing for 141 yards. Eddie Buehler completed 1 of 5 passes for 13 yards and was sacked twice.
Maine took a 9-0 lead early in the second quarter on three field goals by Samuel Tremblay (42, 45 and 37 yards). Sacred Heart took the lead on an 11-yard pass from Poochie Snyder to Jason Palmieri with 19 seconds left in the first half.
Snyder completed 21 of 27 passes for 207 yards and two touchdowns.
Maine is off next week and returns to action on Oct. 17 when it host Bryant.

title: Playground in Bristol to be Named After Late Parks Commissioner
text:
The construction of a new playground at Pemaquid Beach Park dedicated to longtime Bristol resident Sandra Lane is set to start later this fall.
Clyde Pendleton, the chair of the Bristol Parks Commission, said it was Lane’s goal to build a more accessible playground, as the only one in town is at Bristol Consolidated School.
On Sept. 17, the Bristol Parks Commission began seeking bids for the project, which has been in the works for over eight years. The plan is now to name it for Lane, at 13-year member of the parks commission who died in August.
“Sandra was the school bus driver, she was community oriented, she loved kids, the whole nine yards,” Pendleton said.
Pendleton said that Lane drove generations of families throughout the years, dedicating her time to helping the community.
After 46 years of service, Lane received the State of Maine Bus Driver Award, along with the Spirit of America Award in 2014. She was named grand marshal for Olde Bristol Days in 2022, in recognition of her service-oriented and driven spirit.
“At her memorial service, she probably had driven 80% of the people in the room,” Bristol Parks and Recreation Director Shelly Gallagher said.
The new playground will be open and accessible year-round, located next to the ball field at Pemaquid Beach Park. According to the Bristol Parks Commission, the playground will be completed no later than May 2027.
All proceeds from the Pemaquid Beach Triathlons will go directly toward funding the new playground and no tax dollars will go toward the project, Pendleton said.
“If people want to donate towards the playground, donations are welcome and encouraged,” Gallagher said.
For more information, call 563-1800 or go to bristolmaine.org.

title: More than 4,500 pounds of imported chicken stew recalled over missed reinspection
text:
CALIFORNIA (Gray News) - More than 4,500 pounds of imported ready-to-eat chicken stew are being recalled because the products were not reinspected after entering the U.S., federal officials said.
Sempio Food Services Inc., based in Cerritos, California, is recalling about 4,596 pounds of stew imported from South Korea, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Food Safety and Inspection Service.
The chicken stew products were produced on March 30 and have best-by date of September 29, 2027. The following products are part of the recall:
- Cardboard boxes containing pouches of 31.75-oz (900 g) “Sempio Korean Ginseng CHICKEN STEW CLASSIC”
- Cardboard boxes containing pouches of 31.75-oz (900 g) “Sempio Korean Ginseng CHICKEN STEW RICH”
The products bear Korean establishment number “GIA15001” and shipping mark “MK-2026-0422-01”.
The products were shipped to distributors and retailers in Florida, Georgia, Illinois, Maryland, New Jersey, New York, Pennsylvania and Virginia.
There have been no confirmed reports of illness or injury, but officials are concerned some products may still be in consumers’ pantries.
Consumers who purchased the products should not eat them and should throw them away or return them to the place of purchase. Retailers should not sell the products.

title: Shop clerk, son charged with selling illegal kratom amid probe into Ole Miss student deaths
text:
MEMPHIS, Tenn. (WMC/Gray News) - Authorities investigating the deaths of two University of Mississippi students have charged a store clerk and his son with selling an illegal kratom product.
A new federal filing says a toxicology report on Aidan Hamilton and Robert Strang found the substances mitragynine, MGM-15 and MGPI in their systems.
Those same substances were found in “Smax Mango Breeze” pills that investigators found in both students’ rooms after their deaths.
Investigators allege that Puffs Vape, Tobacco and Beer Store in Oxford sold Hamilton the pills twice in the days before his death. Bank records show Hamilton made multiple purchases in September from the store, according to a federal court filing.
The toxicology details come from a motion from federal prosecutors to keep Yahya Mosleh, the manager of Puffs, and his 18-year-old son, Islam Mosleh, in custody.
Mosleh, 51, and his son appeared in federal court on Thursday, where a judge ruled there was probable cause to hand down federal charges against the pair.
In the motion, prosecutors describe the men as posing a danger to the community.
Last week, Lafayette County Metro Narcotics agents sent a confidential informant into Puffs Vape, Tobacco and Beer Store in Oxford to investigate alleged sales of illegal substances, according to the arrest affidavit.
The informant asked if the store sold “7-OH kratom-based pills.”
Records show Yahya Mosleh allegedly said yes before warning the informant to “be careful taking the pills, because people are dying from them.”
Oxford police then executed a search warrant at the store, and 500 units of kratom and kratom-like products were seized. An assortment of “THC cartridges, gummies, pre-rolls and other suspected THC substances” was also recovered.
During the search, detectives found the same brand of Smax Mango Breeze MGM-15, with identical packaging, ingredients and a $39.99 price tag with a smudge on the 9, that had been found near Hamilton.
Prosecutors noted that Islam Mosleh, who attends Oxford High School, had previously drawn complaints from a school resource officer who suspected that Mosleh was selling THC vapes to students at the school. Similar vapes were found in Islam Mosleh’s pockets and backpack.
The Moslehs face federal charges of possession of a controlled substance with intent to distribute. Their attorneys told WMC they have no comment.
When WMC was at the scene of the vape shop on Friday night, four different people tried to walk in, only to be met with a note that the shop is closed until further notice.
Jimmy, who works at Heritage Wine & Liquor next door, said he came to work Thursday at 1 p.m. to a parking lot full of law enforcement and narcotics officers.
He said an employee told him a young man, assumed to be Islam Mosleh, tried to run when police arrived, though he didn’t see it himself.
“As a former college professor, it’s heartbreaking. They get to be not children, but kind of like surrogate children,” Jimmy said. “My bottom line is that I’m not going to say what they did. That’s none of my business. The law will determine that in time, but the loss of young people like that is a terrible tragedy.”
Angelica McKinney, who lives nearby, said she was shocked to learn the store at the center of the investigation was in her neighborhood.
“When I first heard that it was this store here, I was shocked because a lot of people do come here to buy what they need out of here,” McKinney said.
McKinney said she wasn’t necessarily surprised to hear an 18-year-old was accused of selling THC-type vapes.
“Nowadays, kids at the age of 18 think they know it all... Of course there’s something they’re gonna consider if it’s easy money, right?” she said.
She urged parents to have hard conversations about mental health and peer pressure:
“Kids are dealing with depression. So, right now, they’re literally trying to find any and everything to cope with whatever they have going on. So parents just be open to what’s going on with these children nowadays.”
While officials believe it was the Oxford store that sold Hamilton the narcotics found in his system, they say Strang bought his pills from a different store outside the county 20 miles away.
Investigators have not yet said if they’ve determined exactly what killed either student.
Hamilton was laid to rest in Denver on Friday.

title: How Jon Ossoff and Susan Collins are turning a mundane part of their jobs into a reelection pitch
text:
ATHENS, Ga. — After Hurricane Helene barreled through Georgia in the fall of 2024, Sen. Jon Ossoff was the first high-ranking official on the ground in Valdosta, where he took in the damage and promised locals he’d help them get the federal recovery assistance they needed.
“Just about every week, I dial up Georgia mayors and pastors and farmers to find out how I can help,” Ossoff said at a recent campaign rally for his reelection bid against Republican Rep. Mike Collins.
Up the Eastern Seaboard, Maine Sen. Susan Collins keeps a regular itinerary of local events, including ribbon-cuttings and groundbreakings for projects she helped finance as Senate Appropriations Committee chair.
“There’s not a community in Maine that can’t say Susan helped us,” intones the voiceover in a campaign ad for Collins. The five-term senator, who’s not related to the Georgia congressman, is facing Democratic former state legislative leader Troy Jackson in November.
The two senators — Ossoff the Democrat, Collins the Republican — began this election cycle widely viewed as their respective parties’ most vulnerable members. But as Republican Donald Trump’s second presidency and partisan fights on Capitol Hill dominate national political conversation, the senators’ campaigns have played out differently than expected in part because of the more mundane part of their jobs: helping the people back home.
“We in the political world tend to think about the strength of incumbency through the lens of fundraising and national media attention, and those do matter,” said Republican Chris Hartline, once a top adviser at the National Republican Senatorial Campaign Committee. “But the ability to help the local communities you actually represent still matters.”
For Ossoff, it means attracting endorsements from Republican officials, including Valdosta Mayor Scott James Matheson, that have made it harder for Mike Collins to land attacks claiming that the liberal first-term senator from Atlanta doesn’t represent Georgia. For Susan Collins, it means a go-to buffer argument as she runs with the weight of Trump’s lagging popularity and her support for various parts of his agenda.
A month from Election Day, Ossoff has gone from a top GOP target to a widely perceived favorite to defend a seat that Democrats cannot afford to lose as they try to regain a Senate majority. And as Republican incumbents like Ohio Sen. Jon Husted are increasingly viewed as underdogs, strategists in both parties still view Susan Collins’ race as a tossup.
Ossoff draws begrudging respect from Republicans
Ossoff and his aides say the senator tries to deliver on every aspect of what Washington calls “constituent services.”
That could mean federal appropriations, disaster assistance or nuts-and-bolts matters like assisting a voter who is seeking Social Security disability benefits or a missing Social Security check. It includes surprise notes of congratulations or condolences to constituents — something Ossoff sends even to aides of Republican elected officials.
Endorsing Ossoff earlier this year, Matheson, the Valdosta mayor, described himself as a lifelong conservative. But he praised Ossoff for his Helene response. The senator recalled “going block by block” with the mayor and serving “hot meals to folks who had just lost their homes.”
Ossoff points to money secured for a dialysis center in nearby Tifton, Georgia. Mayor Julie Smith, another Republican, has endorsed Ossoff, too, explaining that “he’s been very good for south Georgia.”
Courtney Eskew, whose husband, Joshua, was injured during an Army tour in Afghanistan, pointed to Ossoff’s work for veterans’ care. The couple both grew up in Republican households but said they were volunteering for Ossoff’s campaign.
“Senator Ossoff has been passionately vocal about VA funding, and any time we’ve needed to call to advocate or to ask a question about benefits, his office has done everything we needed,” Eskew said after the couple attended an Ossoff event.
Eskew said it’s a powerful counter to opponent Mike Collins’ attacks that Ossoff is too liberal for the historically conservative state.
Ossoff “doesn’t vote the way I want him to vote” on contentious issues, added Chan Jones, who chairs the Georgia Republican Party’s 8th Congressional District committee. “But as far as the office and the way they’ve carried themselves and handled other aspects of the job, I can’t knock that.”
Jones has his own example as a member of the Bleckley County Recreation Board.
“We were having some trouble with a federal grant,” he said, adding that one call to the senator’s office fixed the issue.
Mainers must decide the value of seniority
Susan Collins is relentless in promoting money she’s steered to Maine — for community colleges and hospital expansions or hyperlocal examples like a program to control the spruce budworm, a threat to the state’s forests and timber industry.
“That will go away with a freshman senator,” she said at a Maine manufacturing conference earlier this year. “It took me years to climb the ladder of seniority.”
No project is too small for her argument. In late August, she attended a ribbon-cutting ceremony for the rehabilitation of St. Croix Apartments in Calais, a city of about 3,000 residents on the Canadian border, more than 200 miles (320 kilometers) from Portland. It’s in a conservative part of the state where GOP candidates need heavy turnout to win statewide.
Collins was there to highlight $3 million she secured to restore 26 affordable housing units for low-income seniors.
“The renovated St. Croix Apartments will provide seniors with safe and affordable homes close to the family, friends and community they love,” Collins said.
The amount is a pittance within appropriations bills measured in the billions. But it’s the kind of work many Maine residents associate with the veteran lawmaker.
In the same campaign stretch, Collins visited a child development center in Bangor to highlight Head Start funding. In the summer, she walked in the Casco Days Grand Parade to raise money for the local fire association and stopped by the dedication of a new fire station in the town of Sweden, population 400.
At the same time, Collins has maintained a stretch in Washington of more than 10,000 consecutive votes — a streak she connects to those results back home.
Collins and Ossoff are following an old script
There are recent examples of candidates succeeding by doing what Collins and Ossoff are trying.
The late Mississippi Sen. Thad Cochran, another powerful committee chairman, withstood a fierce Republican primary challenge to win his final election in 2014 by coaxing Democratic crossover voters in part because of his decades of appropriating money.
Hartline, who worked for Senate Republicans in 2022, pointed to Wisconsin Sen. Ron Johnson as a bright spot in an otherwise tough cycle for the party.
“Johnson knew every corner of Wisconsin because he’d been there,” Hartline said.
Collins, especially, needs that dynamic to outweigh national circumstances.
Democrats, Jackson included, have hammered her for not having done enough to shield Maine from Trump’s tariffs — which she has criticized — and for backing the Iran war, which has raised fuel prices.
But even Jackson supporters recognize Collins’ ability to win five elections when Maine has opted for Democrats in every presidential contest.
Warsame Dualeh, a 45-year-old Jackson supporter, mused about weak opponents — though Collins has drawn aggressive Democratic opposition over the years. And then he acknowledged that the federal money pipeline “very well could be” the reason for Collins’ durability.

title: Ellsworth rides second half surge to beat Mt. Ararat
South Portland tax burden is a source of dread
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The cumulative effect of the following paints a dire picture for South Portland residents. All residents will be impacted and most will suffer the consequences of these tax increases, revenue bonds and other proposals:
- Maine’s median home sale price increased approximately 92% over the past eight years, directly impacting real estate taxes due to city-wide required assessments.
- Annual increases in real estate tax (3.4% for 2026).
- Existing bond debt of $369 annually for the average household.
- Proposed revenue bonds:
  - Police and fire Phase 1 and Phase 2, resulting in a tax increase leading up to $534 by 2030.
  - Pump station/waste water infrastructure resulting in a sewer rate impact estimate of 26%, and leading to an increase of $18.24 by 2029 (per city of South Portland mailer).
- Household waste proposal annual increase of up to $219.
This last proposal was rejected recently.
Unfortunately, the average South Portland homeowner has two choices: continue to absorb huge increases as described or leave our beloved city.
Maine has the oldest population in the U.S. with roughly 23% of its residents 65 or older. Many South Portland residents fall into this category, including me, a 41-year resident/homeowner. It will be a very bleak picture for many if much of the above is implemented.
Joseph Nitsche
South Portland

title: Dashcam video shows a dramatic near-miss with a semitruck during intense rainfall on highway
text:
(CNN) - Dashcam video shows an out-of-control semitruck narrowly avoiding other vehicles on a Nebraska highway Wednesday.
The driver whose camera recorded the video said heavy rain in Omaha was limiting visibility at the time.
The rain also appeared to have caused slick roadways.
The video shows the truck whipping across the highway and ending up perpendicular to traffic.
The National Weather Service said remnants of Hurricane Polo brought Omaha more than four inches of rain in six hours.

title: Colby College hosts #STRONGGIRLS day camp to empower young women
text:
WATERVILLE, Maine (WABI) - Instilling confidence in the next generation- that’s the goal of the #STRONGGIRLS day camp held at Colby College Saturday.
The camp is designed to give young girls ages 10-14 the tools to support themselves through life’s challenges.
“It’s kind of surreal in a way,” said Caroline Hartley, Colby College Athlete
“It just feels like, honestly, like just yesterday that I was one of these girls, kind of trying to figure out my life too, and I just remember how I would always look up to the girls that were older than me.”
60 middle school girls gathered to mingle with peers and mentors and learn about healthy relationships in all areas, from mind and body to social relationships and food.
“So, there are actually 6 modules. It’s strong mind, strong body, strong leadership, strong grit, strong relationships, and strong confidence,” said Leah Lawrence, Impact Program Manager with the Lindsey Vonn Foundation.
Vonn is an Olympic gold medalist skier who created the Lindsey Vonn Foundation as a way to empower young women and connect them with mentors.
“They also get to take home a strong girls journal that Lindsey actually put together a few years ago with some educators, and they are things that she uses to this day,” continued Lawrence.
“We’ve got over 20 student athlete mentors joining them throughout the day and really what our goal is to provide them with tools that can help them move through the world with confidence.”
Middle school can be one of the hardest times in a young girl’s life. Mentors say they hope that this camp can help to inspire confidence and strength in the minds of these young girls.
“It’s kind of like a key part of their life, you know, like growing. Going through middle school can be a really hard kind of phase of, being a little bit more judgmental of themselves or kind of just becoming more aware of what’s going on around them. So being able to grow their confidence and just being kind of receptive of like we were once those girls too, like trying to grow into one ourselves and just reminding them that there’s just so much more that we can reflect on and be grateful for within our lives.” said Hartley.
