title: Trump to rally in Nebraska on Monday ahead of midterms
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - President Donald Trump will hold a rally on Monday at the Pinnacle Bank Expo Center in Grand Island, Neb., as he continues a series of stops in Republican-leaning states ahead of the midterms.
Trump is campaigning for Sen. Pete Ricketts (R-Neb.) and Governor Jim Pillen (R-Neb.). A new Wedgewood poll shows both candidates leading their opponents, with Ricketts ahead by four points.
Ricketts is facing independent candidate Dan Osborn. Pillen is facing former state Sen. Lynne Walz, a Democrat.
The administration’s move to import millions of tons of foreign beef has affected the state’s cattle industry. The industry is also facing costs tied to fertilizer, tariffs, and diesel priced at $6.37.
The president’s approval rating has slid in all 10 key cattle states, according to Civiqs’ rolling online tracking system. Half of Nebraskans approve of the job the president is doing.
The Nebraska stop is one of dozens planned during a multi-day push ahead of the midterms. The president plans to visit swing states as well as reliably red states considered competitive.

title: One month from Election Day, here are the Senate races to watch
text:
One month from Election Day, here are the Senate races to watch
The map of the most competitive races continues to evolve as Republicans shift spending priorities.
One month from Election Day, here are the Senate races to watch
The map of the most competitive races continues to evolve as Republicans shift spending priorities.
With one month left until Election Day, candidates are racing against time to sway voters in critical Senate contests as the map of the most competitive races continues to evolve.
President Donald Trump is campaigning in Ohio on Saturday, where a race between Republican Sen. Jon Husted and former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown could play a decisive role in the balance of power.
Ohio is home to one of seven Senate races currently classified as "toss-ups," according to the Cook Political Report. Others are playing out in Alaska, Iowa, Maine, Michigan, New Hampshire and Texas.
The Associated Press reported Friday that Senate Republicans' top campaign-spending organization is investing more heavily to defend Kansas Sen. Roger Marshall, the GOP incumbent, against Democratic challenger Adam Hamilton, leader of the nation’s largest United Methodist Church. The race has moved into increasingly competitive territory, which is notable considering that Trump carried Kansas by double digits in 2024 and the state has not sent a Democrat to the Senate since 1932.
Meanwhile, the GOP-aligned Senate Leadership Fund is scaling back resources in North Carolina, a swing state where Michael Whatley, a former Republican National Committee chairman, is consistently trailing former Democratic Gov. Roy Cooper in the polls. The seat is currently held by Republican Sen. Thom Tillis, who is retiring.
When asked Friday about the spending shift and whether he is concerned about Whatley's chances, Trump said, "I am because he's a great man, and I am worried about him. I hope he wins."
Democrats are at risk of coming up short while defending Senate seats in New Hampshire and Michigan that the party currently controls.
Democrats need to gain a net of four seats to reclaim the majority in the upper chamber, but that outcome is not a given. The Cook Political Report currently predicts a Democratic pickup of between one and five seats.
Analysts generally believe that Democrats have an easier path to retake control of the House of Representatives.

title: AMC adds the Whitecap Highlands to Maine Woods Initiative
text:
The Alpine-like summit of 3,650-foot White Cap in the heart of the 100-Mile Wilderness affords one of the finest mountaintop vistas in all of Maine. To the north across some 30 miles of heavily forested country stands mile-high Katahdin and its neighbors in Baxter State Park. Looking south, the grand view includes the rest of the White Cap Range, the Barren-Chairback Range, Big Moose Mountain and so much more. Extraordinary!
Much of the land around the White Cap Range has been preserved by the Appalachian Mountain Club over the last two decades or so, to the tune of 130,000 acres. AMC now has its sights set on another piece of the area’s conservation puzzle, the Whitecap Highlands Forest. This 29,500-acre tract on the southern slopes of the range is a mix of fragile high-elevation terrain and cold-water stream habitat for Atlantic salmon and native brook trout.
“The White Cap project is an incredible opportunity to protect a truly stunning, ecologically critical property,” said Steve Tatko, AMC’s vice president of land and conservation. “It really fills in the ‘hole in the donut’ by furthering the protection of the West Branch of the Pleasant River’s headwaters and buffering a scenic section of the Appalachian Trail over Gulf Hagas Mountain, West Peak, Hay Mountain and, of course, White Cap.”
Earlier this year, AMC kicked off a campaign aimed at raising $15 million to support the Whitecap Highlands Forest effort, a goal that, when achieved, will “unlock” an additional $22 million land grant from an anonymous conservation-supporting donor. In the meantime, AMC is working with the interim landowner to manage the land on its behalf, has reopened roads to reestablish public access, and has created new fish passages.
Now in its sesquicentennial year as America’s oldest conservation and recreation organization (1876), AMC established a presence in the 100-Mile Wilderness in 2003 with the purchase of the Katahdin Iron Works Tract. This 37,000-acre parcel includes the eastern four of the Barren-Chairback peaks, Long Pond and the headwaters of the West Branch of the Pleasant River above and along Gulf Hagas, Maine’s “Grand Canyon.”
AMC added the Roach Ponds Tract (29,500 acres) to the north of White Cap in 2009, purchased 4,300 acres around the summit of Baker Mountain (3,528 feet) six years later, and then acquired the Silver Lake Tract (4,400 acres) southeast of White Cap a year after that. Two more land acquisitions followed: the 27,000-acre Pleasant River Headwaters Forest in 2022 and the 29,000-acre Barnard Forest between 2023 and 2025.
AMC’s “Maine Woods Initiative” lands serve as an important anchor in a nearly continuous corridor of conservation lands ranging from Moosehead Lake through the 100-Mile Wilderness to Baxter State Park and Katahdin Woods and Waters National Monument. Including working forest easement lands, the conservation total is in the neighborhood of one million acres, a mind-boggling statistic given that 50 years ago, there was next to none.
In addition to AMC, key players in this conservation mosaic include The Nature Conservancy, National Park Service, the State of Maine, Forest Society of Maine, Maine Audubon, Elliotsville Foundation and Butler Parklands, among others. Baxter State Park, Debsconeag Lakes Wilderness Area, Nahmakanta Public Lands, the Appalachian Trail and Borestone Mountain Sanctuary are some of the notable jewels.
“AMC’s MWI property is remarkable. It’s a big place where we’re doing big things. People are really enjoying it,” Tatko said of this landscape scale conservation model that includes sustainable forest management, multi-use recreation opportunities, outdoor education, and ecological enhancement and protection. “Collaboration with our community partners has been critical to our success and that of the local economy.”
A plan for the Whitecap Highlands Forest hasn’t yet been developed, according to Tatko, but AMC expects to establish new trails connecting the Gulf Hagas area to the White Cap Range ridgeline, good news for hikers looking for new tramping possibilities. This would add nicely to the 200 miles of multiple-use trails on MWI lands currently available.
There are myriad ways to enjoy AMC’s MWI lands, both summer and winter. There’s hiking, paddling, mountain biking, fishing, wildlife watching, stargazing (it’s an International Dark Sky Park), and cross-country skiing and snowshoeing. Along with backcountry and frontcountry camping, AMC also operates three full-service lodges in the Maine sporting camp tradition: Little Lyford near the Little Lyford Ponds, Gorman Chairback on Long Pond and Medawisla on Second Roach Pond.
Carey Kish of Mount Desert Island is a Triple Crown hiker, freelance writer, and author of three hiking guides. Connect with Carey on Facebook and Instagram and at [email protected].

title: Tennessee's prisons chief resigning after failed execution of Christa Pike
text:
Tennessee's prisons chief is resigning after failed execution of Christa Pike
The head of Tennessee's prison system is resigning, Gov. Bill Lee announced Saturday, the first major shake-up since the stunning failed execution of Christa Pike landed her on a ventilator at a hospital.
Related video above: Media witnesses recall what happened during Christa Pike’s failed execution
Frank Strada, commissioner of the Department of Correction, will step down this month, Lee said.
Strada said in a statement that resigning was “in the best interest of Tennesseans” while an independent review determines what happened Wednesday when the state failed to execute Pike despite administering two doses of a lethal drug.
“I believe this review is entirely appropriate and necessary, and I look forward to doing everything I can to help determine exactly what occurred,” Strada said.
Pike was taken to a hospital, where she was on a ventilator and unconscious in the following hours, her attorneys said in a court filing Friday.
Hospital staff were working to save Pike’s life and, as of late Thursday, were trying to clear the two doses of pentobarbital, which the state uses to execute prisoners, lawyers said.
The shocking failure has left both sides of the death penalty debate demanding answers. Lee has ordered an independent review and halted any new executions. Strada said he believes the state “carried out its responsibilities in accordance with the established protocol.”
Pike's legal team welcomed Strada's departure but said, “It does nothing to help Christa now.”
“What happened to her Wednesday reflects a systemic failure that goes far beyond any one person,” the four-lawyer team said. “We hope the governor’s call for a full, independent review will expose the profound problems within Tennessee’s entire death penalty system.”
Pike’s attorneys said they believed problems with the IV lines caused the pentobarbital to flow into her body instead of her bloodstream.
Strada took over the Correction Department in January 2023 after serving as deputy director of the Arizona Department of Corrections. In late 2024, he announced that Tennessee was changing its lethal injection protocol and would use only pentobarbital.
Four people have been executed in Tennessee since 2025, according to the Correction Department.
Pike was 18 when she and her boyfriend tortured and killed a classmate, Colleen Slemmer, in a jealous rage. She later became one of the youngest women to be sent to death row.

title: Time is running out for leadership on healthcare in Maine
text:
Tom Dunne of Cape Elizabeth was the first executive director of the Dirigo Health Agency during the administration of Gov. John Baldacci.
Last fall I wrote an op-ed headlined “Please don’t make me run for governor,” challenging the many candidates to declare how they would lead much needed improvements across Maine’s healthcare system.
After the op-ed appeared, I had conversations with a number of candidates, across party lines. A constant agreement was on the need for change; some had specific ideas; for others, healthcare reform was a relatively new topic.
As a reminder, healthcare makes up about a sixth of our economy — it is big and complicated and
important. The stress of illness is compounded by the stress of an overly expensive and overly complicated system. It is a major pocketbook issue for everyone (except, perhaps, for those taking advantage of the weaknesses and flaws in the current system, making so much more than their counterparts in any other economy of the world).
We are now down to three candidates, one of whom will be our governor, an elected official having formal legal authority and specific responsibilities defined by law. Based on their declarations to date, not one of the three candidates, in healthcare, is positioning to be a leader, someone who will influence, guide or inspire others to a goal.
These candidates are citing slogans, declining to dig in and declare what practical
actions they would take to improve the system. They seem to be throwing out umbrella
statements, hoping to appeal to those voters who will hear what they want to hear while avoiding having to make any statements or provide details that might negatively influence possible voters.
Boiled down, “a public option — funding reform,” “eliminate waste and fraud,” “expand
telemedicine and deal with medical debt” are at best important but small ideas when
compared to the scale of the reform needed across the system. It is almost as if the
candidates are tip-toeing to get elected and then thinking they will “figure it out” later.
Unfortunately, this does not give them a mandate to lead, it just makes them an elected official. As a reminder, we are not stuck in the current system. Maine can lead, adopting a system similar to what Maryland has been working on and similar to the underpinnings of most European systems.
No, it is not “single-payer.” Rather they treat their healthcare systems for what they basically are — geographic monopolies that operate primarily under a global budget system.
There are several ways to fund this type of system (including single-payer). Across the world there are different models to learn from, and to pick from, with an eye to fitting with Maine’s culture and values. There is no perfect solution but there are better options.
Shifting to this sort of system will require strong leadership. Sadly, unless someone steps up over the next 45 days, the Blaine House will soon have a new elected official but not a leader with a mandate for significant reform of this sector.
I think Maine voters are ready for major change and crave greater and more detailed communication from those who aspire to lead.

title: AMC adds the Whitecap Highlands to Maine Woods Initiative
text:
The Alpine-like summit of 3,650-foot White Cap in the heart of the 100-Mile Wilderness affords one of the finest mountaintop vistas in all of Maine. To the north across some 30 miles of heavily forested country stands mile-high Katahdin and its neighbors in Baxter State Park. Looking south, the grand view includes the rest of the White Cap Range, the Barren-Chairback Range, Big Moose Mountain and so much more. Extraordinary!
Much of the land around the White Cap Range has been preserved by the Appalachian Mountain Club over the last two decades or so, to the tune of 130,000 acres. AMC now has its sights set on another piece of the area’s conservation puzzle, the Whitecap Highlands Forest. This 29,500-acre tract on the southern slopes of the range is a mix of fragile high-elevation terrain and cold-water stream habitat for Atlantic salmon and native brook trout.
“The White Cap project is an incredible opportunity to protect a truly stunning, ecologically critical property,” said Steve Tatko, AMC’s vice president of land and conservation. “It really fills in the ‘hole in the donut’ by furthering the protection of the West Branch of the Pleasant River’s headwaters and buffering a scenic section of the Appalachian Trail over Gulf Hagas Mountain, West Peak, Hay Mountain and, of course, White Cap.”
Earlier this year, AMC kicked off a campaign aimed at raising $15 million to support the Whitecap Highlands Forest effort, a goal that, when achieved, will “unlock” an additional $22 million land grant from an anonymous conservation-supporting donor. In the meantime, AMC is working with the interim landowner to manage the land on its behalf, has reopened roads to reestablish public access, and has created new fish passages.
Now in its sesquicentennial year as America’s oldest conservation and recreation organization (1876), AMC established a presence in the 100-Mile Wilderness in 2003 with the purchase of the Katahdin Iron Works Tract. This 37,000-acre parcel includes the eastern four of the Barren-Chairback peaks, Long Pond and the headwaters of the West Branch of the Pleasant River above and along Gulf Hagas, Maine’s “Grand Canyon.”
AMC added the Roach Ponds Tract (29,500 acres) to the north of White Cap in 2009, purchased 4,300 acres around the summit of Baker Mountain (3,528 feet) six years later, and then acquired the Silver Lake Tract (4,400 acres) southeast of White Cap a year after that. Two more land acquisitions followed: the 27,000-acre Pleasant River Headwaters Forest in 2022 and the 29,000-acre Barnard Forest between 2023 and 2025.
AMC’s “Maine Woods Initiative” lands serve as an important anchor in a nearly continuous corridor of conservation lands ranging from Moosehead Lake through the 100-Mile Wilderness to Baxter State Park and Katahdin Woods and Waters National Monument. Including working forest easement lands, the conservation total is in the neighborhood of one million acres, a mind-boggling statistic given that 50 years ago, there was next to none.
In addition to AMC, key players in this conservation mosaic include The Nature Conservancy, National Park Service, the State of Maine, Forest Society of Maine, Maine Audubon, Elliotsville Foundation and Butler Parklands, among others. Baxter State Park, Debsconeag Lakes Wilderness Area, Nahmakanta Public Lands, the Appalachian Trail and Borestone Mountain Sanctuary are some of the notable jewels.
“AMC’s MWI property is remarkable. It’s a big place where we’re doing big things. People are really enjoying it,” Tatko said of this landscape scale conservation model that includes sustainable forest management, multi-use recreation opportunities, outdoor education, and ecological enhancement and protection. “Collaboration with our community partners has been critical to our success and that of the local economy.”
A plan for the Whitecap Highlands Forest hasn’t yet been developed, according to Tatko, but AMC expects to establish new trails connecting the Gulf Hagas area to the White Cap Range ridgeline, good news for hikers looking for new tramping possibilities. This would add nicely to the 200 miles of multiple-use trails on MWI lands currently available.
There are myriad ways to enjoy AMC’s MWI lands, both summer and winter. There’s hiking, paddling, mountain biking, fishing, wildlife watching, stargazing (it’s an International Dark Sky Park), and cross-country skiing and snowshoeing. Along with backcountry and frontcountry camping, AMC also operates three full-service lodges in the Maine sporting camp tradition: Little Lyford near the Little Lyford Ponds, Gorman Chairback on Long Pond and Medawisla on Second Roach Pond.
Carey Kish of Mount Desert Island is a Triple Crown hiker, freelance writer, and author of three hiking guides. Connect with Carey on Facebook and Instagram and at [email protected].

title: Boston Bruins fall to Wild in Minnesota
text:
ST. PAUL, Minn. — Kirill Kaprizov scored twice, Jesper Wallstedt made 26 saves, and the Minnesota Wild beat the Boston Bruins 4-1 on Saturday night.
Quinn Hughes had a goal and assist, and Jared Spurgeon also scored.
With the win, Minnesota improved to 18-4-4 in home openers and its .769 points percentage in those games is second-best in the NHL to Vegas, which is at .850 while going 8-1-1.
Tanner Jeannot scored for Boston, which won 4-3 in overtime at Winnipeg Friday, and allowed just three goals in winning its first two games.
Michael DiPietro made 26 saves for the Bruins in his third career start and first since Jan. 23, 2022, with Vancouver. The 2025-26 American Hockey League MVP with Providence, he led the league with 34 wins, a 1.91 goals-against average and .930 save percentage.
Eight different Wild players had points on Saturday after nine did so in Thursday’s 3-1 season-opening win at Nashville.
Kaprizov tied the game 1-1 with a power-play goal six minutes into the second period, converting a feed from Maxim Shabanov.
He added an empty-net tally with 1:01 to play for his third goal of the season and 11th in eight career games against the Bruins.
Minnesota had a five-on-three power play for 1:52 midway through the second period. Hughes scored with one second left on the latter infraction with a wrist shot that went through Ryan Hartman’s screen for a 2-1 lead.
Boston was scoreless on four power-play chances. Minnesota has killed off all eight short-handed situations through two games after allowing none in the preseason.
Spurgeon added a goal early in the third period with a shot that changed direction off the skate off Nikita Zadorov.
Jeannot scored put the Bruins up 1-0 less than two minutes into the game, converting a touch pass from Mark Kastelic.
Up next
Bruins: Home against Ottawa on Monday night.
Wild: At Buffalo on Tuesday to begin a three-game road trip.

title: Fallen trooper among 3 officers killed in action from the same training class
text:
LOUISVILLE, Ky. (WDRB+WAVE/Gray News) — A Kentucky father said he got chills when he learned Kentucky State Police Trooper Hayden Phillips was shot and killed Monday.
Phillips has a connection to two other officers killed in the line of duty. They all graduated from the same Department of Criminal Justice Training class at Eastern Kentucky University in December 2019.
“It’s weird for sure; my first thought the other day was, ‘Man, is that class cursed,’” Brian Shirley said.
Brian’s son, Jefferson County Sheriff’s Deputy Brandon Shirley, Kentucky State Police Trooper Hayden Phillips and Scott County Deputy Caleb Conley were among 33 graduates from DOJCT class 506.
All three were killed in action.
Brandon Shirley was ambushed in August 2021 while working private security in Louisville at a car lot off Rockford Lane. Conley was shot and killed while conducting a traffic stop on southbound Interstate 75 in Georgetown.
Conley’s murder is similar to what happened to Phillips, who died Monday in Warren County and was also shot during a traffic stop.
Shirley said the coincidence gave him chills.
“It definitely hits home every time I hear an officer has gone down,” he said.
He said when an officer dies, the loved ones left behind become part of a fraternity where no one wants membership, connected by grief.
“Heartache and sorrow, it’s just never going to shut off for them,” Shirley said. “My heart has a giant hole in it, and no matter what I pour into it, I’m never, ever going to fill it up.”
Shirley went to Conley’s funeral in 2023 and said he will connect with Phillips’ family as well.
“Those kids lost their dad,” Shirley said. “She lost her husband.”
They are new members in the club no one wants to join: law enforcement loved ones left behind.
“They say time heals all wounds,” Shirley said. “I don’t know if it gets better or you just get better at dealing with it.”
Police said Emonnie Branch, 51, of Portland, Tennessee, allegedly shot Phillips and fled, triggering a statewide manhunt.
Branch was later arrested in Louisville and charged with murder of a first responder in Phillips’ death. During his arraignment in Warren County Tuesday morning, a judge denied Branch bail.
According to court records from the Tennessee Department of Correction, Branch had at least one active warrant out for his arrest when Phillips stopped him. It was for a probation violation in a fraud case. He pleaded guilty to fraud and impersonation and was sentenced to five years’ probation in July of last year.

title: Why I’m supporting Sen. Susan Collins
text:
Dennis Brockway of Winslow is president of North East Mobile Health Services and a member of the Maine Ambulance Association. The views expressed here are his own.
I want to voice my strong support for Sen. Susan Collins.
As a member of the Maine Ambulance Association and president of North East Mobile Health Services, I have had the opportunity to see firsthand the challenges facing emergency medical services in Maine, particularly in our rural communities. Over the years, Sen. Collins has sponsored, co-sponsored or supported numerous pieces of legislation aimed at strengthening EMS and improving access to emergency medical care.
Her commitment to rural healthcare goes well beyond words.
Sen. Collins played an important role in securing $50 billion for the Rural Health Transformation Program during congressional negotiations and pushed to expand the program and broaden the range of rural healthcare providers eligible to participate. Maine subsequently received approximately $190 million in first-year funding through the program.
When Maine’s award was later placed in jeopardy after the state missed federal milestones and the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) raised concerns about implementation, Sen. Collins personally intervened with CMS Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz in an effort to help preserve Maine’s funding.
Her work on behalf of rural EMS extends much further. Sen. Collins helped author the SIREN program, which provides grants to rural EMS agencies for recruitment, training, equipment and other critical needs. She has consistently supported efforts to strengthen the EMS workforce and improve access to emergency care in rural communities.
My support for Sen. Collins, however, is based on more than legislation.
In my dealings with her over the past 20 years, I have found her to be honest, respectful and willing to listen, even when people disagree with her. That matters to me. Maine has a long tradition of independent-minded public servants who put their responsibility to the state ahead of partisan politics. Sen. Margaret Chase Smith embodied that tradition, and I see much of that same Maine independence in Sen. Collins.
I recognize that many Mainers disagree with Sen. Collins on important issues. They have every right to do so. But after decades in public life and numerous hard-fought campaigns, she has been subjected to an extraordinary level of scrutiny. Through it all, she has maintained a reputation for integrity and a commitment to serving Maine.
Seniority also matters. Sen. Collins has accumulated decades of experience, relationships and influence in Washington. Maine is a small state, and having a senator in a position to influence federal policy and funding can have very real consequences for our rural hospitals, ambulance services and communities.
For me, this election should not simply be about party labels. It should be about who can most effectively represent Maine.
Based on what I have witnessed personally over the past two decades, I believe Susan Collins has earned the opportunity to continue doing that work.

title: Maine honors two firefighters killed in line of duty among others at memorial service
text:
AUGUSTA, Maine (WABI) - The ceremonial bell echoed across the Capitol grounds Saturday at the annual Firefighter Memorial Service, honoring the 42 Maine firefighters lost this year.
The Firefighters Memorial, across from Capitol Park, was dedicated in 1997 by then-Gov. Angus King, said Ken Desmond, president of the Maine State Federation of Firefighters.
Desmond has attended every year since, and said Saturday’s turnout was reminiscent of the service in 2001 after the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks.
“Obviously I’m old enough to remember the ceremony around 9/11 and just how the communities came together to support the fire service. This year has been pretty much the same,” echoed Bill Gillespie, Liberty Fire Chief and President of the Maine Fire Chiefs Assocation. “Maine has suffered a lot of tragedy this year, including myself and Waldo County.”
Montville firefighter Jacob Spaulding and Lt. Katherine Paige of Belmont Fire laid the wreath at the memorial. Both suffered major injuries in the Searsmont explosion.
Among those in attendance was Sen. Susan Collins, who said during her remarks: “This annual memorial service is always powerful and inspiring, but it has a special significance this year. As we honor 2 firefighters who made the ultimate sacrifice battling the horrific explosion at Robbins Lumber in Searsmont last May.”
Searsmont Assistant Fire Chief Wayne Woodbury and Morrill firefighter Andrew Cross were each honored with 20 bell tolls, signifying their line-of-duty deaths.
“As far as line of duty deaths, having two at the same incident is significant for Maine in the last decade or so,” explained Maine State Fire Marshal Shawn Esler. “But to be honest with you, one firefighter death in the line of duty is too many.”
Saturday’s service not only served as a commemoration of the lives lost, but as a call to action to address the challenges and future of the Maine fire service.
Gillespie said Maine’s fire service remains among the least expensive because of its reliance on volunteers. With volunteerism down and departments statewide facing critical staffing shortages, he said changes must be made.
“We need to figure out a way to create more volunteer opportunities for firefighters. We need to figure out a way to get them trained. We need to figure out a way for them to have time off from work so they can get trained. So all these initiatives are things that we’re looking at to try to better the fire service in the future,” described Gillespie.
Esler went on to explain those changes come through collaboration among the Fire Marshal’s Office, Fire Commission and legislators at the State House.

FBI has commissioned a classified and internal ‘Patel Report’ about times when it ‘fell short’
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The FBI is issuing a classified report to its workforce examining what it says are chapters from the bureau’s history “where this institution fell short,” according to an internal message obtained Friday by The Associated Press.
It was unclear what episodes from the FBI’s past are chronicled in the new “Patel Report.” But the document’s existence is in keeping with Director Kash Patel’s vocal criticism of the leaders who preceded him and with his determination to rid the FBI of agents he contends have politicized the bureau in the past. Patel’s critics say he is the one who has weaponized the FBI and that his scrutiny of his predecessors and their decision-making is part of an effort to rewrite history in favor of President Donald Trump.
Patel pledged at his confirmation hearing last year that he would not look “backward,” but as director, he has encouraged investigations of former senior officials and presided over sweeping terminations, including of employees who participated in years-old investigations of Trump, were photographed taking a knee during a 2020 racial justice protest and contributed to a disputed analytical memo about Catholic extremism.
“The Patel Report looks backward because accountability demands it,” says a message to the workforce signed by the FBI’s co-deputy directors, Christopher Raia and Andrew Bailey. The message describes the report as marking the “closing of one chapter in our history and the beginning of another complete with a brighter future ahead.”
Bailey announced his resignation earlier this week, and his last day is Friday. The FBI declined to comment on the report.
The message also says: “We cannot change what happened before we arrived. But we can confront it honestly. We can recognize failures instead of protecting them. We can hold people accountable. We can fix what was broken. And we can build safeguards strong enough to ensure the mistakes of the past are never allowed to define this institution again. These steps are consistent with any institution of excellence that is constantly striving for improvement.”
It was unclear if the report made recommendations or demanded any action to address what the FBI now regards as past shortcomings.
The FBI message says the report is meant to “promote fierce organizational accountability” and rebuild “public trust.” But Patel’s critics say the politically charged investigations into perceived adversaries of Trump that the FBI has embarked on under his watch, as well as the punishment of agents who participated in investigations into the Republican president to which they were assigned, have eroded faith in the nation’s premier federal law enforcement agency.

title: Mormon leader decries explosion in sports gambling, prediction markets
text:
SALT LAKE CITY (AP) — A leader of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints warned Saturday that an explosion in gambling driven by online prediction markets and sports betting is fostering greed, particularly among youths, while producing “nothing of value.”
D. Todd Christofferson, one of the top three leaders of what is known widely as the Mormon Church, said rampant betting among teenagers and young adults is robbing time from their studies and relationships as smartphones make gambling possible anywhere.
“For us as Latter-day Saints, overarching all other concerns is the fact that gambling is morally wrong. Gambling is built on the desire to obtain something for nothing,” Christofferson said at the faith’s twice-annual general conference.
The declaration that prediction markets are gambling puts the conservative church at odds with President Donald Trump. The Republican’s administration has argued the platforms such as Kalshi and Polymarket don’t constitute gambling and therefore shouldn’t be subjected to state gambling bans such as the one enacted this year in Utah, where the church is based.
Prediction markets allow wagers on anything from whether it will rain in Los Angeles or if the United States will go to war.
“Or even, if you can imagine, the timing of the Second Coming,” Christofferson said Saturday. “Where do you go to collect on that bet?”
Opposition to gambling is common among religious organizations. The Methodist Church refers to it as “a menace to society.” The Southern Baptist Convention, the largest Protestant denomination in America, has condemned gambling several times and in 2025 declared sports gambling inconsistent with biblical principle.
Gambling is forbidden in Islam and considered a vice among Hindus. In the Catholic Church, gambling is not in itself a sin, but is considered potentially problematic.
For more than a century, Utah kept gambling almost entirely out of the state. There are no casinos, no lotteries and no racetracks that allow bets. The prohibition is rooted in the ideals of Mormons who view gambling as a path to selfishness and addiction.
“The rise of predictive markets, and the legalization of sports gambling, this is just really taking off all across the country,” said Matthew Bowman, a professor of religion and history at Claremont Graduate University in California. “And a lot of institutions — religious, state and otherwise — are grappling with this problem.”
Saturday’s speech comes as the church has been wading into political issues under President Dallin Oaks, a former Utah Supreme Court justice who became the faith’s top leader last October. Church leaders this year have opposed state ballot measures that would establish rights to abortion in Idaho and Nevada.
Yet the institution’s approach to political issues — using public statements and behind-the-scenes lobbying to convey its message — has become more calculated in recent years, Bowman said.
The shift followed public blowback to the church’s stance against California’s Proposition 8, a 2008 ballot measure that sought to ban gay marriage. In that case, Bowman said church leaders encouraged its members to get directly involved.
__
Associated Press writer Holly Meyer contributed to this story from Nashville, Tennessee.

title: Meet the air traffic controller who flies himself to work
text:
PUEBLO, Colo. (AP) — Jake Hutzler spends his workdays directing planes from an airport tower. Once a week, he gets there by strapping a propeller to his back and taking to the skies of Colorado.
Before his commute, the 28-year-old air traffic controller lays out a large wing on the road outside his apartment complex, fires up the motor and starts running. Within seconds, his feet leave the ground.
For the next 20 minutes, Hutzler flies at a leisurely 35 mph (56 kph) above the expansive fields around Pueblo, a city near the Front Range mountains. He soars over a highway, a water tower and finally the airport while listening to his favorite music.
Before taking off, Hutzler calls the tower where he works and lets his colleagues know he’s coming. Once airborne, he keeps them updated on where he’s at and how high he’s flying.
“I’m very small and I don’t show up on radar,” Hutzler said, “so they’ll want to kind of keep track of my location and get updates on my progress.”
As the airport comes into view, he waits for the OK to land on the airport’s ramp. Pulling down on toggles to slow down the paramotor, he lets his feet dangle and meets the ground with a brief jog. He packs up the wing, strips off his jacket to reveal his collared work shirt and begins his shift telling planes when it’s safe to land and take off.
‘A view that almost nobody gets to experience’
For someone who has been fascinated with flying since childhood, it’s a particularly satisfying commute. Hutzler says it’s as close as you can get to flying like a bird.
“In a paramotor, you have a view that almost nobody gets to experience,” he said. “You have no cockpit, nothing in front of you. You’re just sitting there in the air and total freedom to go wherever you want.”
His grandfather used to take him up in a small four-seat aircraft. In college, Hutzler put in about 20 hours toward getting a pilot’s license, but the costs were too high for him to continue.
Everything changed when he came across a viral video of a man flying a paramotor to McDonald’s and eating his hamburger on the flight home.
“After I saw that, I was like, ‘I’m sold,’” he said. “I gotta do that.”
Flying became a family affair
Hutzler started training to fly the contraption — also known as powered paragliding — in 2021 in Florida and later became an instructor.
Part of the appeal is just how accessible paramotors are. There’s no license required and the price tag is a fraction of the cost of many other forms of flying. However, they’re still subject to federal rules on ultralight vehicles, including that they can only be operated during the day and fliers must avoid congested cities and towns.
The sport became a part of Hutzler’s life story. He trained the woman he would go on to marry, and when he was ready to propose he used fake engine trouble on his paramotor to lure her to the contraption, where he had left a ring. On their wedding day, their paramotors were with them at the altar. Now he’s looking forward to the day their 2½-year-old daughter is old enough to go on a tandem ride.
But after Hutzler started working in air traffic control earlier this year, his job left him less time to fly.
The solution: Start flying to work.
He approached his manager about commuting by paramotor and they went through the rule book and made sure he’d have two-way communication with the tower when he entered their airspace. He made his first flight to work in June and has been doing it ever since, weather permitting.
But paramotoring is a very fair-weather sport. It only takes about 10 mph (16 kph) of wind — basically a light breeze — to keep Hutzler on the ground. It can also be problematic if the sun heats the ground and causes updrafts — making for an extremely bumpy ride.
The airborne commute isn’t actually faster
With the time needed to set up the paramotor and put away all the gear, the trip takes slightly longer than driving to work. But, he said, it’s so much more fun.
“You could be having your favorite song playing in your headphones, and you just can relax and take in this awesome experience,” he said.
___
Golden reported from Seattle. Associated Press transportation writer Josh Funk contributed from Omaha, Nebraska.

title: 4 teens killed in crash after police use PIT maneuver ends chase sparked by shooting
text:
TYLER, Texas (KLTV/Gray News) - A police chase sparked by a shooting ended in a crash that left four teens dead in Texas, authorities said.
According to the Tyler Police Department, on Sept. 27, officers were called to the 1500 block of Lake Placid Road in response to suspicious gunshot noises in the area. The caller also described a vehicle the alleged shooters were driving.
Around 4 a.m., police received a call from a local hospital saying they were treating two victims with gunshot wounds from the incident.
Officers investigating the incident saw the suspect vehicle and attempted to make contact. However, the vehicle drove away from the area and officers began a pursuit through Tyler that continued onto Highway 31 East at a high rate of speed.
According to the release, Texas Highway Patrol joined the chase as it exited the city. One trooper used a precision immobilization technique, known as a PIT maneuver, to end the pursuit, according to the department.
The vehicle crashed and the pursuit ended around 5:30 a.m. near County Road 211, officials said. Three occupants of the suspect vehicle died at the scene and one occupant was taken to the hospital, where that person later died, according to the release.
Police identified the occupants as Jaffet Cuarenta, 17, Adrielle Vazquez, 17, and Emigdio Gutierrez, 17, all of Tyler, and a 15-year-old from Smith County whose name was not released because of age.
The victims of the earlier shooting had non-life-threatening injuries and were identified as a 17-year-old male from Tyler and an 18-year-old female from Smith County. Their names are being withheld at this time, officials said.

title: UMaine football drops 5th straight game
text:
Nick Laughlin of Cape Elizabeth scored early in the fourth quarter to pull Maine within six, but the Black Bears couldn’t get any closer and suffered their fifth straight loss, falling to Sacred Heart 24-16 on Saturday in Orono.
Maine falls to 1-5 overall and 1-2 in the Coastal Athletic Conference. The Black Bears have not won since beating Towson in their season opener on Aug. 27.
Sacred Heart improves to 2-3 overall and 2-2 in the conference.
Laughlin scored on a 2-yard rush with 12:03 left to make it 21-15. Maine gave up a 40-yard field goal to Ryan Bocklet on the ensuing Sacred Heart possession, then drove to the Pioneers’ 37-yard line before turning the ball over on downs with 1:40 left.
Maine forced a Sacred Heart punt and started a drive at its own 43 with 1:16 left. The Black Bears gained one first down, but quarterback Caden Drezek threw four straight incomplete passes from the Sacred Heart 47 to end Maine’s hopes.
Drezek, who saw the bulk of the snaps after starting the season as the backup, went 12 for 28 passing for 141 yards. Eddie Buehler completed 1 of 5 passes for 13 yards and was sacked twice.
Maine took a 9-0 lead early in the second quarter on three field goals by Samuel Tremblay (42, 45 and 37 yards). Sacred Heart took the lead on an 11-yard pass from Poochie Snyder to Jason Palmieri with 19 seconds left in the first half.
Snyder completed 21 of 27 passes for 207 yards and two touchdowns.
Maine is off next week and returns to action on Oct. 17 when it host Bryant.

title: Cornell president calls alleged gang rape ‘deeply disturbing,’ pledges greater transparency
text:
(AP) - Cornell’s president called the alleged gang rape of a student at a fraternity house in 2024 “deeply disturbing” on Saturday and said it would weigh on the university for years to come, as he pledged greater transparency amid mounting outrage over the school’s handling of the case.
In an eight-minute video message to the Cornell community, Michael Kotlikoff described the past week as one of the most difficult in the university’s history and acknowledged troubling questions about the investigations that followed the allegations.
“My heart aches when I think of what she experienced,” Kotlikoff said. “It raises heartbreaking and troubling issues about sexual assault, dehumanization, and aspects of party culture, alcohol, and drug use.”
“I believe we as an administration and we as a community must do better,” he continued.
Kotlikoff reaffirmed his commitment to supporting an independent investigation of the case called for by New York Gov. Kathy Hochul and said Cornell’s Board of Trustees would announce details next week. He also expressed support for Hochul’s decision to turn the criminal investigation over to the state attorney general.
Scrutiny has mounted in recent days over Cornell’s response to allegations that the woman was sexually assaulted by multiple fraternity members in 2024. The woman, identified in court documents as Jane Doe, has sued the university and seven former students.
During a student assembly hearing Thursday that gave students an opportunity to voice concerns and discuss proposals to improve Cornell’s response to sexual assault, several speakers called for Kotlikoff’s resignation.
Kotlikoff acknowledged frustration that Cornell has not communicated enough about its handling of the case, saying that has led to distrust. While citing “real legal and privacy limits” on what the university can disclose, he pledged greater transparency and more opportunities for students, parents and others to engage with university leaders.
He also committed Cornell’s support to legislative efforts to change New York’s sexual assault laws.
The case has renewed scrutiny of a New York law that makes it difficult to prosecute sexual assaults involving people who voluntarily consume alcohol or drugs, even if they became too intoxicated to consent.
Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten cited the law in defending his initial decision not to pursue charges, saying the woman’s original statement to police described voluntary drug use and sexual activity.
Critics have long sought to close what they call the “voluntary intoxication loophole,” which distinguishes between people incapacitated by drugs administered without their consent and those who voluntarily became intoxicated. Hochul has pledged to push for changes to the law.

title: AI-generated robocalls? Why you could be seeing even more unwanted phone calls
text:
PHOENIX (KPHO/Gray News) — With the midterm elections quickly approaching, you may already be noticing more robocalls on your phone than usual.
Legal robocalls to cellphones require the recipient’s consent. But a group is now asking the federal government to waive that requirement.
The Club for Growth asked the Federal Communications Commission for an emergency waiver to make AI-generated robocalls without prior consent.
“As far as I’m concerned, if they’re handing out medals for bad ideas, this is a strong contender for the gold,” Patrick Crotty, an attorney with the National Consumer Law Center, said.
According to the petition, “the Club and its affiliated political committees would like to use AI-powered calling tools to engage in noncommercial, political speech to inform and gather input from potential voters more effectively (e.g., in more languages) and more efficiently.”
The Club for Growth says similar rules already apply to landlines.
Crotty said if the consent requirement is removed, political robocalls would increase by as much as 40 times compared with previous midterm elections.
“We’d probably expect something closer to 15 billion robocalls,” he said.
The Club for Growth did not immediately respond to a request for an interview.
The FCC is currently taking public comments on the petition.

title: UMaine men’s hockey opens 50th season with win over Holy Cross
text:
The University of Maine’s men’s hockey team opened the program’s 50th season with a 4-1 victory over Holy Cross on Friday night as Robert Morris University transfer left wing Tanner Klimpke scored a pair of power-play goals in the opening 7:33 and sophomore center Brock James tallied an important insurance goal in the third period.
Senior goalie Albin Boija made 18 saves to earn his first victory since a 6-5 overtime win at UMass Lowell on Jan. 24 and graduate student left wing and captain Owen Fowler added an empty-net goal for the Black Bears, who killed off a 34-second two-man disadvantage late in the third period.
Sophomore Danick Leroux made 26 stops for the Crusaders and Matt Kursonis scored a shorthanded goal.
The two teams will play again on Saturday night at 7 at the DCU Center Arena in Worcester.
“The work ethic was good. Every guy out there worked hard,” said UMaine sixth-year head coach Ben Barr, who has now won his last five season-openers. “We made some mistakes. It wasn’t perfect.”
Senior Klimpke, a 16-goal scorer at Robert Morris a year ago and a second team All-Atlantic Hockey America selection, took advantage of an extended power play to stake UMaine to a 2-0 lead with goals 2:39 apart.
And it was Bemidji State transfer defenseman Isa Parekh and senior center Sully Scholle who earned the assists on each goal.
Ben Riche picked up a cross-checking penalty for the Crusaders and the UMaine coaching staff also used a successful challenge in which Holy Cross’ Owen Kim was assessed a five-minute major for contact to the head at the 3:45 mark.
That gave UMaine a five-minute power play including a full two-minute five-on-three.
Klimpke opened the scoring on the five-on-three at the 4:54 mark when Parekh fed him a nice cross-ice pass and he one-timed it past Danick Leroux.
The two-teamed up again with a five-on-four power play goal at the 7:33 mark with Parekh passing across to Klimpke.
“We worked on our power play a lot. We were well-prepared. We knew what they were going to do. We built some chemistry there and (Parekh) was able to find me for two pretty open ones, which was good,” said Klimpke who added that it “definitely feels good to get off to a (good) start.
“Hopefully, I can keep it rolling into the rest of the season,” added the Calgary, Alberta native.
That gave Klimpke four goals in three games dating back to last season when he had two goals in a 5-2 victory over Sacred Heart in the second game of their best-of-three AHA semifinal round series which was eventually won by Sacred Heart, two games to one.
“It was important to score on those power plays. If we don’t score there, that would be a big momentum shift,” said Barr, who credited director of hockey operations Nick Fonzi for making the call for the challenge based on his video review.
Junior center Kursonis cut the lead in half at the 5:05 mark of the second period as he scored a nifty shorthanded goal off a two-on-one with Riche, who picked up an assist.
Falmouth’s James extended the lead six minutes into the third period when he was set up nicely by sophomore defenseman Lukas Peterson and he converted into the open net.
Alaska-Anchorage transfer Judah Makway also earned an assist on the goal.
Peterson and Arizona State transfer Sam Alfano assisted on the goal by Fowler, which was his sixth over his last six games dating back to last season.

title: USDA considers adapting farm-style safety net for fishermen
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Top federal agriculture officials visited Maine this week to evaluate whether crop insurance can be expanded to protect the state’s multimillion dollar lobster industry.
The visit by U.S. Department of Agriculture Undersecretary Richard Fordyce and Risk Management Agency Administrator Pat Swanson comes as the agency increasingly looks to integrate seafood producers into traditional agricultural safety nets.
Federal crop insurance allows farmers to buy government-subsidized policies that pay out in weeks to months after natural disasters or market drops cause severe revenue losses. In contrast, lobstermen rely on federal fishery disaster declarations that can take three to five years to distribute aid, which industry analysts call far too slow for small operators.
“We are a small-boat, owner-operated fishery made up of thousands of independent businesses, so programs designed for agriculture or other food-producing sectors will not necessarily translate neatly to lobster,” said Patrice McCarron, director of the Maine Lobstermen’s Association.
However, McCarron called the visit “an important first step” toward determining whether existing USDA programs can be adapted or new approaches developed to better support Maine lobstermen in their role as food producers for the world.
During a dockside roundtable in Stonington on Tuesday, industry leaders emphasized that lobstermen face severe market swings and price crashes rather than physical catch loss alone. Fordyce, a corn and soybean farmer from Missouri, noted that lobstermen favored revenue protection over simple yield guarantees.
“Just talking with the lobstermen, I think they were probably more inclined to try to find a product or try to find a path forward that would be more supportive of total revenue,” Fordyce said. “I was quite surprised by the data that’s available as far as supporting catch numbers.”
Last year’s  lobster catch was valued at $461.4 million — 7.5% below the 10-year average, and, when adjusted for inflation, 20% down from 2024, state data shows.
Curt Brown, president of Bold Coast Seafood in Prospect Harbor, hosted the delegation and highlighted the shared reality between ocean and land harvesters.
“I was struck by how many of the same challenges we face in seafood are also challenges that farmers across the country face every day,” Brown said. “There is a lot we can learn from each other.”
Seafood industry consultant Noah Oppenheim said bringing Midwest agricultural leaders to coastal Maine provided crucial perspective, especially the similarities between the rural fishing communities in Maine and the rural farming communities in the Midwest.
While the visit was focused on ways to manage the industry’s risks, representatives also used the time to drive home other ways the agency can help water-based food producers like they support land-based farmers, including equal access to loan, grant, purchasing and marketing programs.
“The agency seems wide open to focus on all of this at once,” Oppenheim said. “Congress knows this is a bipartisan feel-good issue. We need to be eating more domestic seafood. It’s the right thing to do to have seafood be an equal part of our food system.”
Oppenheim said opportunities for fishermen have expanded since the USDA created its Office of Seafood in April. One of its top priorities is to find ways for fishermen to tap into the same federal programs and safety nets as the nation’s potato and dairy farmers.
Addressing expectations regarding a timeline, Fordyce cautioned that any official expansion must ultimately be approved by the Federal Crop Insurance Corporation board. However, because local advocates have worked on the issue for several years, he said “a lot of that preliminary work has been kind of done.”
While a full rollout for lobster insurance remains down the road, Fordyce emphasized that establishing direct working relationships between Washington officials and Maine coastal leaders was the immediate, vital outcome of the trip.
This story was originally published by the Maine Trust for Local News. Penny Overton can be reached at poverton@pressherald.com.

title: ‘Please, don’t wait’: With weeks left to live, woman shares breast cancer story to help others
text:
BATON ROUGE, La. (WAFB/Gray News) - A Baton Rouge woman says she is sharing her breast cancer story in hopes of helping other women.
Whitney Brooks, 34, was diagnosed with Stage 3 breast cancer at age 27.
The disease has since progressed to Stage 4 and spread throughout her body, leaving her unable to walk, use the restroom or feed herself without help.
In July, Brooks was placed on hospice and given a 90-day prognosis.
“I think that’s one of the main reasons I don’t go to sleep,” Brooks said. “I just think, what if I don’t get up? What if this is my last breath?”
Brooks said she has days when she wants to keep fighting and moving forward, as well as days when she feels like giving up.
“I know some days I feel like I want to keep moving, keep going,” she said. “But some days, I want to throw in the towel and not want to do it anymore.”
Now, Brooks is using her final days to encourage other women to pay attention to changes in their bodies and seek medical care.
Brooks said she first noticed something was wrong when she was just 25 years old.
While taking a shower, she felt a lump in her breast.
“I just thought, oh, that’s a boil. It’ll go away,” Brooks said.
But the lump did not go away.
Brooks said her now-wife, Dana Foreman, eventually urged her to go to Woman’s Hospital to have it checked.
“It was positive for cancer,” Brooks said.
Two years later, Brooks was diagnosed with breast cancer.
“Cancer really doesn’t have an age. It doesn’t have a number,” Brooks said.
According to the American Cancer Society, about one in eight women will develop invasive breast cancer during their lifetime.
The five-year relative survival rate for breast cancer that has not spread beyond the breast is nearly 100%.
Brooks said fear played a role in why she did not initially get the lump checked.
“Please, don’t wait,” she said. “Don’t let fear sink in, because that’s what I did. I allowed fear to sink in and stop me.”
Doctors encourage women to be familiar with how their breasts normally look and feel and to talk with a health care provider about changes that concern them, including a new lump, changes in breast size or shape, skin changes or unusual discharge.
Despite the uncertainty surrounding what comes next, Brooks said she is trying to focus on the time she has left and to enjoy a nice vacation.

title: Maine’s Democratic voters should not fall for Collins’ pitch
text:

title: Nanna's House to benefit from 2026 Maine Marathon
text:
Nanna's House to benefit from 2026 Maine Marathon
Nanna's House and three other local nonprofits are the beneficiaries of this weekend's Maine Marathon.
Nanna's House to benefit from 2026 Maine Marathon
Nanna's House and three other local nonprofits are the beneficiaries of this weekend's Maine Marathon.
Nanna's House, a nonprofit in South Portland, is one of four beneficiaries of the 2026 Maine Marathon. Founder and Executive Director Beth Fournier started the organization four years ago as a way to help foster families like her own.
“When kiddos come into care, they don’t typically come with anything," she said. "That visual of coming with a black trash bag, it actually does happen.” Fournier collects donations of personal care and comfort items that can be sent with a child when they are placed with a new foster family.
A small shed behind the Point Community Center is stocked with items like clothes, hygiene kits, shoes, books, toys, diapers, wipes, strollers and blankets. The shed is accessible to caseworkers at all times, so they can pick up anything a child or family may need whenever they need it.
Fournier said, “To see that there is a need in the community, and that I can help be that bridge between the need and the resources, has just made me feel like this is worth it." She named Nanna's House after her mom, someone who inspired her to give and help others.
“At my parents’ house, you don’t have to come with a diaper bag," she said. "You show up how you are, and you leave clean and happy and fed, and that’s our goal.” Everything in the shed is new, and it's all free.
Many items have been donated, but Fournier does purchase some with the help of monetary donations. The nonprofit will get $5,700 from the Maine Marathon. Maine Community Bank donates the race registration fees to local charities each year.
Fournier has never run a marathon but has enjoyed learning more about the race. She said, “It’s been really cool to see the process and how it all works and just the generosity of all the volunteers to be able to put this marathon on solely for the purpose of giving back to nonprofits like Nanna’s House.”
In its first year, the organization helped 10 kids. In Year 4, that number climbed to 250. “It’s both heartbreaking and so encouraging at the same time because those are all kids," Fournier said. "Those are all faces. Those are all lives that are being changed forever."
The other beneficiaries, each getting $20,000, are Camp No Limits, Day One and Pine Tree Society.

title: Calling for sanity from my sickbed in Maine
text:
Bill Hiss lives in Lewiston.
It does seem odd to be writing an op-ed from a hospital bed, with ninth-floor views to Mount Washington, and people bustling to and fro night and day. Being a healer here is like serving on a submarine: tiny spaces, machinery everywhere and staff maneuvering past each other.
But perhaps it’s a helpful time for a literal grayhead — I am 82 — to share three thoughts while attached to an IV pole.
First, seeing the staff at Maine Medical Center is a blunt reminder of how utterly insane, cruel and counterproductive for America is this federal administration’s hostility to immigrants. At least as I see them at work, perhaps 10%-20% of the doctors, 30%-40% of the RNs, 70% of the LPNs and the vast majority of the support staff of housekeepers, food staff, etc., are immigrants.
Hope to stay alive? Get meds at 2 a.m.? Need food brought to your bedside? Pay attention, folks: immigrants are doing much of the work we need to stay alive.
Within the last hour, I was seen by two infectious disease physicians, one an immigrant from Vietnam, the other from an Arab country, who will care for me over the six-week treatment for a spine infection. As a minister, I see the same pattern in hospitals, rehab centers and nursing homes: the immigrants are irreplaceable labor. The same is true of agricultural workers, meat packing, hospitality, restaurants, truck drivers and countless other fields.
Second, being caught in the tragic contractions of Central Maine Medical Center for nine weeks before being referred to Maine Medical Center has been a (literal) painful reminder that perhaps it is time to rethink our medical delivery system.
I have a fine education, can get information, can afford medical expenses and have a high-end Medicare Advantage policy. But all summer I was caught in one communication or insurance snafu after another. This federal administration and our for-profit insurance industry have their fingers around our throats. If I cannot figure it out with my advantages, what in God’s name are the 70%-80% of America’s lower economic bands to do when faced with a serious medical problem?
Third, seeing the barrage of negative TV ads reminds me that hopefully sooner — by
November — we will need to find common-sense, middle-ground spaces in our social contracts. Tragically for America, President Trump’s view of the world is based on his own mental illness of narcissism, hatreds, racism, insults, pathological incessant lying, policy ignorance and the instincts of a lifelong real estate con man. 
Equally tragic, the Republicans in Congress have been almost completely compliant with his daily whims, disrupting everything from fuel and food prices to international treaties to respect for our constitutional protections. Every day a new threat, a new distraction: masked and armed ICE officers at polling places, snipers on his garish monument to himself, threats to our closest allies, all while he and his family are raking in billions in illegal sweetheart deals.
Two of my fellow Lewiston citizens, running as Republicans for higher office, have yard signs that are purple, and one of these fellow citizens told me when she knocked on my door that this was deliberate, to try to send a signal that she hoped people would see her as a moderate. Well, I would like to believe so.
These two women are not MAGA cartoons spewing hate; they have worked faithfully in their current public offices. But how are we to interpret their candidacies in the light of Sen. Susan Collins claiming to be a moderate, while voting for what Trump wanted 95% of the time? My hope is that they will demonstrate clearly a rejection of MAGA cruelty and illegality.
And yes, if they are elected, I hope to offer thoughts on how we find more sensible middle ground for our country.

title: Woman told Cornell investigators she ‘felt like bait’ during alleged gang rape
text:
(AP) - A woman who says she was gang-raped at a Cornell University fraternity told the school’s investigators last year that she “felt like bait” as the attackers were “like lions around me,” according to records from the school’s disciplinary investigation.
The documents, reviewed Friday by The Associated Press, include excerpts of interviews Cornell’s investigators did with the woman and the men she accused and shed more light on the university’s handling of the case.
While heavily redacted, the records offer a fuller but sometimes conflicting timeline of events and a glimpse at how the men responded to the allegations. Some disputed the woman’s account and said they weren’t involved in any assault.
The woman, identified in court papers only as Jane Doe, sued Cornell and seven former students last month, alleging she was given ketamine and repeatedly assaulted at a fraternity house in October 2024.
She went to campus police three weeks after the encounter and gave a detailed account of what happened, but the local district attorney decided not to file criminal charges or push for more investigation after reviewing a police summary of her interview.
Only the school’s investigation, under the federal Title IX law, persisted, with a goal of deciding discipline for the students involved.
Lawsuit by one of the accused men reveals details on investigation
This week, a lawyer for one of the accused men filed documents from the school’s investigation in a lawsuit that seeks to overturn the university’s punishment and remove it from his academic record. They include a 99-page report on a campus hearing panel’s disciplinary findings and a summary of events submitted by the university’s lawyers.
Though only a fraction of the thousands of pages amassed in the investigation, the records show the breadth of the university’s inquiry — including 50 interviews with 32 witnesses and 12 days of hearings.
Late Thursday, Gov. Kathy Hochul appointed Attorney General Letitia James as a special prosecutor to lead a renewed criminal investigation, saying she had lost faith in Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten.
According to the Title IX documents filed in court, which are only a portion of the entire investigation, the woman and several of the men gave investigators similar accounts of drug use and sexual activity that took place at the Chi Phi fraternity house — but differed sharply in how much of it was consensual.
Snapchat messages drew other men
The woman had been invited there by a fraternity member for whom she had long held strong romantic feelings and sexual interest, according to the disciplinary panel’s findings. The panel found that she initially consented to sex with that man and one of his friends, though she later alleged in her lawsuit that she had been pressured into taking ketamine, marijuana and alcohol and was too intoxicated to consent.
Then other men began showing up in the room, some drawn by a message one of the fraternity brothers sent to a Snapchat group at 1:42 a.m. using a vulgar term to advertise that a woman’s body was freely available. Later, another person in the chat asked if the “shop” was still open.
The woman told investigators that her intoxication had rendered her partly defenseless. She said she remembered smoking marijuana and said she knew she took ketamine, her first time doing so, but didn’t have an independent memory of it. The drug, she said, left her in a state of “vague consciousness.”
“You look like an operating human being,” she told school investigators at a hearing in May of 2025. ”You don’t look dead or asleep necessarily. So, lights are on, but nobody’s home. Your brain is not functioning at its proper level.”
She said some of the men inhaled drugs off her unclothed body.
“I felt like bait. I felt like lions around me. It just was a totally debilitating place to be in,” she told investigators.
Accused student says he only entered room for a wellness check
One of the men the woman accused of snorting drugs off her body — but not participating in other elements of the assault — denied her account.
He told investigators he was in the room for no more than five minutes, and didn’t go there for sex.
“That was not our intentions at all. We were just checking out to see if everything” was OK, he said.
He insisted that he did not see the woman naked at any time — she was under bed coverings, he said — and did not partake in drug use. He said he sat on a couch and chatted for a few minutes, then left after the woman and another man there both indicated they were all right.
A Cornell disciplinary panel later cleared him of sexual assault or exploitation allegations, but found him responsible for attempted sexual exploitation because it didn’t believe his claim to have gone to the room for altruistic reasons.
The fraternity member, who is challenging Cornell’s disciplinary process in court, also posted in the Snapchat conversation, saying what was happening in the room was not a joke, adding: “Firsthand pov not a bit.” The student later told investigators he did not remember sending the message, according to Cornell’s account.
Woman’s lawsuit seeks tougher penalties
In her lawsuit, Jane Doe accused two of the other men who entered the room of performing sex acts on her without her consent, while she was partially incapacitated. She accused another man of kissing her without her consent. According to the Title IX documents, Jane Doe told investigators two other men stood at the foot of the bed acting “more like voyeurs than anything.”
The lawsuit seeks to hold all seven men liable for rape. She is asking for unspecified damages.
Cornell hasn’t detailed the results of its investigation, but said it resulted in some students being expelled.
The man who filed the lawsuit challenging his punishment was allowed to stay at Cornell, but he was ordered to stay away from the woman, take a class on sexual harassment and bystander intervention, and write a paper reflecting on the circumstances for which he was found responsible and include a proposal to train other students on preventing sexual harassment.

title: Famed Hawaii sea arch collapses, prompting warnings of unstable cliffs
text:
A famed Hawaii sea arch collapses, prompting warnings of unstable cliffs
A scenic cliff on the wave-swept coast of Hawaii's Big Island has collapsed, the National Park Service said.
Related video above: As super El Niño strengthens, study suggests that climate change is intensifying El Niños
The Holei Sea Arch, located in Hawaii Volcanoes National Park, was about 90 feet (27.4 meters) high before it collapsed sometime between Sept. 23 and Sept. 27, possibly when the park was temporarily closed during Tropical Storm Nolo.
Its collapse into the Pacific Ocean was not unexpected; however, it marks “the latest transformation of the park’s remote and rugged coastline,” the NPS said in a Facebook post. People reacting to the post called it a sign of nature taking its course.
Officials at the park service warned visitors to stay away from the site since it is unstable and presents a serious falling hazard.
“Photos on social media show people entering the closed area near where the sea arch once stood, putting themselves and first responders at great risk of falling and drowning,” the NPS said.
The popular tourist site was formed about 550 years ago. The name Holei comes from a small endemic plant in the milkweed family.

title: Trump announces payments to seniors to help pay Medicare premiums ahead of midterm elections
text:
(AP) - President Donald Trump is promising more payments to voters just ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections — this time, to more than 20 million seniors, giving them $90 each to help pay for Medicare premiums.
The announcement, made late Friday night by Trump on social media, comes after the president last month said about 1 million people would get rebate checks of $500 for Affordable Care Act premiums. He has also promised on the campaign trail to send every American adult $5,000 if Republicans retain control of the House and Senate in the midterm elections.
That pledge — which would require approval from Congress — would likely cost more than $1 trillion, adding to the deficit and worsening inflation.
Trump highlighted his $5,000 promise at a rally in Vandalia, Ohio, on Saturday night, and told supporters that 70,000 families in the state would receive the ACA rebates “within the next couple of days.” He also reminded voters about the $1,776 payments to military members, announced in December — though he mused that they should have been timed better.
“Maybe I should have waited a year,” he said. “To be honest, I said that. Should I wait for before the election?”
Polls show Americans increasingly blame Trump for the high cost of gasoline and groceries with just 17% approving of his handling of inflation. Trump has sought to shrug off concerns about affordability, saying the economy is booming.
The White House said the $90 payments for seniors will come from the Medicare Improvement Fund, established by Congress in 2008 as flexible funding to improve program operations and payments to health care providers.
Medicare Part B enrollees can expect to receive a one-time payment in October, either through direct deposit or by check, the White House said. Total monthly costs for the program — which covers costs like doctor’s visits, ambulance services and lab tests — start around $200 and vary with income.
To be eligible, seniors must be living in the U.S. and not be already receiving premium assistance from Medicaid or paying adjusted monthly premiums based on income, according to the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services. Seniors enrolled in Medicare Advantage, a private plan alternative to traditional Medicare coverage, are not eligible for the payment. More than half of eligible Medicare beneficiaries have Medicare Advantage, according to healthcare research nonprofit KFF.
Previous administrations have not used the Medicare Improvement Fund in this way, although Congress has periodically taken out money from the fund to pay for other priorities, said Larry Levitt, KFF’s executive vice president for health policy. For example, $20.74 billion was used for the creation of the Affordable Care Act in 2010.
“The Medicare Improvement Fund language is quite broad and gives substantial discretion to the administration,” Levitt said.
