title: UAE says FlyDubai co-pilot attacked captain with cockpit’s crash axe
text:
CAIRO (AP) — The co-pilot accused of attacking the captain of an Israel-bound flight with an ax and trying to seize the controls was an Omani national who had been barred from flying on his country’s airline because of concerns about extremist views, officials said Saturday.
The co-pilot has been identified as Hamam al-Hammami, according to three people with knowledge of the situation, including a Gulf and a Western diplomat, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to the media.
The United Arab Emirates, which is leading the investigation, said the co-pilot attacked with the cockpit’s crash ax and tried to take control of the plummeting plane in a “terrorist attack” Wednesday. His actions nearly crashed the flight with 182 people on board before passengers and others rushed in and subdued him.
The new details raised questions about how thoroughly FlyDubai vets potential employees, and how the co-pilot’s presence on a flight filled with Israeli passengers got past Israel’s strict security protocols.
Israel has said it has agreements with foreign carriers to keep pilots of nations without diplomatic ties from flying there. Israel and Oman don’t have formal diplomatic relations. The UAE government has earned a reputation for effective measures against extremist activities but has bristled in the past over criticism of security lapses.
The incident occurred at a sensitive time for Israel, a week before the anniversary of the Hamas-led attack on Oct. 7, 2023, that sparked the war in Gaza. It also came weeks before a highly contentious election in which security, and Oct. 7 security failures, have been central issues.
FlyDubai hired the co-pilot after Oman Air barred him
Separately, a regional official and a person familiar with the matter said the co-pilot had been barred from flying by Oman over concerns that he had adopted extremist views. The official said he was moved to an administrative job at Oman Air. Both spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss the ongoing investigation. They gave no details about the alleged extremist views.
The co-pilot was later hired by UAE-based airline FlyDubai, the person said. It wasn’t immediately clear to what extent the co-pilot was vetted. The Gulf diplomat said he had undergone standard security checks before being hired, but it appears that the checks focused on whether he had been convicted of criminal charges and didn’t go deeper into examining his background for potential signs of radicalization.
The regional official also said security agencies from four regional countries were working to establish the co-pilot’s motives, aided by the United States and other Western governments. The Gulf diplomat said the investigation, which hasn’t concluded, hasn’t found any connections with militant groups, suggesting that the co-pilot acted on his own.
The regional official said the co-pilot was born in the UAE and his mother is Syrian. He obtained Omani nationality from his father, also an Omani national. The regional official also said the co-pilot had traveled to Syria, with no details.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Friday said the co-pilot had undergone “Islamist radicalization,” but provided no evidence. There was no immediate comment Saturday from Israel’s government.
A social media account was deleted the day of the flight
A FlyDubai spokesperson said in an email that the airline could not comment beyond its official statements and acknowledged “there are many questions at this stage.” There was no immediate comment from Oman Air, and Oman’s government has said nothing publicly in response to repeated questions since the incident.
In a statement to The Associated Press, Royal Air Maroc, Morocco’s national carrier, said the co-pilot “completed a three-month theoretical training period with the airline in 2025, as part of the pre-employment process. At the end of this training period, his application was not selected for employment.” There were no details.
Keith Coles, a spokesperson for Buckinghamshire New University in England, told the AP that al-Hammami previously completed a distance-learning course in aviation management there but “did not undertake any pilot training.” There were no details on the timing.
Little else was immediately known about the co-pilot’s background. His Instagram account was active until the day of the flight and then deleted.
Philip Baum, a visiting professor of aviation security at Coventry University in England who wrote a book about aircraft hijackings and bombings, said background check systems differ from country to country and there are limits on what types of information can be shared.
“In terms of aviation security itself, obviously we want to have as robust background checks as possible. But there are huge limitations on doing background checks in any case, especially in cross-border checks,” he said.
Captain and passengers have described drama on board
Airlines are generally required to carry crash axes in the cockpit that could be used in an emergency to break open a window to escape or break open a panel to access a fire.
The captain, who was badly wounded, has said he used his remaining energy while being attacked to unlock the cockpit door, allowing people who had noticed alarming sounds to come in, tackle the co-pilot and stabilize the flight while passengers screamed.
In a phone call with Israel’s Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Saturday, the flight’s captain, Smit Machchhar, said that before the attack, the co-pilot wanted to pray, and that he turned away out of respect. He said he felt a blow to the back of his head a few minutes later, and then the blows kept coming.
Netanyahu told Machchhar that he was amazed at his courage and his ability to stay cool under impossible conditions. “You saved so many souls. ... You saved the spirit of the world,” he said.
The plane made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia after a descent so extreme that part of the rudder was torn away, and aviation experts have marveled that it didn’t crash. FlyDubai has said crew traveling on the plane helped to stabilize it and land. They haven’t been publicly identified.
The captain and co-pilot were later taken to the UAE. The passengers, most of them Israeli, flew home later Wednesday on a separate plane, to cheers.
___
Mednick reported from Tel Aviv, Israel, and Anna from Jerusalem. AP Washington bureau chief Anna Johnson in Washington, Transportation Writer Josh Funk in Omaha, Nebraska, and reporter Sam Metz in Jerusalem contributed.

title: 4 teens killed in crash after police use PIT maneuver ends chase sparked by shooting
text:
TYLER, Texas (KLTV/Gray News) - A police chase sparked by a shooting ended in a crash that left four teens dead in Texas, authorities said.
According to the Tyler Police Department, on Sept. 27, officers were called to the 1500 block of Lake Placid Road in response to suspicious gunshot noises in the area. The caller also described a vehicle the alleged shooters were driving.
Around 4 a.m., police received a call from a local hospital saying they were treating two victims with gunshot wounds from the incident.
Officers investigating the incident saw the suspect vehicle and attempted to make contact. However, the vehicle drove away from the area and officers began a pursuit through Tyler that continued onto Highway 31 East at a high rate of speed.
According to the release, Texas Highway Patrol joined the chase as it exited the city. One trooper used a precision immobilization technique, known as a PIT maneuver, to end the pursuit, according to the department.
The vehicle crashed and the pursuit ended around 5:30 a.m. near County Road 211, officials said. Three occupants of the suspect vehicle died at the scene and one occupant was taken to the hospital, where that person later died, according to the release.
Police identified the occupants as Jaffet Cuarenta, 17, Adrielle Vazquez, 17, and Emigdio Gutierrez, 17, all of Tyler, and a 15-year-old from Smith County whose name was not released because of age.
The victims of the earlier shooting had non-life-threatening injuries and were identified as a 17-year-old male from Tyler and an 18-year-old female from Smith County. Their names are being withheld at this time, officials said.

title: UMaine men’s hockey falls in OT against Holy Cross after late rally
text:
A dramatic late rally by the University of Maine men’s hockey team went for nought on Saturday night.
The Black Bears scored goals 48 seconds apart in the final 3:27 to force overtime, but senior right wing Connor Welsh scored 1:33 into the overtime on a delayed penalty to give Holy Cross a 3-2 victory in the Cross City Classic at the DCU Center in Worcester, Massachusetts.
Both teams are now 1-1 as UMaine had earned a 4-1 triumph on Friday night at the Hart Center on the Holy Cross campus in Worcester.
Goals by junior centers Matt Kursonis in the first period and Noah Eyre in the third period gave Holy Cross a 2-0 lead and a cross checking penalty on UMaine alternate captain Sully Scholle with just 4:30 left, his second penalty of the period, made a possible comeback a very slim proposition.
But Holy Cross’ Preston Lounsbury was assessed a tripping penalty just 30 seconds later and UMaine junior defenseman and Bemidji State transfer Isa Parekh scored on the four-on-four with 3:27 remaining before teammate Lee Parks, a junior right wing and UMass Lowell transfer, notched the equalizer 48 seconds later.
In the three-on-three overtime, UMaine was going to be assessed a penalty so Holy Cross was able to replace goalie Danick Leroux with an extra attacker. Welsh fired the puck past the glove side of UMaine goalie Petter Wickstrom Stumer to win it.
Will Elias and Owen Kim garnered assists. Canisius transfer Wickstrom Stumer was making his UMaine debut.
“It’s a tough way to lose,” said UMaine coach Ben Barr. “I can’t fault the effort at all this weekend.”
He said the game-winning goal resulted from a bad decision.
“We had the puck and decided to go one-on-three and we turned it over. And then you had a forward playing defense and we take a penalty. It was a mental error,” Barr said.
He said the game-winning goal, along with the Kursonis goal, came on shots from odd angles that beat Wickstrom Stumer clean to the short side.
“We needed to make that save,” said Barr, who feels both should have been stopped but added that Wickstrom Stumer works hard and is a great kid who will learn from it.
Leroux finished with 26 saves on 28 shots while Wickstrom Stumer wound up with 23 on 26.
Barr said Leroux was outstanding all weekend and the Crusaders blocked a ton of shots.
“[Leroux] got in our head a little. We got a little too cute with the puck around the net,” he noted.
Kursonis opened the scoring at the 8:57 mark of the first period by gathering in the puck between the face-off circles and snapping a shot past Wickstrom Stumer for his second goal of the weekend.
Anthony Biakabutuka and Lounsbury picked up assists.
Following a scoreless second period, Eyre expanded the lead on the power play as he swatted home a third rebound after Wickstrom Stumer had stopped his first two shots. Elias and Owen Kim earned assists.
UMaine took five consecutive penalties in the third period and had to kill off a two-man disadvantage that spanned 1:55.
Perekh, who had two assists on Friday night, flipped home a rebound for his first goal in a Black Bear uniform with Will Gerrior and Tanner Klimpke picking up assists.
Parks tied it by depositing a Lukas Peterson rebound behind Leroux.
Despite being shorthanded for a healthy portion of the third period, UMaine outshot Holy Cross 13-5 in the frame.
Lounsbury’s penalty was the only Crusader penalty in the period.
UMaine will face seventh-ranked Quinnipiac, the ECAC favorite in the preseason poll, for its home openers on Friday and Saturday nights at 7 p.m. at the Alfond Arena.
Quinnipiac opened its season with a 10-2 thrashing of New Hampshire and a 6-3 win over defending Hockey East Tournament champion Merrimack.
Holy Cross will visit Arizona State for a pair next weekend.

Cornell president calls alleged gang rape ‘deeply disturbing,’ pledges greater transparency
text:
(AP) - Cornell’s president called the alleged gang rape of a student at a fraternity house in 2024 “deeply disturbing” on Saturday and said it would weigh on the university for years to come, as he pledged greater transparency amid mounting outrage over the school’s handling of the case.
In an eight-minute video message to the Cornell community, Michael Kotlikoff described the past week as one of the most difficult in the university’s history and acknowledged troubling questions about the investigations that followed the allegations.
“My heart aches when I think of what she experienced,” Kotlikoff said. “It raises heartbreaking and troubling issues about sexual assault, dehumanization, and aspects of party culture, alcohol, and drug use.”
“I believe we as an administration and we as a community must do better,” he continued.
Kotlikoff reaffirmed his commitment to supporting an independent investigation of the case called for by New York Gov. Kathy Hochul and said Cornell’s Board of Trustees would announce details next week. He also expressed support for Hochul’s decision to turn the criminal investigation over to the state attorney general.
Scrutiny has mounted in recent days over Cornell’s response to allegations that the woman was sexually assaulted by multiple fraternity members in 2024. The woman, identified in court documents as Jane Doe, has sued the university and seven former students.
During a student assembly hearing Thursday that gave students an opportunity to voice concerns and discuss proposals to improve Cornell’s response to sexual assault, several speakers called for Kotlikoff’s resignation.
Kotlikoff acknowledged frustration that Cornell has not communicated enough about its handling of the case, saying that has led to distrust. While citing “real legal and privacy limits” on what the university can disclose, he pledged greater transparency and more opportunities for students, parents and others to engage with university leaders.
He also committed Cornell’s support to legislative efforts to change New York’s sexual assault laws.
The case has renewed scrutiny of a New York law that makes it difficult to prosecute sexual assaults involving people who voluntarily consume alcohol or drugs, even if they became too intoxicated to consent.
Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten cited the law in defending his initial decision not to pursue charges, saying the woman’s original statement to police described voluntary drug use and sexual activity.
Critics have long sought to close what they call the “voluntary intoxication loophole,” which distinguishes between people incapacitated by drugs administered without their consent and those who voluntarily became intoxicated. Hochul has pledged to push for changes to the law.

title: Bride’s sheepadoodle steals the show in viral wedding video
text:
DOOR COUNTY, Wis. (WBAY/Gray News) - When a bride decided to have her dog be part of her wedding, she couldn’t have expected that he’d end up being the star of the show.
Emily Cowles and her husband, Josh, married Aug. 22 in Door County, Wisconsin.
“Door County is just like heaven. It’s my happy place. So, we go back frequently. And yeah, that’s where we wanted to get married,” Cowles said.
The couple had decided that Cowles’s 5-year-old sheepadoodle, Swayze, needed to be part of their celebration.
“He is just a bright light to anybody who meets him. He’s so goofy and a great snuggler. Everybody calls him a Muppet. He’s just the best,” Cowles said.
Cowles had the idea to strap a GoPro onto Swayze and capture the celebration from the dog’s point of view.
Cowles posted the video of Swayze’s perspective of the wedding online. It has since gone viral, drawing millions of views.
“All of a sudden, the shares started going up. I’m like, what is going on? Then suddenly The Dodo’s reaching out, we got published in People, and then we woke up to being on Good Morning America. I’m like, what is going on?” Cowles said.
Cowles said the best part isn’t the attention the video received but the moments she didn’t know were caught on camera, including one between Swayze and her 91-year-old grandmother.
“He, like, took refuge in spending time with her for like 20 minutes. It was so sweet. And you can just hear him talk or her talking to him. And it was just so, so sweet to watch back,” Cowles said.
Cowles said she and Josh will keep those unscripted moments for years to come.
“There’s going to be a day when not all those people are going to be around. And especially Swayze. Um, so we’re going to be able to look back and it’s just going to bring a smile to our face for the rest of our lives,” Cowles said.
Cowles said Swayze has taken the newfound attention in stride.
“He’s so humble. We’re trying not to let it go to his head,” Cowles said.

title: More than 4,500 pounds of imported chicken stew recalled over missed reinspection
text:
CALIFORNIA (Gray News) - More than 4,500 pounds of imported ready-to-eat chicken stew are being recalled because the products were not reinspected after entering the U.S., federal officials said.

- Cardboard boxes containing pouches of 31.75-oz (900 g) “Sempio Korean Ginseng CHICKEN STEW RICH”
The products bear Korean establishment number “GIA15001” and shipping mark “MK-2026-0422-01”.
The products were shipped to distributors and retailers in Florida, Georgia, Illinois, Maryland, New Jersey, New York, Pennsylvania and Virginia.
There have been no confirmed reports of illness or injury, but officials are concerned some products may still be in consumers’ pantries.

title: Trump touts G7 plan to release oil and diesel reserves to address high prices
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Trump touts G7 plan to release oil and diesel reserves to address high prices
The G7 announced a plan to release 100 million barrels of oil and fuel products to combat high prices largely caused by the war with Iran.
Trump touts G7 plan to release oil and diesel reserves to address high prices
The G7 announced a plan to release 100 million barrels of oil and fuel products to combat high prices largely caused by the war with Iran.
The Group of Seven nations announced an agreement Friday to release 100 million barrels of oil and diesel reserves in the coming weeks to address fuel prices driven higher by the conflict with Iran.
The G7 includes the United States, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the U.K.
President Donald Trump praised the plan and said the diesel release would happen immediately.  
The announcement comes after diesel prices hit a record high last month, though the national average has since fallen to roughly $6.36 per gallon as of Saturday morning, according to AAA.
These price shocks have squeezed farmers who rely on diesel to operate equipment and transport crops, with downstream effects on grocery prices for everyday Americans.
Trump has faced pressure to address high fuel prices ahead of the midterm elections, but has maintained that the added costs are temporary and worthwhile to ensure Iran does not obtain a nuclear weapon.
Experts told The Associated Press that the G7 agreement should help lower prices in the short term, but the move also risks depleting stockpiles intended for emergencies amid continued uncertainty about the direction of the conflict.
Some Republicans had also urged Trump to ban U.S. diesel exports to ease prices, but the G7 agreement takes that tool off the table as it relates to member countries.
"Europe has a lot of diesel, and they're going to be making a major world contribution, and so are we, and we're not going to be doing the export ban. We're going to be doing what we're supposed to do, but I did ask them, and we're going to have a lot of oil very shortly, as soon as Iran ends, which won't be long," Trump said.

title: Time is running out for leadership on healthcare in Maine
text:
Tom Dunne of Cape Elizabeth was the first executive director of the Dirigo Health Agency during the administration of Gov. John Baldacci.
Last fall I wrote an op-ed headlined “Please don’t make me run for governor,” challenging the many candidates to declare how they would lead much needed improvements across Maine’s healthcare system.
After the op-ed appeared, I had conversations with a number of candidates, across party lines. A constant agreement was on the need for change; some had specific ideas; for others, healthcare reform was a relatively new topic.
As a reminder, healthcare makes up about a sixth of our economy — it is big and complicated and
important. The stress of illness is compounded by the stress of an overly expensive and overly complicated system. It is a major pocketbook issue for everyone (except, perhaps, for those taking advantage of the weaknesses and flaws in the current system, making so much more than their counterparts in any other economy of the world).
We are now down to three candidates, one of whom will be our governor, an elected official having formal legal authority and specific responsibilities defined by law. Based on their declarations to date, not one of the three candidates, in healthcare, is positioning to be a leader, someone who will influence, guide or inspire others to a goal.
These candidates are citing slogans, declining to dig in and declare what practical
actions they would take to improve the system. They seem to be throwing out umbrella
statements, hoping to appeal to those voters who will hear what they want to hear while avoiding having to make any statements or provide details that might negatively influence possible voters.
Boiled down, “a public option — funding reform,” “eliminate waste and fraud,” “expand
telemedicine and deal with medical debt” are at best important but small ideas when
compared to the scale of the reform needed across the system. It is almost as if the
candidates are tip-toeing to get elected and then thinking they will “figure it out” later.
Unfortunately, this does not give them a mandate to lead, it just makes them an elected official. As a reminder, we are not stuck in the current system. Maine can lead, adopting a system similar to what Maryland has been working on and similar to the underpinnings of most European systems.
No, it is not “single-payer.” Rather they treat their healthcare systems for what they basically are — geographic monopolies that operate primarily under a global budget system.
There are several ways to fund this type of system (including single-payer). Across the world there are different models to learn from, and to pick from, with an eye to fitting with Maine’s culture and values. There is no perfect solution but there are better options.
Shifting to this sort of system will require strong leadership. Sadly, unless someone steps up over the next 45 days, the Blaine House will soon have a new elected official but not a leader with a mandate for significant reform of this sector.
I think Maine voters are ready for major change and crave greater and more detailed communication from those who aspire to lead.

title: Head Start was there for my family. Maine children need it protected.
text:
The BDN Opinion section operates independently and does not set news policies or contribute to reporting or editing articles elsewhere in the newspaper or on bangordailynews.com
Megan Newsome is a parent and advocate living in Lisbon.
When my son Brayden was born, our family was facing a lot at once. I had been diagnosed with cancer while I was pregnant. He arrived about six weeks early and spent time in the NICU. By the time Brayden was about a year old, I was receiving WIC, the federally funded nutrition program for women, infants and children. WIC staff asked whether I had childcare and told me about Early Head Start.
I knew very little about the program then. It quickly became a godsend.
At the time, Brayden was not yet walking. He could not feed himself or hold his own cup. Within weeks of starting Early Head Start, he was pulling himself up, holding his cup and learning to use a spoon and pick up food on his own.
His teachers paid attention to who he was and how he learned. Brayden is left-handed. When teachers recognized that and encouraged him to use the hand that came naturally to him, it showed me that they saw my son as an individual.
Head Start also gave me something I deeply needed while facing cancer: trusted people who could care for my child during the workday. Knowing my son was cared for and learning gave me comfort during an incredibly difficult time.
The support did not stop at the classroom door. Head Start connected us with mental health counseling, clothing, diapers, food banks and help during the holidays — all supports we needed to make sure Brayden had what he needed to learn and grow, at home and in the classroom. There was always someone I could turn to.
Brayden is now 3 and has moved from Early Head Start into Head Start. He is now on track developmentally, and this is a crucial moment in his learning. If he needs additional help before elementary school, I want us to recognize it early and have support in place.
That is why proposed changes to Head Start concern me so deeply. Families could lose developmental screenings, medical and dental services, counseling and other support that helps children grow and prepare for school.
For some children, Head Start may provide the only developmental screening they receive. It’s the front door to health care, dental care, and mental health support. If those services disappear, important needs could go unnoticed until a child enters school and faces a harder path forward.
Larger classrooms and fewer teachers would also make it harder to provide the individual attention that helped Brayden. Teachers need time to know each child, understand how they learn and recognize when they may need additional support.
Head Start works because all these pieces work together. It is not simply a place where parents leave their children. It helps children build confidence and skills while connecting parents with trusted people and practical resources. Weakening any part of that model weakens the program families count on.
I know what Head Start made possible for my son and me. I also know other families rely on it for that same stability and partnership.
The public has only until Oct. 6 to comment on the proposed changes, but Congress can act even after that. I am asking Sens. Susan Collins and Angus King and Rep. Jared Golden, who represents Maine’s 2nd Congressional District, my home district, to listen to Maine families, oppose the proposed rule, and protect the standards and services that make Head Start so effective.
Children deserve to enter school with their strengths recognized and the support they need already in place. Parents deserve trusted partners as they build strong futures for their families.
Head Start gave my family both.

title: Family dog euthanized after attacking and killing 3-year-old child, authorities say
text:
SULLIGENT, Ala. (WTVA/Gray News) — Authorities say a dog attacked and killed a toddler this week in Alabama.
The reported attack occurred on Friday morning at a home on Walnut Street in Sulligent, according to the Lamar County coroner.
Authorities said the dog attacked a 3-year-old boy, who later died at the hospital.
Sulligent Police Chief Michael Franklin said the boy’s family owned the dog.
After the attack, the family surrendered the animal to police, who took the dog to a veterinarian in Russellville for euthanasia.
Franklin said the health department ordered the euthanasia and testing of the dog.
Sulligent authorities did not say if any charges were expected to be filed in the case. The family was not immediately identified.

title: Trump urges calls to senator’s personal cellphone in push for permanent daylight saving time
text:
(AP) - President Donald Trump on Saturday pressured Republican Sen. Tom Cotton of Arkansas to support a bill to make daylight saving time permanent, posting the personal cellphone number of the chairman of Senate Intelligence Committee and urging Americans to call it.
The Sunshine Protection Act passed the House in July, but it faces roadblocks in the Senate where some Republicans are strongly opposed. Proponents, including the White House, argue that the change would provide more daylight during the times that Americans are most active. Detractors said permanent daylight saving time would lead to darker and potentially more hazardous winter mornings when children will be waiting for school buses and parents will be driving to work in darkness.
It was a remarkable escalation on Trump’s part of a longstanding fixation shared by both men — with Trump supporting making daylight saving time permanent, and Cotton vociferously opposed — at a time just weeks before the midterms, when Republicans would prefer that the president focus on talking about affordability issues and the party’s achievements. Cotton is also up for reelection this November, although that race is not expected to be competitive.
Trump calls daylight saving time ‘depressing’
Daylight saving time is that period between spring and fall when clocks in most parts of the United States are set one hour ahead of standard time. Not all states observe it — and under the bill, states can opt out of the change if their respective legislatures act to do so before the bill’s enactment.
“It’s a lot of work for a lot of people, running around for two days, changing all the clocks in the house,” Trump told reporters as his left the White House on Saturday for a rally in Vandalia, Ohio. “It discombobulates everybody,” he said.
Trump said the time change gives golfers less time on the greens and tennis players less time on the courts. He blamed Cotton for stopping the bill. “So, everyone in Arkansas, a State I love, and won 3 times, the last by by 34 points, tell Tom to, GET IT DONE! It will be appreciated by all,” Trump said on social media on Saturday morning, kicking off the fight.
Trump included a phone number with an Arkansas area code. The Associated Press called the number, but no one answered and the voicemail box was full.
Cotton, a member of Republican leadership, reiterated his opposition to permanent daylight saving time in a social media post of his own Saturday afternoon. He is not the only GOP senator who opposes the policy, though he has been among the most vocal opponents.
“No one likes changing the clock, me included, but Congress has enacted permanent Daylight Savings Time multiple times before and repealed it each time once Americans experienced absurdly late sunrises in the winter,” Cotton wrote. “Arkansans don’t want their kids going to school in the pitch dark, and I’ll always put Arkansas first.”
The fight over changing the clock went on all Saturday
Trump promptly fired back in another post. “If Tom Cotton were putting Arkansas first, he would give them an extra hour of daylight and, more importantly, they wouldn’t have to run all over their houses, farms, work places, and everywhere else, twice a year, having to change their Clocks, and often forgetting to do so,” Trump said, adding that “that is really putting Arkansas FIRST.”
As his motorcade was rolling back to the White House from his golf course, Trump added that “a table full of very distinguished people just told me that they HATE, immediately after a mandatory time change, going home at night – and it’s DARK.”
“It’s depressing!” Trump continued. “One of the gentleman stated that, ‘I just hate going home in darkness.’ It’s also, in Crime Ridden Blue States, a lot more dangerous to be walking home in the dark!”
A 2025 poll from The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research shows that if forced to choose, most Americans would prefer to keep that extra hour of daylight in the evening. Only 12% of U.S. adults favor the current system of daylight saving time, which requires people in most states to change their clocks twice a year, while 47% oppose it and 40% are neutral.
Members of Congress have long been interested in the potential benefits and costs of daylight saving time since it was first adopted as a wartime measure in 1942. The Senate passed a bill four years ago to make daylight saving time permanent, but it stalled in the House.
This is not the first time Trump has released personal information about a senator
While competing for the 2016 Republican presidential nomination, the late Sen. Lindsey Graham of South Carolina described Trump as “unfit for office” after Trump denigrated the military service of Sen. John McCain of Arizona. Trump then released Graham’s personal cellphone number. That prompted a viral video in which the senator dramatically destroyed a series of flip phones.
Graham later became a close ally of Trump. In contrast, although they share many of the same policy positions, Trump and Cotton are not known to be close.
Cotton, one of the Republican Party’s most prominent national security voices, has advocated for a more hawkish approach on Iran, particularly as Trump entertains pauses in military strikes amid the seven-month war. In Trump’s first term, Cotton was a critic of the president’s attempts at overhauling the nation’s sentencing laws, calling the proposal a “jailbreak.”
Earlier this year, Cotton had temporarily defied Trump’s attempts at stalling the confirmation process for his own nominee for director of national intelligence, Jay Clayton. The president had wanted to ensure his interim pick for the intelligence job, Bill Pulte, would be able to serve in that role at least briefly when the former director, Tulsi Gabbard, left the job.
But the appointment of Pulte, who had no known national security credentials, drew bipartisan condemnation from Capitol Hill and Cotton had tried to expedite Clayton’s confirmation process, which could have prevented Pulte from being installed as acting director.
But Trump ultimately ordered Clayton to not appear before Cotton’s committee for his confirmation hearing, and Pulte served in the job for several weeks this summer. Clayton was eventually confirmed by the Senate in late July.
___
Associated Press writer Mary Clare Jalonick in Washington contributed to this report.

title: Driver hit and killed by their own dump truck, troopers say
text:
ONSLOW COUNTY, N.C. (WITN/Gray News) - Troopers say the driver of a dump truck was hit and killed by their vehicle in North Carolina, according to officials.
Officials say it happened around 1:30 p.m. on a private driveway near Old Folkstone Road near U.S. 17.
Troopers say the driver’s truck was stuck, and another dump truck at the scene helped them get unstuck.
Afterwards, troopers say the driver got out of their truck, and their vehicle moved forward and pinned them between the two trucks.
The driver died at the scene, according to troopers.
At this time, the driver’s identity has not been released.

title: A famed Hawaii sea arch collapses, prompting NPS warnings of unstable cliffs
text:
HAWAII VOLCANOES NATIONAL PARK, Hawaii (AP) — A scenic cliff on the wave-swept coast of Hawaii’s Big Island has collapsed, the National Park Service said.
The Holei Sea Arch, located in the Hawaii Volcanoes National Park, was about 90 feet (27.4 meters) high before it collapsed sometime between Sept. 23 and Sept. 27, possibly when the park was temporarily closed during Tropical Storm Nolo.
Its collapse into the Pacific Ocean was not unexpected; however, it marks “the latest transformation of the park’s remote and rugged coastline,” the NPS said in a Facebook post. People reacting to the post called it a sign of nature taking its course.
Officials at the park service warned visitors to stay away from the site since it is unstable and presents a serious falling hazard.
“Photos on social media show people entering the closed area near where the sea arch once stood, putting themselves and first responders at great risk of falling and drowning,” the NPS said.
The popular tourist site was formed about 550 years ago. The name Holei comes from a small endemic plant in the milkweed family.

title: Why I’m supporting Sen. Susan Collins
text:
Dennis Brockway of Winslow is president of North East Mobile Health Services and a member of the Maine Ambulance Association. The views expressed here are his own.
I want to voice my strong support for Sen. Susan Collins.
As a member of the Maine Ambulance Association and president of North East Mobile Health Services, I have had the opportunity to see firsthand the challenges facing emergency medical services in Maine, particularly in our rural communities. Over the years, Sen. Collins has sponsored, co-sponsored or supported numerous pieces of legislation aimed at strengthening EMS and improving access to emergency medical care.
Her commitment to rural healthcare goes well beyond words.
Sen. Collins played an important role in securing $50 billion for the Rural Health Transformation Program during congressional negotiations and pushed to expand the program and broaden the range of rural healthcare providers eligible to participate. Maine subsequently received approximately $190 million in first-year funding through the program.
When Maine’s award was later placed in jeopardy after the state missed federal milestones and the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) raised concerns about implementation, Sen. Collins personally intervened with CMS Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz in an effort to help preserve Maine’s funding.
Her work on behalf of rural EMS extends much further. Sen. Collins helped author the SIREN program, which provides grants to rural EMS agencies for recruitment, training, equipment and other critical needs. She has consistently supported efforts to strengthen the EMS workforce and improve access to emergency care in rural communities.
My support for Sen. Collins, however, is based on more than legislation.
In my dealings with her over the past 20 years, I have found her to be honest, respectful and willing to listen, even when people disagree with her. That matters to me. Maine has a long tradition of independent-minded public servants who put their responsibility to the state ahead of partisan politics. Sen. Margaret Chase Smith embodied that tradition, and I see much of that same Maine independence in Sen. Collins.
I recognize that many Mainers disagree with Sen. Collins on important issues. They have every right to do so. But after decades in public life and numerous hard-fought campaigns, she has been subjected to an extraordinary level of scrutiny. Through it all, she has maintained a reputation for integrity and a commitment to serving Maine.
Seniority also matters. Sen. Collins has accumulated decades of experience, relationships and influence in Washington. Maine is a small state, and having a senator in a position to influence federal policy and funding can have very real consequences for our rural hospitals, ambulance services and communities.
For me, this election should not simply be about party labels. It should be about who can most effectively represent Maine.
Based on what I have witnessed personally over the past two decades, I believe Susan Collins has earned the opportunity to continue doing that work.

title: Letter: Waldo County will benefit from Breanna Pinkham Bebb
